CHAPTER 3

第三章

DISILLUSIONMENT

幻灭

———————————

“I married the girl of my dreams; but I woke up to the stuff of nightmares.”

“我娶了梦寐以求的女孩；但醒来后却发现一切都像噩梦一样。”

—from a client interview with the author

——摘自作者与客户的访谈

With the advent of resentment, you will enter the second stage of your relationship journey—disillusionment. 11 I remember as a boy I used to love Western movies and TV shows. I fantasized about being a cowboy, wearing a white hat, and entering a town to help the poor townsfolk rid themselves of the menacing bad guy in the black hat. What I liked most about those shows was the look of the town with its hotel, saloon, general store, and the stable where I—I mean, where the good guy would keep his horse. I loved the clean lines and immaculate paint jobs on the buildings, and the fine clothing of all the inhabitants—except of course for the town drunk, who always appeared dirty and unkempt. I loved the barroom brawls where the hero could be punched in the face thirty times and never even lose his hat, much less get bruised.

随着怨恨的产生，你将进入关系旅程的第二阶段——幻灭。<sup>11</sup> 我记得小时候我特别喜欢西部电影和电视剧。我幻想自己是个牛仔，戴着白帽子，进城帮助穷苦的镇民们摆脱戴着黑帽子的恶棍。我最喜欢那些剧集的地方是小镇的景象：旅馆、酒吧、杂货店，还有马厩——我是说，好人把马拴在那里。我喜欢建筑简洁的线条和一尘不染的油漆，以及所有居民精致的衣着——当然，除了那个总是脏兮兮、邋里邋遢的镇上醉汉。我喜欢酒吧里的打斗场面，英雄就算被打了三十拳，帽子也不会掉，更别说身上有淤青了。

Then I saw the pictures of real western towns and their inhabitants, and my dreams were shattered. There is no way a white hat would stay white in those places. Most of the early western towns were filthy, comprised mainly of hastily erected shacks and canvas tents. And forget about painting them. They were lucky to have a bucket of whitewash thrown on them. And the people? Well you could describe them as many things but “well-dressed” would not be among the top ten adjectives. Most of them looked like the town drunk in my favourite shows. I can still remember the feeling of “reality” setting in, when the picture of my dreams was blown apart.

然后我看到了西部小镇及其居民的真实照片，我的梦想瞬间破灭。在那些地方，白帽子根本不可能保持洁白。早期的西部小镇大多肮脏不堪，主要由匆匆搭建的棚屋和帆布帐篷组成。至于粉刷，那就更别提了。能有人往墙上泼一桶白灰就不错了。至于镇上的人？你可以用很多词来形容他们，但“衣着体面”绝对排不上前十。他们大多数看起来就像我最喜欢的电视剧里的醉汉。我至今仍记得那种“现实”袭来的感觉，我的梦想瞬间崩塌。

Disillusionment tends to have a rather negative connotation, often associated with feelings of anger, despair, and even betrayal. In fact the meaning of the word indicates a freedom from illusion. This is a good thing. 12 Human beings carry a deep reverence and thirst for the Truth. Without the power to dispel the illusions which block our awareness of this Truth, we would be in an eternal prison, never completely satisfied or at peace. Relationships have an amazing power to dispel our illusions about the nature of Love. It begins as soon as our disappointment causes us to realize that perhaps we were mistaken. Perhaps this person is not the source of my happiness. A first, we may draw the conclusion that we simply chose the wrong mate, and then begin the search once again. But the disappointment will continue as long as the expectations are there, eventually leading even the most die-hard fantasizer 13 to realize that the source of our needs just ain’t out there. I’ve often felt that disillusionment is a gift from my own Soul, intended to help me break out of the trap of believing that my source of happiness is “out there.”

幻灭往往带有负面含义，常常与愤怒、绝望甚至背叛等情绪联系在一起。事实上，这个词的含义是摆脱幻觉。这是一件好事。<sup>12</sup> 人类对真理怀有深深的敬畏和渴望。如果我们没有能力驱散那些阻碍我们认识真理的幻觉，我们将永远被囚禁，永远无法获得真正的满足和平静。人际关系拥有神奇的力量，可以驱散我们对爱的本质的幻想。这种力量始于失望让我们意识到自己或许错了。或许这个人并非我幸福的源泉。起初，我们可能会得出结论，自己只是选错了伴侣，然后再次开始寻找。但只要期望犹存，失望就会持续，最终甚至会让最顽固的幻想家<sup>13</sup> 也意识到，我们需求的源泉根本不在外面。我常常觉得，幻灭是我灵魂赐予我的礼物，旨在帮助我摆脱认为幸福的源泉“在别处”的陷阱。

However, the process of disillusionment can be a very gradual one, like the taking down of a cathedral brick by brick. It begins when our needs do not get met, and we fail in our attempts to educate our partners as to exactly how they should be fulfilling us. At this point we resort to…

然而，幻灭的过程可能非常缓慢，就像一块砖一块砖地拆毁一座大教堂。它始于我们的需求得不到满足，以及我们试图教导伴侣如何满足我们却以失败告终。此时，我们便会诉诸……

***

MISGUIDED BEHAVIOUR

错误的行为

———————————

“The Devil made me do it!”

“都是魔鬼让我这么做的！”

-Anonymous

-匿名的

In her book, “Positive Discipline” 14 Jane Nelsen explains that when a child’s needs for belonging and significance are not met, the child experiences discouragement. The intensity of the discouragement varies from child to child, but typically leads to a certain degree of misguided behaviour and misplaced goals. Ms. Nelsen outlined four expressions of misguided behaviour, stating that a misbehaving child is not a bad child, but simply a discouraged one. The four behavioural expressions of discouragement are:

简·尼尔森在其著作《正面管教》<sup>14</sup>中解释说，当孩子的归属感和价值感需求得不到满足时，他们就会感到沮丧。这种沮丧的程度因人而异，但通常会导致一定程度的错误行为和错位的目标。尼尔森女士概述了四种错误行为的表现形式，并指出行为不端的孩子并非坏孩子，而只是感到沮丧。这四种沮丧的行为表现形式是：

• Attention Getting (Look at me! Look at me!)

• 引人注目（看我！看我！）

• Power Struggle (I’m not gonna do it and you can’t make me!)

• 权力斗争（我不会这么做，你也强迫不了我！）

• Revenge (I’m gonna hurt you as much as you hurt me.)

• 复仇（我会以牙还牙，让你也尝尝你伤害我的滋味。）

• Assumed Inadequacy (Why bother trying—I don’t matter anyway.)

• 自我否定（何必费力尝试——反正我也无关紧要。）

The words in the brackets are mine. The first two behaviours are attempts to get the two primary needs met, while the bottom two point to a more severe sense of discouragement, where there is a belief that the need will never be met and thus the pain of discouragement drives the child to more destructive (often self -destructive) behaviour.

括号里的文字是我加的。前两种行为是为了满足两个基本需求而做出的尝试，而后两种行为则指向一种更为严重的挫败感，在这种挫败感中，孩子认为需求永远无法得到满足，因此挫败的痛苦驱使孩子做出更具破坏性（通常是自毁性）的行为。

Since adult relationships have a marvellous way of bringing old pain up to the surface, you will discover in your relationship that childhood 15 behaviour that you thought you had left behind is still with you, albeit in a much more sophisticated form. As the resentment from unsatisfied expectations arises, you will also begin to re-experience the discouragement that you faced as a child around those same unmet needs. This will lead you to react with the same misguided behaviour you attempted when you were young. Misguided behaviour is actually an attempt to manipulate your partner, and signals that you are trying to stave off disillusionment by controlling him or her. If he or she will not meet your needs freely, then you will just have to trick him/her into it. If the first two behaviours fail you can always resort to revenge in order to at least level the playing field. As a last resort you can simply give up and withdraw into a phlegmatic or melancholic shell, where you may experience a certain degree of discontent, but where the real pain cannot reach you.

由于成年人的关系总能巧妙地将旧伤重新唤起，你会发现，你以为早已摆脱的童年行为模式其实依然存在，只不过形式更加复杂。随着未满足的期望带来的怨恨涌上心头，你也会重新体验到童年时期因同样需求未被满足而产生的挫败感。这会导致你用年少时尝试过的错误方式来应对。这种错误行为实际上是在试图操纵你的伴侣，表明你试图通过控制对方来避免失望。如果对方不愿主动满足你的需求，你就会想方设法欺骗对方。如果前两种方法都失败了，你还可以选择报复，至少以此来平衡双方的关系。作为最后的手段，你可以选择放弃，把自己封闭起来，陷入冷漠或忧郁的情绪中。在那里，你或许会感到些许不满，但真正的痛苦却无法触及你。

***

ATTENTION GETTING

引人注目

———————————

When you watch the antics of a couple trying to control each other, 16 and you look at it from the perspective of misguided behaviour resulting from early childhood discouragement, you begin to realize that Roy Harper was right: grown-ups are just silly children. But as long as we want to remain beguiled by illusion, we will use adult logic and reasoning to justify our manipulations (if we dare examine them at all!). We will persist in acting so as to draw special attention from our partners. We will act sweet, nice, capable, strong, funny, intelligent, wise, tolerant, brave, afraid, weak (in a cute, sexy sort of way, of course), spaced out, with it, cool, hot… and the list goes on. There are numerous ways to attract our partner’s attention, with more variations on the theme being thought up every day.

当你观察一对情侣试图控制对方的种种滑稽举动时，<sup>16</sup> 并从童年早期挫折导致的错误行为角度来看待这一切，你就会开始意识到罗伊·哈珀是对的：成年人其实也像傻孩子一样。但只要我们想继续沉浸在幻觉中，我们就会用成年人的逻辑和推理来为自己的操控行为辩解（如果我们胆敢审视这些行为的话！）。我们会坚持不懈地表演，以博得伴侣的特别关注。我们会表现得温柔、善良、能干、坚强、风趣、聪明、睿智、宽容、勇敢、胆怯、柔弱（当然，是以一种可爱性感的方式）、心不在焉、机智、酷、性感……等等等等。吸引伴侣注意力的方法数不胜数，而且每天都有新的花样涌现。

However, there is no manipulation so effective that your partner will never get tired of it and begin to feel the pressure of expectation lurking beneath it. After all, if your partner sees the same thing every day, s/he will very soon stop noticing it, and become more aware of the manipulations behind your behaviours. When you realize that you are not being noticed or appreciated, the discouragement increases, and you may find yourself moving into the second mode of manipulation…

然而，没有任何一种操控手段能让你伴侣始终保持警惕，不会感到厌倦，也不会感受到潜藏在背后的期待压力。毕竟，如果你的伴侣每天都看到同样的事情，他/她很快就会习以为常，并更加察觉到你行为背后的操控意图。当你意识到自己没有被注意到或欣赏时，沮丧感会加剧，你可能会发现自己开始使用第二种操控手段……

***

POWER STRUGGLE

权力斗争

———————————

“When the fighting starts, Hell puts out the welcome mat.”

“当战争爆发时，地狱会铺开欢迎地毯。”

—Anonymous

-匿名的

I call it a Power Struggle because there is an effort made by both sides to be seen as powerful, and therefore significant. As the relationship continues, however, it becomes more than that. As the sense of discouragement grows, the Power Struggle becomes an attempt to gain control over the direction of the relationship, with each person trying to change the thoughts, words, and behaviour patterns of the other.

我称之为权力斗争，因为双方都试图展现自己的力量，从而彰显自身的重要性。然而，随着关系的深入，它远不止于此。随着挫败感的加剧，权力斗争演变为对关系走向的掌控，双方都试图改变对方的想法、言语和行为模式。

Those quirky little idiosyncrasies that you used to find so cute in your partner now become petty annoyances that soon lead to outright disgust. 17 His loud laughter which was an amusing novelty now grates on your spinal cord. Her once-fascinating stories now set your teeth on edge and make you want to scream from boredom. You’ve now begun to get on each other’s nerves. At this point, your choices seem to be: 1) change—by force or coercion—your partner’s habits, speech mannerisms, clothing style, length of hair, etc., (2) learn the tolerance of a saint, or (3) get rid of your partner and find a more appropriate one. Most adults, for various reasons, choose number 1, and thus the Power Struggle begins in earnest!

那些你曾经觉得伴侣身上可爱至极的小怪癖，如今却变成了令人厌烦的琐碎小事，很快就演变成彻底的厌恶。他那曾经让你觉得新鲜有趣的大笑，如今却让你感到脊背发凉。她曾经让你着迷的故事，如今却让你感到厌烦透顶，甚至想尖叫。你们开始互相看不顺眼。此时，你的选择似乎只有三个：1）通过强迫或胁迫的方式改变伴侣的习惯、说话方式、穿衣风格、头发长度等等；2）学会像圣人一样宽容；或者3）甩掉现在的伴侣，另寻一个更合适的。大多数成年人出于各种原因，都会选择第一个选项，于是，一场真正的权力斗争就此拉开帷幕！

We often think of Power Struggles as taking the form of loud arguments that can sometimes involve throwing objects at each other or maybe even the exchange of gunfire. But the manipulations of the Power Struggle can take on many other expressions, which can include cold silences, mutual avoidance, caustic sarcasm, or the simple exchange of mean, angry looks. I can always tell when a certain couple I know is fighting as soon as I enter their house; it’s as quiet as a graveyard, but as tense as the climax of a horror movie. Yet my two friends are unbearably polite with each other, never breaking the façade that hides a personal conflict of nuclear proportions. Whereas I know another couple who, when fighting, will scream themselves hoarse, their faces sometimes only inches apart from each other’s. Between these two extremes are innumerable methods of engaging in Power Struggle—all equally dangerous to the success of a relationship, and all with an equally incredible potential for bringing us a vision of True Partnership.

我们通常认为权力斗争表现为激烈的争吵，有时甚至会演变成互相投掷物品，或者开枪交锋。但权力斗争的手段远不止于此，它还可以表现为冷漠的沉默、互相回避、尖刻的讽刺，或者仅仅是交换充满敌意的眼神。我总能在一进门就察觉到我认识的某对夫妇正在争吵；屋里静得像死人窝，却又紧张得像恐怖电影的高潮。然而，我的这两个朋友却总是彬彬有礼，始终保持着伪装，掩盖着一场如同核弹级冲突的内心煎熬。而我认识的另一对夫妇，一旦吵架，就会扯着嗓子大喊大叫，有时脸都贴到一起了。在这两种极端之间，存在着无数种权力斗争的方式——它们都同样会损害一段关系的成功，同时也同样蕴藏着让我们看到真正伙伴关系的无限可能。

Being confronted with disenchantment with your partner brings you face to face with the process of disillusionment. When you fight, you are only trying to remain blind to what is behind the curtain of fantasy. But when you tire of trying to maintain a false sense of control, you can peek behind it. What lurks behind that curtain is the beginning of the journey in earnest.

对伴侣感到失望，意味着你正经历着幻灭的过程。争吵时，你只是试图对幻想背后的真相视而不见。但当你厌倦了维持虚假的控制感时，你就可以窥探真相了。隐藏在那层帷幕之后的，才是真正旅程的开始。

***

OF CARROTS, WATERMELONS, AND PAIN

胡萝卜、西瓜和疼痛

———————————

“There was a faith-healer of Deal

“迪尔镇有一位信仰治疗师。”

Who said, ‘although pain isn’t real,

谁说过，“虽然痛苦不是真实的”，

If I sit on a pin

如果我坐在一根针上

And it punctures my skin

它刺破了我的皮肤

I dislike what I fancy I feel .’”

我不喜欢我自以为是的感觉。

—Anonymous

-匿名的

It is amazing to see the change in couples once the Power Struggle stage begins. They may have begun their relationship with smiles of pure excitement and pleasure on their faces, and stars in their eyes whenever they looked at each other. But when the sense of disillusionment seeps in, the smiles are replaced by frowns, and the stars in the eyes become fires of anger—sometimes even hatred. So what happened? Why do we treat our partners like our greatest enemies? Let me illustrate what I believe is the cause of this unhappy change in the relationship.

一旦进入权力斗争阶段，情侣之间的变化令人惊叹。他们或许在恋爱之初脸上洋溢着纯粹的兴奋和喜悦，每次对视都眼中闪烁着爱的光芒。但当失望的情绪逐渐滋生，笑容被愁容取代，眼中的爱意也变成了愤怒的火焰——有时甚至是仇恨。究竟发生了什么？为什么我们会把伴侣当作最大的敌人？让我来阐述一下我认为导致这种不幸关系转变的原因。

Many people I know, myself included, carry the negative childhood memories of being forced to eat some kind of food that we didn’t want to eat. For me it was boiled carrots.

我认识的很多人，包括我自己，都有过被迫吃自己不想吃的食物的不愉快童年记忆。对我来说，那就是煮胡萝卜。

My parents bought very few fresh vegetables. The kind I had to eat had already been overcooked and packed in a can, only to be brought into our house, poured into a pot and boiled again ! There was a rule in our home, which stated that no one could leave the table until they had eaten everything on their plate; give my parents full marks for commitment, they made sure that rule was followed to the letter.

我父母很少买新鲜蔬菜。我吃的那些蔬菜都是罐头装的，煮过头了，拿到家里来，倒进锅里又煮了一遍！我们家有条规矩，盘子里的食物必须吃完才能离开餐桌；我父母真是太有担当了，他们确保这条规矩被一丝不苟地执行。

One night a week for many years found me staring at those sickly orange cubes that I was sure were scientifically designed to make little boys gag and/or vomit—taking a few thousand brain cells or a vital organ in the bargain. I tried everything to avoid putting those carrots down my throat! I thought of holding my breath, stuffing them into my mouth, and casually walking to the bathroom to eject them into the toilet. I tried to feed them to my dog. I smuggled some tissue into the kitchen and, when my parents left the room or weren’t looking, I would slide the things off my plate and onto the tissue paper in my lap to gather them into a soggy, pulpy mass. I would even try to spread them around the plate to give the appearance of “a few scraps” remaining. But the schemes rarely worked more than once, if at all. I was usually caught in the act, and thereby left with the sickening task of trying to digest the carrots that were now not only soggy and disgusting, but cold and mushy as well.

多年来，每周总有一个晚上，我都会盯着那些令人作呕的橙色方块，我确信它们是经过科学设计，专门用来让小男孩作呕甚至呕吐的——顺便还能夺走几千个脑细胞或者某个重要器官。我尝试过各种方法来避免把这些胡萝卜吞下去！我想过屏住呼吸，把它们塞进嘴里，然后若无其事地走到卫生间，把它们吐进马桶。我还试着喂给我的狗吃。我偷偷带了一些纸巾到厨房，趁父母离开房间或不注意的时候，把胡萝卜从盘子里滑到腿上的纸巾上，把它们聚拢成一团湿漉漉的糊状物。我甚至会试着把它们摊开在盘子周围，假装还剩下“一些残渣”。但这些计谋很少能成功，即使成功，也往往只能成功一次。我通常都会被当场抓获，然后不得不面对令人作呕的消化过程——这些胡萝卜不仅湿漉漉的、令人作呕，而且还又冷又烂。

Then something changed. It was one of those nights when, after a good hour or so of delay, I finally wrestled the last awful chunk of overcooked vegetable down my throat, and sighed in relief that it didn’t reappear in a more disgusting form. Afterwards a huge piece of chocolate cake was placed in front of me. It was rich and moist with a thick chocolate icing, and it weighed about a pound. This kind of dessert was as rare as gold in our house. Then my mother spoke the most beautiful words to a kid’s ears: “There’s seconds if you want more.” The cake was gone in less than two minutes, and the second piece didn’t take much longer. My father smiled and asked me, “Why can’t you eat your carrots that fast?” The answer I had then, but was smart enough not to say out loud was “Well Dad, I never see you put any food you don’t like on your plate!”

然后，事情发生了变化。那天晚上，我拖延了一个多小时，终于费力地把最后一块难以下咽的煮过头的蔬菜咽了下去，长舒一口气，庆幸它没有以更恶心的形式再次出现。之后，一大块巧克力蛋糕摆在了我的面前。蛋糕口感浓郁湿润，上面覆盖着厚厚的巧克力糖霜，重约一磅。这种甜点在我们家简直比黄金还珍贵。这时，妈妈对我说了句最动听的话：“如果你还想吃，可以再来一块。”蛋糕不到两分钟就被我吃光了，第二块也很快就被我吃完了。爸爸笑着问我：“你为什么吃胡萝卜吃得这么慢？”我当时心里有个答案，但很聪明地没有说出口：“爸爸，我从没见过你把不喜欢吃的东西放到盘子里！”

My answer to that question now is that it is a basic human tendency: we will struggle to avoid, delay or reject an unpleasant experience regardless of its inevitability. I even chose to suffer the lesser discomfort of being stuck on a hard chair for hours in the vain hope that the carrots would miraculously disappear form my plate, rather than face the harsher reality of letting those repulsive orange things anywhere near my lips.

现在我对这个问题的回答是，这是一种基本的人类倾向：无论不愉快经历是否不可避免，我们都会竭力避免、拖延或拒绝。我甚至宁愿忍受几个小时坐在硬椅子上这种相对较小的不适，只盼着胡萝卜能奇迹般地从盘子里消失，也不愿面对让那些令人作呕的橙色东西靠近嘴唇的残酷现实。

We follow the same principle in our relationships. We enter the Power Struggle with our partner in order to avoid, delay, or reject an unpleasant feeling that is surfacing from within us . From where did this pain originate? To understand this, we must return once again to the issue of childhood needs. In Chapter One I stated that as children we were driven by two major desires: the need to belong (the need for inclusion), and the need to feel important. When these needs were not met, we experienced great pain, sometimes to the point of heartbreak. In order to save ourselves from the hurt, we had to distance ourselves from whatever or whoever seemed to be causing it. “My mother is not making me feel important. This hurts a lot. I have to push this pain away and make it disappear.” In the process of trying to distance ourselves from the pain, we also distanced ourselves from the perceived source of the pain—in this example, Mom. And so there we were: discouraged, isolated from the most important people in our lives, and trying desperately to push away the heartbreak.

我们在人际关系中也遵循同样的原则。我们与伴侣陷入权力斗争，是为了逃避、拖延或压制内心涌现的不愉快感受。这种痛苦究竟源于何处？要理解这一点，我们必须再次回到童年需求的问题上。我在第一章中提到，孩童时期，我们受两种主要欲望的驱使：归属感（被接纳的需求）和被重视的需求。当这些需求得不到满足时，我们会经历巨大的痛苦，有时甚至会心碎。为了避免受伤，我们不得不远离任何似乎造成痛苦的人或事。“妈妈没有让我觉得自己很重要。这很痛苦。我必须把这种痛苦推开，让它消失。”在试图远离痛苦的过程中，我们也疏远了我们认为的痛苦来源——在这个例子中，就是妈妈。于是，我们陷入了这种境地：沮丧，与生命中最重要的人隔绝，拼命地想要摆脱心碎的痛苦。

But the pain does not disappear. It rarely—if ever—does until we deal with it properly. This was the hardest thing for me to understand in my earlier relationships—that my partner was merely making me aware of some pain I had been carrying inside me for a very long time, and trying not to feel. What I am most amazed by is the subtlety of my denial of the pain’s existence. It takes an exceptional person to be able to catch the first signals that some old pain is coming up, and an even more exceptional one to choose to face it responsibly, without pushing their partner away from the intimate space they had been sharing. This is an important point: very often a conflict will arise immediately after a period when the couple was enjoying a time of intimacy. They may have felt very warm towards each other, the sex may have been especially intimate, there may have been more humour, or tenderness than usual. It is as if the love we experience in those moments of intimacy gives us the strength to unconsciously call up the unfinished business or unhealed wounds of our past, so that they can be given the loving attention they did not receive at that traumatic time. Therefore, it is a call to transformation which is the prelude to a serious conflict or relationship crisis. Before I realized this, I had four different explanations regarding why fights got started in my relationships.

但痛苦并不会消失。除非我们妥善处理，否则它几乎不会——甚至根本不会——自行消失。在我早期的恋爱关系中，最难理解的就是这一点：我的伴侣只是让我意识到，我内心深处一直隐藏着某种痛苦，而我一直试图压抑着它。最令我惊讶的是，我竟然如此巧妙地否认了这种痛苦的存在。能够察觉到旧伤复发的最初迹象，需要非凡的洞察力；而能够负责任地面对它，同时又不将伴侣推离他们曾经共享的亲密空间，则需要更加非凡的勇气。这一点至关重要：很多时候，冲突会在伴侣享受了一段亲密时光之后立即出现。他们可能彼此感觉非常温暖，性生活可能格外亲密，也可能比平时更加幽默或温柔。仿佛我们在亲密时刻体验到的爱，赋予我们力量，让我们无意识地唤起过往未竟之事或未愈合的伤痛，以便给予它们在创伤时期未曾得到的关爱。因此，这是一种转变的呼唤，也是严重冲突或关系危机的前兆。在我意识到这一点之前，我对人际关系中争吵的起因有四种不同的解释。

EXPLANATION #1: There is a conflict here because you started it. Therefore I am not fighting; I am merely protecting my boundaries which you are so thoughtlessly invading.

解释一：这里之所以有冲突，是因为你先挑起的。因此，我不是在反击；我只是在捍卫我的界限，而你却如此轻率地侵犯了我的界限。

EXPLANATION #2: There is a conflict here because, although it may look like I started this one, all I was doing was pointing out some inappropriate behaviour on your part, and while I was pointing it out, I just happened to think of a few more areas in which you needed some correction, such as how you behave on or close to your period, etc. You just can’t take constructive advice—you call it criticism, but I’m being as nice as I can be, considering your mood.

解释二：这里存在冲突，因为虽然看起来好像是我先挑起的，但我只是指出你的一些不恰当行为。在指出这些行为的同时，我又想到了你其他一些需要改正的地方，比如你在经期前后的一些行为等等。你就是听不进建设性的建议——你称之为批评，但考虑到你的情绪，我已经尽可能委婉了。

EXPLANATION #3: There is a conflict here because you are wrong, and too pigheaded to admit that I’m right about this issue. Now I am forced to get angry, because it’s the only way to make you understand how wrong you are.

解释三：这里存在冲突，因为你错了，而且固执己见，不肯承认我在这个问题上是对的。现在我不得不生气，因为这是让你明白自己错得有多离谱的唯一方法。

EXPLANATION #4: There is a conflict here, not because I’m hurt—I’m just upset. Anyone would be if you talked to them the way you talk to me! You call it constructive advice, but it sounds like heartless criticism to me.

解释四：这里确实存在冲突，不是因为我受到了伤害——我只是感到很生气。如果你用这种语气跟别人说话，任何人都会生气！你称之为建设性建议，但在我看来，这简直就是冷酷无情的批评。

For the longest time I did not understand that I fought with someone to protect myself from feeling a very old and serious pain that I had been carrying inside me, unhealed and unnoticed. The other person’s behaviour simply caused that old pain to reach my awareness. I also did not understand that what I said or did could cause those same reactions in my friends and partners. It may be important to remember that we often choose to fight rather than face our pain because it is simply easier to be angry than it is to feel heartbroken. Don’t forget that discouragement arrived immediately after the hurt—when you consider looking at what’s behind the conflict, you face a discouraging voice telling you the pain is too big for you to handle. This reminds me of another story:

很长一段时间以来，我都不明白，我与人争吵是为了保护自己，不去感受内心深处一直隐藏着的、未愈合且未被察觉的、由来已久的、沉重的伤痛。对方的行为只是让那份旧伤重新浮现，触及了我的意识。我也不明白，我的言行也会在我的朋友和伴侣身上引发同样的反应。或许我们应该记住，我们常常选择争吵而不是直面痛苦，因为愤怒远比心碎更容易承受。别忘了，伤痛之后往往紧接着就是沮丧——当你试图探究冲突背后的原因时，你会听到一个令人沮丧的声音，告诉你痛苦太过沉重，你根本无法承受。这让我想起了另一个故事：

A landlord of mine once told me that he grew up in the area I was moving into. He said it was mainly farmland when he was a child, and that his father grew watermelons. He bragged about how big the melons were, and spread his arms to indicate that they were about four feet long. A while later I realized that to a boy of about seven, an average watermelon would seem enormous. As he grew bigger, the size of the watermelon in his memory grew as well. 18

我的一位房东曾经告诉我，他是在我即将搬去的这片区域长大的。他说他小时候那里主要是农田，他父亲种西瓜。他吹嘘说西瓜有多大，还张开双臂比划着说大约有四英尺长。过了一段时间我才意识到，对于一个七岁左右的男孩来说，一个普通的西瓜看起来就已经非常巨大了。随着他长大，他记忆中的西瓜也越来越大。<sup>18</sup>

You can apply the same logic to childhood pain. Sure, it must have seemed enormous when you were young—maybe even overwhelming. But it is possible that growing up brings with it the capacity to see the pain from a different perspective. The pain may not be quite so overwhelming as it once was. A more conscious and mature approach to Power Struggles will give you the chance to not only face your old wounds, but to free yourself from their damaging consequences. And what are those consequences? They are the limitations of our…

同样的道理也适用于童年的伤痛。当然，年幼时，这些伤痛或许显得无比巨大——甚至令人难以承受。但成长或许会让你拥有从不同角度看待伤痛的能力。伤痛可能不再像以前那样难以承受。以更清醒、更成熟的态度面对权力斗争，不仅能让你直面旧伤，还能让你摆脱其带来的伤害。而这些伤害究竟是什么呢？它们就是我们自身的局限性……

***

BELIEFS: THE WATERMELONS OF THOUGHT

信念：思想的西瓜

———————————

“Sow a thought and reap an action. Sow an action and reap a habit. Sow a habit and reap a character. Sow a character and reap a destiny.”

“种下思想，收获行动；种下行动，收获习惯；种下习惯，收获性格；种下性格，收获命运。”

—Dan Wells

——丹·威尔斯

The above quote has stuck with me ever since I first heard it. It states that, once you catch a thought and give it a home inside you, you set off a chain reaction with wide-ranging, and long-lasting, results. In his book “Having it All,” Arnold Patent states that the average human being has about fifty thousand thoughts a day, most of them “old thoughts.” 19 A lot of them began from childhood and have been hanging around ever since. It’s like having a tape recorder in your head with an endless reel, repeating the same thoughts over and over again. Thought is a key ingredient of belief. If thought is the seed, plant it, and you will reap the watermelon of a belief.

自从第一次听到这句话，它就一直萦绕在我心头。它指出，一旦你捕捉到一个念头，并让它在你心中扎根，你就会引发一系列连锁反应，产生广泛而持久的影响。阿诺德·帕滕特在他的著作《拥有一切》中提到，普通人每天大约会产生五万个念头，其中大部分是“旧念头”。<sup>19</sup> 许多旧念头始于童年，并一直萦绕在你心头。这就像你的脑子里装着一台无限循环的录音机，一遍又一遍地重复着同样的想法。思想是信念的关键要素。如果说思想是种子，那么把它种下，你就能收获信念这颗西瓜。

Supposing you had a painful experience as a child. For instance, say your father promised to take you camping, and it was something you really wanted to do. Then it didn’t happen. Maybe dad got very busy at work and had to give up his vacation. Maybe he got sick, or maybe he just forgot. Since most children don’t have a very expanded view of the world, it wouldn’t much matter what reason your Dad gave you. You would probably experience a degree of disappointment. In the pain of that disappointment, thoughts would come into your mind to interpret your experience. What if one of those thoughts was, “Dad doesn’t care about me!”? What if another thought tagged along for the ride, something like, “Nobody loves me.”? If similar disappointments took place, those thoughts may well turn into a belief that you are basically unlovable. If that belief is played over and over in your mind for years, you might come to take that belief as fact. What is a person who believes she or he is unlovable likely to experience from time to time in her/his close relationships?

假设你小时候有过一段痛苦的经历。比如说，你爸爸答应带你去露营，而你一直很想去。结果却没去成。也许爸爸工作太忙，不得不放弃假期；也许他生病了；也许他只是忘了。由于大多数孩子对世界的认知有限，爸爸给出的理由其实并不重要。你很可能会感到失望。在失望的痛苦中，你的脑海中会浮现出各种想法来解读这段经历。如果其中一个想法是：“爸爸根本不在乎我！”呢？如果另一个想法也随之而来，比如：“没有人爱我。”呢？如果类似的失望反复出现，这些想法很可能会演变成一种信念：你根本不值得被爱。如果这种信念在你脑海中反复出现多年，你最终可能会把它当成事实。那么，一个认为自己不值得被爱的人，在亲密关系中可能会经历什么呢？

From this perspective, it is evident that past trauma does not simply disappear as you grow up. At the root of each limiting belief is a painful experience that has not gone away. We are all Dr. Frankensteins, having created monster beliefs that rampage through our lives and wreak lesser or greater degrees of havoc. There is not one belief that you have about yourself or this world that is true. Nor do any beliefs serve you if they encourage perceptions of yourself as small or bad. Yet many people harbour such beliefs, never knowing their source and rarely understanding that these beliefs are just houseguests; they do not have to be permanent residents. A helpful step may be to find out where these beliefs are living.

从这个角度来看，过去的创伤并不会随着成长而消失。每一个限制性信念的根源都在于一段挥之不去的痛苦经历。我们每个人都像弗兰肯斯坦博士一样，创造出了肆虐我们生活、造成或多或少破坏的“怪物”信念。你对自身或这个世界的所有信念，没有一个是绝对正确的。任何信念，如果让你觉得自己渺小或糟糕，都对你毫无益处。然而，许多人却深陷于这样的信念之中，从未探寻其根源，也鲜少意识到这些信念只是暂时的房客，它们并非永久的住户。或许，找出这些信念的根源所在，会是一个有益的尝试。

***

THE GHOSTS OF OUR PAST

我们过去的幽灵

———————————

“The past is left, but right behind,

“过去已成往事，但就在身后。”

lingering, haunting shadows.”

挥之不去的、令人不安的阴影。

—C. G. Moon

——C·G·穆恩

About a year and a half into my marriage, when my wife and I were fully entrenched in a Power Struggle, I realized that I made a huge mistake with my wedding vows. Su Mei and I each created our own vows and spoke them in front of hundreds of witnesses. They were full of promise, poetry, and loving intentions. Tears fell from my eyes as I sincerely promised to love Su Mei unconditionally, to honour and respect her through good times and bad, and to allow no pain to come between us. They were sincere commitments that I had every intention of keeping. The problem was, as beautiful as the sentiments were, they were neither realistic nor practical. In other words they were not promises that I could keep. If I really wanted to keep my word, my vows would have sounded more like, “I promise, that in the process of learning to love you unconditionally , I will push every button you’ve got, cause you to feel more pain than you can presently imagine, induce you to say things to me that would shock a New York taxi driver, and make you regret the day you met me. Also, when you do the same to me, I will respond to you with all the maturity of a three year old, with petulance and tantrum as my two main weapons. I will constantly forget that we are two human beings simply doing our best. I will regularly fall into the trap of expecting you to be my absolute source of happiness. Eventually I will grow up and learn the true purpose of our relationship, but until then, all I can say is that it’s going to hurt, and I’m sorry.” Now those are vows that I would have no problem living up to!

结婚大约一年半后，我和妻子陷入了一场权力斗争，我才意识到自己在结婚誓词上犯了个大错。我和苏美各自撰写了誓词，并在数百位见证人面前宣读。誓词充满了承诺、诗意和爱意。我热泪盈眶，真诚地承诺无条件地爱苏美，无论顺境逆境都尊重她、敬重她，不让任何痛苦阻隔我们。这些都是我真心实意想要遵守的承诺。问题是，尽管这些誓词美好动人，却既不现实也不可行。换句话说，这些承诺我根本无法兑现。如果我真的想信守诺言，我的誓言应该更像是这样：“我保证，在学会无条件爱你的过程中，我会触碰你所有的痛点，让你感受到你现在无法想象的痛苦，让你说出连纽约出租车司机都会震惊的话，让你后悔遇见我的那天。同样，当你也这样对我时，我会像个三岁小孩一样，用任性和耍脾气来回应你。我会经常忘记我们只是两个尽力而为的普通人。我会经常掉进你成为我幸福的唯一来源的陷阱。最终我会长大，明白我们关系的真正意义，但在那之前，我只能说，这会很痛苦，我很抱歉。” 这才是我绝对能做到的誓言！

When we enter any relationship, we bring to it all the old pains, traumas and unfinished business of our past. Whenever we were hurt as children, and the pain was not healed—which is often the case—we buried the pain so that we didn’t have to feel it all the time. Why? Well, besides the fact that we simply don’t want to feel pain of any kind, the truth is that some of our childhood pain is so great that sometimes when we were hurting, we thought the pain would kill or disable us unless we somehow got rid of it.

当我们进入一段新的关系时，我们会把过去所有的伤痛、创伤和未了的心愿都带进去。童年时期，如果我们受到伤害，而这些伤痛又没有被治愈——这种情况很常见——我们就会把痛苦埋藏起来，以免时时感受到它。为什么呢？除了我们根本不想感受任何痛苦之外，事实是，有些童年的伤痛太过强烈，以至于我们有时会觉得，除非摆脱它，否则这种痛苦会要了我们的命，或者让我们丧失行动能力。

I remember once when I was young I lost our dog’s collar. This angered my father considerably. He tormented me with slaps and verbal abuse for what seemed to me to last at least an hour. The slaps I could handle—their marks disappeared within the day—but the emotional bruising did not leave so quickly. I needed my father’s forgiveness and love. When forgiveness and love were not forthcoming, it hurt me so deeply that I thought my heart was going to break. However, a few hours later I was running around outside, laughing and playing with my brother. One might think that due to the resilience of children around pain, I simply forgot about the ugly incident with my father and got on with my life. However, years later I recalled the incident. I re-experienced the pain I felt as a six-year-old boy being yelled at and hit by a father from whom I needed love, and once more felt my heart break.

我记得小时候有一次弄丢了我们家狗的项圈。这让父亲非常生气。他用耳光和言语虐待我，我觉得至少持续了一个小时。耳光我可以忍受——痕迹一天就消失了——但精神上的创伤却久久无法愈合。我需要父亲的原谅和爱。当他没有给予我原谅和爱时，我感到无比痛苦，仿佛心都要碎了。然而，几个小时后，我又在外面跑来跑去，和哥哥一起欢笑玩耍。人们可能会认为，由于孩子天生具有很强的适应能力，我很快就忘记了和父亲的那次不愉快的经历，继续过着自己的生活。然而，多年以后，我又想起了这件事。我再次体验到了六岁时被父亲责骂和殴打的痛苦，而我本该从父亲那里得到爱，我的心再次破碎。

I know from my work as a therapist that I am not unusual when it comes to how I handled pain as a child and as an adult. Many of us experienced painful episodes we thought would literally break our hearts, or cripple us unless we took some measures to escape the hurt. So we created a basement in our mind—the subconscious—where we could store our suppressed pain and lock it away, eventually forgetting about it altogether. Like a storage closet that we open only when we want to throw some unwanted article into it, the subconscious mind is a depository full of unwanted, painful memories that we never knew how to deal with or resolve. But unlike a storage closet, the subconscious mind kept growing in order to allow us to keep stuffing the discomfort away, thus avoiding the call to confront the pain openly.

作为一名治疗师，我知道我的经历与许多人并无二致，无论是在童年还是成年时期，我处理痛苦的方式都大同小异。我们许多人都经历过痛苦的事件，我们以为这些痛苦会彻底击垮我们，或者让我们痛苦不堪，除非我们采取措施逃避伤痛。于是，我们在内心深处——潜意识——建造了一个地下室，用来储存和锁住我们压抑的痛苦，最终将其彻底遗忘。就像一个储物柜，我们只有在想扔掉不需要的东西时才会打开，潜意识就像一个仓库，里面装满了我们不想要的、痛苦的记忆，而我们却不知道该如何处理或解决这些记忆。但与储物柜不同的是，潜意识不断膨胀，让我们得以继续隐藏这些不适，从而逃避直面痛苦的呼唤。

So, you may ask, what’s the problem? If the subconscious keeps growing with whatever junk we throw into it, why not keep stuffing the pain in there? What’s the point in suffering if you can avoid it? I would be the first to agree with you, except for a few snags with the idea. One snag is that in order to avoid feeling the pain as a child, I had to reject any bond with my father. I withdrew from him as much as I could and maintained a distance throughout my early life, with the emotional wound standing between us. The other major snag, as mentioned earlier, is that painful incidents are instrumental in the formation of most of the limiting beliefs we have about ourselves and the world around us. For instance, the experience I suffered with my father over the dog collar may have caused me to believe that he did not love me. From that belief I could extrapolate that, since my father was to me a figure of great authority, no male authority figure would love me. Consequently, I may live out my life fearful of teachers, police, doctors, bosses, etc. Fear limits us from acting freely and according to our nature. Going further with that example, if I live in fear of all these figures, what does that make me believe about myself? Maybe that I’m a wimp or a weakling, a no-good screw-up, a failure. What we believe we are often determines what kind of work we choose, what kind of friends we have, where we live, the quality of our sex lives, and most other aspects of our existence, probably even including our choice for the kind of car we drive. You might argue that it is very hard to believe one incident of being slapped around by my father would create such a debilitating belief and poor sense of self worth in me, and I would probably agree with you. As stated before, the seed of belief is created from a singularly painful incident, but is reinforced by subsequent episodes of similar nature. The example was given to illustrate that painful situations from our past that have not been healed will negatively influence our beliefs about ourselves. Once the pain is dealt with in a healthy manner, the belief can change accordingly.

所以，你可能会问，问题出在哪里？如果潜意识会不断吸收我们塞进去的各种垃圾信息，为什么不把痛苦也塞进去呢？如果可以避免痛苦，那痛苦的意义何在？我本来会第一个同意你的观点，但这个想法也有一些问题。其中一个问题是，为了避免童年时期的痛苦，我不得不切断与父亲的一切联系。我尽可能地疏远他，在早年生活中一直与他保持距离，我们之间始终存在着一道情感创伤。另一个主要的问题是，正如前面提到的，痛苦的经历往往会塑造我们对自身和周围世界的大部分限制性信念。例如，我和父亲因为狗项圈而产生的冲突可能让我觉得他不爱我。基于这种信念，我推断，既然父亲在我心中是权威人物，那么任何男性权威人物都不会爱我。因此，我可能会终生生活在对老师、警察、医生、老板等等的恐惧之中。恐惧限制了我们自由行动，也限制了我们按照自己的本性行事。进一步来说，如果我生活在对这些人恐惧之中，我会对自己产生怎样的看法呢？也许我会觉得自己是个懦夫、是个弱者、是个一无是处、是个失败者。我们对自己的认知往往决定了我们选择什么样的工作、结交什么样的朋友、住在哪里、性生活质量如何，以及我们生活的其他方方面面，甚至可能包括我们选择开什么样的车。你可能会说，很难相信被父亲打了一巴掌这件事会让我产生如此根深蒂固的信念和低自尊，我大概也会同意你的看法。正如前面所说，信念的种子源于一次痛苦的经历，但随后类似事件的发生会强化这种信念。举这个例子是为了说明，过去那些没有得到治愈的痛苦经历会对我们对自己的认知产生负面影响。一旦痛苦得到健康处理，信念也会随之改变。

We all live according to who we believe we are. If you truly believe that you are successful, your failures will not keep you from ultimate success; if you believe you’re a failure, even your biggest successes can be experienced as failures. All beliefs formed out of an unhealed pain will be limiting. Since these beliefs about ourselves are inextricably woven to past traumas that can rarely be clearly remembered, much less changed, how can we ever be free from our limitations? This is what makes relationships such invaluable gifts in our lives. Your present relationship offers you the opportunity to revisit past trauma and heal those experiences, thereby correcting the mistaken beliefs that were formed from those incidents.

我们都活在自己对自身的认知之中。如果你真心相信自己是成功的，那么失败并不会阻碍你最终的成功；如果你认为自己是失败者，那么即使是最大的成功，在你眼中也可能如同失败一般。所有源于未愈合伤痛的信念都具有局限性。由于这些关于自身的信念与过往创伤密不可分，而这些创伤往往难以清晰地回忆起来，更遑论改变，我们又该如何摆脱这些局限呢？正因如此，人际关系才显得如此珍贵。你现在的这段关系为你提供了一个机会，让你重新审视过去的创伤，疗愈那些经历，从而纠正那些由过往事件形成的错误信念。

***

GOING HOME

回家

———————————

“If you haven’t left home peacefully, you haven’t left at all.”

“如果你没有和平地离开家，那就等于没有离开。”

—C.G. Moon

——C.G. Moon

Henry, a colleague of mine, told me of a visit he made back to his hometown. He was invited to dinner by Ron, an old school chum, and his wife Betty (not their real names). As a couple they were not doing well, steeped in the hellish waters of Power Struggle. Henry found himself sitting at the dinner table, listening to Betty as she went on and on about what a no-good bum her husband was. She would spread her complaints around, sometimes talking to my colleague, then suddenly swinging over to lash out at Ron before returning to Henry again. It sounded something like this: “This guy is a bum, Henry! He works at a job for a few months and then he quits. He’s so useless—he never sticks to anything. Why don’t you do something with your life, for Chrissake, Ron? Why don’t you go back to school and make something of yourself? Tell him, Henry! He’s got no brains! He can’t take care of his family, he’s so useless! He should go kill himself in a car accident—at least the insurance money would take care of us. That’s all you’re good for, Ron, is killing yourself! Why don’t you…” and so on. As my colleague’s ears were assaulted by the verbal barrage, he would look over at his friend who kept his eyes on the food, saying almost nothing through the entire diatribe, except to offer the occasional shrug and say, “What do you want from me, anyway?” Then his shoulders would sag and he would relapse into silent eating.

我的同事亨利跟我讲了他回老家探亲的经历。他受邀去老同学罗恩和他的妻子贝蒂（均为化名）家吃晚饭。这对夫妻关系并不好，深陷权力斗争的泥潭。亨利坐在餐桌旁，听着贝蒂不停地抱怨她丈夫是个多么没出息的混蛋。她一会儿跟亨利抱怨，一会儿又突然转向罗恩发泄一番，最后才回到亨利身上。听起来大概是这样的：“亨利，这家伙是个游手好闲的家伙！他干几个月活就辞职了。他真是个废物——什么事都坚持不下去。看在上帝的份上，罗恩，你为什么不做点有意义的事呢？为什么不回学校好好学习，让自己出人头地呢？告诉他，亨利！他没脑子！他养不起家，真是个废物！他应该去车祸中丧命——至少保险金能养活我们。罗恩，你除了自杀就没别的用处了！你为什么不……”诸如此类。我的同事被这连珠炮似的谩骂折磨得耳朵嗡嗡作响，他瞥了一眼朋友，只见朋友一直盯着食物，几乎一言不发，只是偶尔耸耸肩，说：“你到底想从我这儿得到什么？”然后肩膀垮了下来，又开始默默地吃东西。

What struck Henry so powerfully was the amazing familiarity of the situation. There were times throughout his childhood and adolescence when he would find himself sitting at the dining table with Ron while Ron’s mother complained to Henry about how useless her son was. It was almost as if Betty had gone to acting school solely to learn how to play the part of Ron’s mother—that’s how uncanny the similarity was between the two most important women in Ron’s life. (Henry pointed out to me that Betty is a really wonderful, caring, loving woman—at that juncture in their relationship, just like in all Power Struggles, Ron was doing his best to bring out the worst in her, and Betty the worst in him.)

最让亨利感到震撼的是，眼前的情景竟如此似曾相识。在他童年和青少年时期，他常常会和罗恩一起坐在餐桌旁，听着罗恩的母亲向他抱怨儿子有多么没用。贝蒂仿佛专门去表演学校学习过如何扮演罗恩的母亲——罗恩生命中最重要的两个女人之间的相似之处简直令人难以置信。（亨利告诉我，贝蒂其实是一位非常棒、非常体贴、非常慈爱的女人——在他们关系的那个阶段，就像所有权力斗争一样，罗恩竭尽所能地激发贝蒂最糟糕的一面，而贝蒂也竭尽所能地激发罗恩最糟糕的一面。）

Henry told me that his friend had a very painful childhood, and that he had developed a very poor sense of himself as a man. It was obvious to all of Ron’s friends that his mother treated him horrendously. So why would he turn around and marry someone who would verbally abuse him like his mother had? And why would Betty marry someone so unsatisfying to her? I’m sure that when Ron and Betty first met, Betty wasn’t thinking, “Man, what a loser this guy is—I hope he asks me to marry him!” And I’m equally sure Ron wasn’t thinking, “Geez, who let this horrible nag onto the planet? Lucky I found her before someone else snatched her up!” They only began to see these unattractive aspects of each other as they got closer. But as ugly as that scene at the dinner table might appear to the observer, Ronald was actually being given a second chance. As a child, he had no idea how to respond to his mother’s dissatisfaction, and so could only suffer her criticism and reinforce beliefs about himself accordingly. Now, with Betty, life was giving him the opportunity to find a healthier response, one that could heal both his and Betty’s wounds. These opportunities for healing the past are offered to all relationships, whether the people involved take advantage of them or not. Who says there’s no going back?

亨利告诉我，他的朋友童年非常痛苦，因此对自己作为男人的形象非常不自信。罗恩所有的朋友都看得出来，他的母亲对他极其恶劣。那么，他为什么会转身娶一个像他母亲那样对他进行言语虐待的人呢？贝蒂又为什么会嫁给一个让她如此不满意的人呢？我敢肯定，罗恩和贝蒂初次见面时，贝蒂绝对不会想：“天哪，这家伙真是个窝囊废——我希望他能向我求婚！”我也同样肯定，罗恩当时肯定不会想：“哎呀，谁把这个唠叨的讨厌鬼放生到这世上？幸好我赶在她被别人抢走之前找到了她！”他们只是在彼此了解加深之后才开始看到对方这些不讨喜的方面。虽然餐桌上的那一幕在旁观者看来或许很不堪，但实际上，罗恩得到了第二次机会。小时候，他不知道该如何回应母亲的不满，只能默默忍受她的批评，并因此更加坚定自己的信念。如今，遇到贝蒂，生活给了他一个机会，让他找到一种更健康的应对方式，一种能够治愈他和贝蒂彼此创伤的方式。所有关系都存在这种治愈过往的机会，无论当事人是否把握。谁说没有回头路呢？

***

KILLED BY FRIENDLY FIRE

被友军火力击毙

———————————

“Yet each man kills the thing he loves….”

“然而，每个人都会杀死自己所爱的东西……”

—Oscar Wilde

——奥斯卡·王尔德

In relationships, the process of moving emotionally closer to someone and sharing more of our life with that other person causes us to re-experience past wounds that we would normally be blissfully unaware of. For example, a bank teller might get angry at me and call me a jerk. My wife might get angry at me and call me a jerk. Which one is likely to hurt more? I have hardly any emotional connection with the teller, whereas the connection I have with my wife is as strong, or almost as strong, as the one I had with my mother when I was a child. My wife calling me a jerk could more effectively trigger a subconscious memory of a time when my mother lost patience with me and expressed it in a way that hurt my feelings. So any pain associated with my mother can be accessed, and forgiven if I so choose, through my relationship with my wife. My job is to remember, whenever I am tempted to get into a fight, that most, if not all, of the pain I’m feeling is not caused by my wife. It comes from the past.

在人际关系中，当我们与某人建立更亲密的情感联系，并与他们分享更多生活点滴时，我们会重新体验到那些我们通常浑然不觉的过往伤痛。例如，银行柜员可能会对我发火，骂我混蛋。我的妻子也可能会对我发火，骂我混蛋。哪一种更让我痛苦？我和柜员几乎没有任何情感联系，而我和妻子的感情却像我小时候和母亲的感情一样牢固，甚至几乎一样牢固。妻子骂我混蛋，更有可能触发我潜意识里母亲曾经对我失去耐心，并以伤害我的方式表达出来的记忆。因此，任何与母亲相关的伤痛，都可以通过我和妻子的关系触及，如果我愿意，也可以选择原谅。我的任务是，每当我想要争吵时，都要记住，我感受到的大部分痛苦，如果不是全部的话，都不是妻子造成的。它源于过去。

Therefore when I fight with my wife, I’m only making things worse for myself. I’m compounding my misery by not dealing directly with the pain from my past, and I am doing my best to make my wife miserable by insisting that she is the sole cause of my pain. Together we are choosing to distract ourselves by focusing on some crucial issue, such as why I think the sofa should be at a sixty-degree angle rather than at the forty-five she is so stubbornly insisting upon. The most important point to remember when you find yourself being sucked into some form of Power Struggle is this: I am never upset for the reasons I think I am . To expand this point, let me give you some examples of what kinds of subjects have been used to fuel a Power Struggle. Among them are arguments I have witnessed professionally, socially, and within my own marriage:

因此，当我与妻子争吵时，我只会让自己的情况变得更糟。我没有直接面对过去的伤痛，反而加剧了自己的痛苦；我坚持认为妻子是我痛苦的唯一根源，这无疑是在竭尽全力让她也感到痛苦。我们都选择用一些无关紧要的小事来分散注意力，比如为什么我认为沙发应该摆成60度角，而不是她固执地坚持的45度角。当你发现自己陷入某种形式的权力斗争时，最重要的是要记住：我生气的原因从来不是我以为的那些。为了进一步说明这一点，让我举一些例子，说明哪些话题会被用来引发权力斗争。这些例子包括我在工作中、社交场合以及我自己的婚姻中目睹过的争吵：

• A couple arguing over the high school their children will attend. (The children were not even in the first grade.)

一对夫妇正在争论他们的孩子将来要上哪所高中。（孩子们当时甚至还没上一年级。）

• Two lovers dispute concerning who the next president of the United States should be (neither of them votes, and only one is American).

• 一对恋人争论谁应该成为下一任美国总统（他们都没有投票权，而且只有一人是美国人）。

• A couple heatedly debating the angle at which a sofa should be placed. 20

一对夫妇正在激烈争论沙发应该摆放的角度。20

• A couple on the brink of divorce because of a disagreement about whether the bird they saw was a crow or a raven (to date there is still no resolution concerning this vital topic).

• 一对夫妇因为对他们看到的鸟是乌鸦还是渡鸦存在分歧而濒临离婚（迄今为止，关于这个重要问题仍未得到解决）。

• Two old friends of over twenty years refuse to talk to each other because one owes the other a hundred dollars.

• 两位相识二十多年的老朋友因为其中一人欠另一人一百美元而断绝了往来。

• A married pair, unsure of what they are arguing about, but taking an opposite position to whatever the other one says (e.g.: “Snow is white.” “No it isn’t! Haven’t you ever heard of yellow snow?”).

• 一对已婚夫妇，不确定他们在争论什么，但无论对方说什么，他们都持相反的立场（例如：“雪是白色的。”“不，它不是白色的！你没听说过黄雪吗？”）。

To me, what makes Power Struggle even more painful is that the fight is between two people who truly care for each other. It’s just that the surfacing pain is so great that it blinds us to the love that, in our heart of hearts, we long to share with each other. If we could find a way to resolve our pain, we would certainly discover how wonderful we really are, and what a monumental mistake it was to let the traumas of our past determine what we believe we are in the present.

对我而言，权力斗争最令人痛苦之处在于，这场斗争发生在两个真心关爱彼此的人之间。只是，表面的痛苦如此强烈，以至于蒙蔽了我们的双眼，让我们看不到内心深处渴望与彼此分享的爱。如果我们能找到化解痛苦的方法，我们一定会发现自己是多么美好，也会意识到，让过去的创伤左右我们对自我的认知是多么巨大的错误。
