Suddenly I became aware of the world—how enormous it was, and how small I was in comparison to it. I remember an intense melancholy overcoming me, gradually pushing out the blissful peace that had filled me just a few seconds earlier.

我的女儿塔拉在写这篇文章时五岁。她喜欢画人，但尤其喜欢画小女孩。通常，她画的小女孩比她画的房子要大。<sup>45</sup> 塔拉似乎仍然觉得自己很大，这反映在她的画作中，尽管随着她与周围世界的联系越来越紧密，她可能会失去这种宏伟感。房子会变大，小女孩会变小。这让我想起我五岁时的一次经历，在一个阳光明媚的日子里，我坐在路边。突然间，我意识到这个世界——它是多么浩瀚，而我与之相比又是多么渺小。我记得一种强烈的忧郁感袭来，逐渐驱散了几秒钟前还充满我的幸福宁静。

Looking back on that incident now, I wonder if my sadness emerged from the loss of some inner connection I was enjoying before I “woke up” to my external surroundings. I do know that it was after this experience that I became more and more aware of what was going on around me—the emotional changes in my family, the establishment of friends as more or less permanent and important fixtures in my world, and the sense of a world that was expanding daily. In effect, I was becoming consciously oriented towards the outside world, and the sense of smallness that had been growing in me without my conscious awareness was now a very real self-perception. My external orientation became involved with the pursuit of bigger and bigger goals in what I believe was an attempt to recapture the lost feeling of “omnipotence” I had enjoyed as a child. However, no accomplishment or personal victory could ever satisfy the longing, and I was ultimately left with the old perception of myself as basically unimportant—a small dot in a large cosmos.

现在回想那件事，我不禁思考，我的悲伤是否源于失去某种内在联系——在我“觉醒”到外部世界之前，我曾享受着这种联系。我知道，正是在那次经历之后，我开始越来越意识到周围发生的一切——家人的情感变化，朋友们逐渐成为我生活中不可或缺的重要存在，以及世界日益扩张的感觉。实际上，我开始有意识地关注外部世界，而之前在不知不觉中滋生的渺小感，如今变成了一种真切的自我认知。我对外部世界的关注与追求越来越大的目标紧密相连，我认为这是一种试图重拾童年时期那种“无所不能”的感觉的尝试。然而，任何成就或个人胜利都无法满足这种渴望，最终，我还是回到了最初的认知：我本质上微不足道——浩瀚宇宙中微不足道的一粒尘埃。

The relationship process brings you to a confrontation with that smallness, and calls on you to know the Truth about yourself. Nowhere is this more intense than in the Introspection stage; for although it is the most difficult level of relationship to deal with, what it offers is invaluable: Soul. Having immersed itself in the concrete reality of ego, Soul begins in earnest to shed its skin and make its true power known at this stage. Now you would imagine that something this momentous would be hard to conceal, with the soul’s radiance dramatically piercing through the darkness in a way that would make the most beautiful sunrise look like a dull flashlight in comparison. In fact the typical human experience at this stage is almost the opposite. This is why it is often the most difficult of relationship experiences.

关系的过程会让你直面自身的渺小，并召唤你去认识关于你自己的真相。在内省阶段，这种体验尤为强烈；尽管这是关系中最难处理的阶段，但它所提供的却是无价之宝：灵魂。灵魂沉浸于自我具体的现实之中，在这个阶段，它开始真正地蜕去外壳，展现其真正的力量。你或许会认为，如此重大的转变难以掩藏，灵魂的光芒会戏剧性地穿透黑暗，使最美丽的日出都黯然失色。但事实上，在这个阶段，典型的人类体验几乎恰恰相反。正因如此，它往往是关系中最艰难的阶段。

There are more traps in the Introspection Stage than in any of the other levels. That may not sound very encouraging, especially when you consider that we probably still have a lot of work to do in the Glamour and Disillusionment stages. I want to assure the reader (and myself) that Introspection is not meant to be the end of the line for your relationship—unless you want it to be, of course. Sometimes relationships must end because they are too abusive, or because the couple has been stuck for too long. Or maybe both have come to the peaceful resolution that it is time to move forward, but not together. In no way do I want to suggest that any or all relationships should stay together for life. But if you feel in your heart that you want to keep going in your present relationship or life situation, maybe what is offered in this chapter can give you some inspiration.

内省阶段的陷阱比其他任何阶段都多。这听起来可能不太令人鼓舞，尤其考虑到我们可能在魅力阶段和幻灭阶段还有很多工作要做。我想向读者（也向我自己）保证，内省阶段并非你们关系的终点——当然，除非你们自己希望如此。有时，关系的结束是必然的，因为彼此之间存在太多的虐待，或者是因为双方陷入僵局太久。又或许，双方都已达成共识，是时候各自向前看了，但不再一起。我绝不是想暗示任何或所有关系都应该白头偕老。但如果你内心深处仍然希望继续维持目前的关系或生活状态，那么本章的内容或许能给你一些启发。

***

THE GOOD, THE BAD, THE UGLY…AND THE SACRED

好人、坏人、丑人……以及神圣之物

———————————

“To love is to love it all.”

“爱就是爱一切。”

—Anonymous

-匿名的

Let us once more review the process of relationship in the form of a simple model that delineates the stages an individual passes through as s/he comes closer to her or his partner:

让我们再次回顾一下恋爱关系的进程，用一个简单的模型来描述一个人在与伴侣关系日益亲密的过程中所经历的各个阶段：

THE GOOD
美好
Glamour, Sentiment, Romance,
魅力、情感、浪漫、
Excitement Caused by the Need for Love
对爱的渴望带来的兴奋
Soul level: A gift / lesson offered; Recognizing an Old Friend
灵魂层面：一份礼物/教诲；认出一位老朋友

THE BAD
Disillusionment, Power Struggle, Control,
Manipulation, Old Pain Surfaces
Soul level: Communication, Acceptance, Commitment to Accountability

负面因素：幻灭、权力斗争、控制、操纵、旧伤复发；灵魂层面：沟通、接纳、承担责任。

THE UGLY
丑陋的
Introspection, Shadow Figures, Sacrifice Patterns,
内省、阴影人物、牺牲模式、
Fatigue, Malaise, Nostalgia for the Glamour of Romance,
疲惫、不适、对浪漫魅力的怀念、
Repulsion Towards Mate or Vice Versa, Death Temptations
对伴侣的排斥或反之亦然、死亡的诱惑、
Soul level: Awakening to One’s Direction,
灵魂层面：觉醒于自身方向、
Uncovering the Ego Conspiracy, Birth of Commitment
揭露自我阴谋、承诺的诞生

SOUL—CENTERED RELATIONSHIP
以灵魂为中心的关系
Revelation, The First Guardian on the Threshold, Discernment,
启示，门槛上的第一位守护者，辨别力，
Beginning of Emotional, Mental and Personality Integrations,
情感、心理和人格整合的开始，
Conscious Loving Relationship, Purpose Life Work, Vision
有意识的爱的关系，人生目标，愿景

Of course it is possible that a person could go through the first three levels of relationship without being aware of the actual progress that takes place on a Soul level—I know this from first-hand experience. You can endure most of the harmful aspects, while enjoying very few loving ones, should you be unwilling to take responsibility for your life. And even if you take advantage of the opportunities in the previous stages, this does not guarantee that you will make it successfully through the next one—although it does increase your chances. 46 The maturity and awareness you gain by mastering communication and responding to your pain peacefully in the Disillusionment Stage will be of immeasurable assistance to you in the Introspection Stage, but there are elements of Introspection that are unique to this stage alone, for here the internal life of relationship begins in earnest.

当然，一个人有可能在经历关系的前三个阶段后，仍然没有意识到灵魂层面上的实际进展——我对此深有体会。如果你不愿意为自己的人生负责，你或许能够忍受大部分有害的方面，却只能享受到极少的美好。即使你充分利用了前几个阶段的机会，这也不能保证你能够顺利度过下一个阶段——尽管这确实会增加你成功的几率。<sup>46</sup> 在幻灭阶段，你通过掌握沟通技巧并以平和的方式应对痛苦而获得的成熟和觉察，将在内省阶段为你提供莫大的帮助。但内省阶段也包含一些独有的元素，因为在这个阶段，关系的内在生活才真正开始。

As difficult as it was for me to change my old mindsets—from the idea that there were good guys and bad guys, 47 that there was an absolute right and absolute wrong, 48 and that marriage was a fifty-fifty proposition 49 —I became convinced that there was no way I could be happy in my relationships unless I committed to being 100% accountable for everything I perceived in them. And I could not fulfill that commitment to accountability if I were unwilling to face everything that was inside me.

尽管改变我原有的思维模式——比如认为世间有好人和坏人<sup>47</sup>、有绝对的对错<sup>48</sup>以及婚姻是双方各占一半<sup>49</sup>——对我来说十分困难，但我最终确信，除非我承诺对我在感情关系中感知到的一切负起百分之百的责任，否则我不可能在感情关系中获得幸福。而如果我不愿意面对自己内心的一切，我就无法履行这份责任。

Introspection is the act of looking inward to examine all of one’s thoughts and feelings with the ultimate goal of being at peace with—and loving—everything inside you. In the process you also discover the roadblocks to happiness, such as the good guy/bad guy, right/wrong, and fifty/fifty modes of thinking. Without a commitment to Introspection, the negative aspects of your split mind will be thrown outside into the realm of relationship. Your partner inevitably assumes the facets of your “ugliness.” Your choice then becomes whether you will avoid that ugliness, attempt to destroy it, or remove it from your life (by removing you-know-who!). One thing is certain—it will be very hard to truly love the ugliness without accepting it as yours, for you cannot love anything while keeping it separate from you.

内省是指向内审视自己的所有想法和感受，最终目标是与内心的一切和解，并爱上它们。在这个过程中，你也会发现通往幸福的障碍，例如好人/坏人、对/错以及五五开的思维模式。如果不进行内省，你分裂思维中的负面因素就会被抛入人际关系中。你的伴侣不可避免地会承受你“丑陋”的一面。这时，你的选择就变成了：是逃避这些丑陋，试图摧毁它们，还是将它们从你的生活中移除（通过移除你懂的那个人！）。有一点是肯定的——如果你不接受丑陋是你的，就很难真正爱它，因为你无法在将任何事物与你割裂开来的同时去爱它。

The honest examination of your inner reality you see reflected in your partner will help you to come to a true and peaceful understanding of yourself. Although what you find within you may at first be terribly unattractive, you will also be blessed with the opportunity to see that there is nothing within you that cannot be accepted. And in the acceptance, what you once saw as ugly will itself become love. 100% personal accountability will not only help resurrect a dead relationship, it will resurrect the parts of you that you thought were dead, or never realized had existed.

诚实地审视你内心深处的真实自我，你会发现它反映在你的伴侣身上，这将帮助你真正平和地了解自己。虽然你最初可能会发现一些令你难以接受的自我，但你也将有幸看到，你内心深处没有什么是不能被接纳的。在接纳的过程中，你曾经视为丑陋的部分，最终会转化为爱。百分之百的自我负责不仅能帮助挽救一段濒临破裂的关系，还能唤醒你内心那些你以为已经消亡，或者从未意识到其存在的部分。

Let’s get back to the old myth that relationships are a fifty/fifty proposition. You cannot have a fifty/fifty relationship, because it implies only a fifty percent commitment on your part, meaning you are committed to the relationship half of the time. You cannot be completely committed fifty percent of the time. If you believe that you are only responsible for fifty percent of the relationship, you will only be giving half of what you are capable of giving. Since everything you see is a projection, you will perceive that your partner is only giving half of what s/he can give, while both of you simultaneously insist that you are doing your share and accuse the other of holding back.

让我们回到那个老生常谈的误区：恋爱关系应该是五五开的。五五开的关系是不可能的，因为它意味着你只投入了百分之五十的精力，也就是说你只在一半的时间里投入其中。你不可能在百分之五十的时间里都全身心投入。如果你认为自己只对这段关系负有百分之五十的责任，那么你只会付出你能力的一半。由于你所看到的一切都是投射，你会觉得你的伴侣只付出了对方能力的一半，而你们双方却同时坚持自己已经尽到了应尽的责任，并指责对方有所保留。

At the Introspection Stage, an opportunity surfaces for you to realize that you and your partner are connected on a fundamental level of being, and you can understand that the manner in which you treat your partner is actually how you are treating yourself. Thus an imperative emerges, requiring you to accept and integrate your shadow side, give up competition and offer support, give sincere encouragement when your mate is feeling inadequate, become a discerning influence rather than a prosecutorial or indiscriminate one, choose empowerment over pity, and join your partner in the emptiness that is at the center of the human condition. The Introspection stage brings home the message, in words made from stardust, 50 that whatever you give to your partner you are giving to yourself. Once you have entered this stage, it is likely that your entrance will be heralded by the experience of the most debilitating form of misguided behaviours...

在内省阶段，你将有机会意识到你和伴侣在根本层面上是相连的，并明白你对待伴侣的方式实际上就是你对待自己的方式。因此，一种迫切的需求油然而生：你需要接纳并整合自身的阴暗面，放弃竞争，转而提供支持；当伴侣感到力不从心时，给予真诚的鼓励；成为一个有洞察力的引导者，而非一个指责或不加区分的引导者；选择赋能而非怜悯；并与伴侣一同面对人类境况核心的空虚。内省阶段以星尘般的语言，50 传递着一个深刻的信息：你给予伴侣的一切，最终都会给予你自己。一旦你进入这个阶段，很可能你会经历一些最令人痛苦的错误行为……

***

ASSUMED INADEQUACY

假定不足

———————————

“Nobody minds. Nobody cares. Pathetic, that’s what it is.”

“没人介意。没人关心。真可悲。”

—Eeyore, when everyone forgot his birthday. “Winnie-the-Pooh,” by A. A. Milne

——屹耳，当大家都忘了他的生日时。《小熊维尼》，A·A·米尔恩著

There are two basic ways to travel the path of relationship. We can either (1) pursue our needs endlessly, manipulating others when we have to, taking what we can get when we can get it, and compromising when all else fails, or (2) we can learn about who we are by letting go of expectations, communicating to reach a mutually fulfilling resolution, and constantly choosing happiness for our partners and ourselves equally. Most of us move back and forth between these approaches. If, however, we get caught on the downward-spiralling path of a relationship oriented towards personal need—creating demands on our partners, fighting, manipulating, etc.—the need will not be satisfied, and a sense of discouragement is bound to grow. Ultimately this leads to the pattern of behaviour known as Assumed Inadequacy.

处理人际关系主要有两种方式。我们可以选择（1）无休止地追求自身需求，必要时操纵他人，能得到什么就得到什么，万不得已就妥协；或者（2）放下期待，通过沟通达成双方都满意的解决方案，并始终平等地为伴侣和自己选择幸福，从而更好地了解自己。大多数人会在这两种方式之间摇摆不定。然而，如果我们陷入以个人需求为导向的恶性循环——对伴侣提出要求、争吵、操纵等等——那么需求将无法得到满足，沮丧感也必然会与日俱增。最终，这会导致一种被称为“假定不足”的行为模式。

If, in your childhood, you faced so much discouragement that you decided it was no use trying to get your needs met from the person or people around you, you might have chosen to simply give up. From that point on you assumed that all your efforts would ultimately come to naught, so why bother trying to get attention, recognition, invitations to join in...why bother trying to be loved? Might as well give up and hope that everyone will just leave you alone. How much Assumed Inadequacy you had to deal with all depends on the type of person you are.

如果你童年时期遭遇了太多挫折，以至于你觉得从身边的人那里获得满足毫无意义，你或许会选择彻底放弃。从那时起，你便认定自己所有的努力最终都会徒劳无功，那么何必费心去争取关注、认可、参与的邀请……何必费心去渴望被爱呢？不如就此放弃，祈祷所有人都能放过你。你所经历的“自我否定”程度，完全取决于你是怎样的人。

Naturally you developed coping mechanisms to deal with this heartbreak, or else you probably would have succumbed to some debilitating mental, emotional, or physical sickness. By emotionally distancing yourself from the people who did not meet your needs, you managed to survive. Paving over the traumas with denial and forgetfulness, you picked yourself up and adjusted to a world that seemed to promise that you could have what you needed if you found the right person or people to give it to you. Perhaps you tried to earn it through some astounding achievement, or worked really, really hard for it. When you transitioned into adolescence, you may have turned to your peer group for a sense of significance. As a young adult perhaps you sought importance and belonging in a romantic relationship with a potential life partner, or sought for your importance in a career.

你自然而然地发展出应对这种心碎的机制，否则你很可能早已被某种严重的精神、情感或身体疾病所击垮。通过与那些无法满足你需求的人保持情感上的距离，你得以生存下来。你用否认和遗忘掩盖创伤，重新振作起来，适应着这个世界——这个世界似乎承诺，只要找到合适的人，你就能得到你想要的一切。或许你曾试图通过惊人的成就来赢得它，或者为此付出了巨大的努力。进入青春期后，你可能转向同龄群体寻求价值感。成年后，你或许在与潜在伴侣的恋爱关系中寻求重要性和归属感，或者在事业中寻求价值。

Whatever avenue you chose, there is a good chance that sooner or later, you found yourself on the verge of facing that old experience of wanting to give up on your chosen source of love altogether. Almost all people see terminating a physical situation as a wise, even life-saving, approach when the overwhelming sense of inadequacy threatens to drown them. Nowhere is this idea more powerful than in the area of intimate relationships. This is because such relationships always have the tendency to draw you back to the deepest life experiences available to you at the time. The closer you get to your partner, the greater the potential to awaken the feelings of inadequacy you experienced as a child when you came to believe that you were not important enough to be loved by Mom, Dad, or other family members.

无论你选择哪条路，你都很有可能迟早会再次面临那种想要彻底放弃你所选择的爱情来源的念头。几乎所有人都认为，当强烈的自卑感几乎将自己淹没时，结束一段肉体关系是一种明智之举，甚至是救命之举。这种想法在亲密关系中尤为强烈。这是因为亲密关系总是倾向于将你拉回到当时你所能体验到的最深刻的人生经历。你与伴侣越亲近，就越有可能唤醒你童年时期那种自卑感——那时你觉得自己不够重要，不值得被父母或其他家人爱。

In many relationships, the attempts to reach fulfilment through the significant other are ultimately met with a sense of failure, and with it a feeling of supreme discouragement. The warmth of love and acceptance is perhaps lacking. Words that are exchanged—even by those who practice heartfelt communication—might seem lifeless and ineffectual. A fog of confusion permeates the air, and a sense of direction is lost or confounded. At such times, a thought could sneak into your mind that you might have never really believed you would hear yourself saying: “Maybe it’s over.”

在许多关系中，试图通过伴侣获得满足感的努力最终都以失败告终，随之而来的是深深的沮丧。爱与接纳的温暖或许已经缺失。即使是那些真心沟通的人，彼此的言语也可能显得苍白无力。迷茫和困惑弥漫，方向感迷失或困惑。在这样的时刻，一个念头可能会悄悄溜进你的脑海，你或许从未想过自己会说出这样的话：“也许一切都结束了。”

I have heard that disheartening voice a number of times when my wife and I hit a seemingly impermeable wall. Sooner or later we were led through it to a better place, but the next time we hit that wall, the voice sounded even more convincing and the supreme discouragement and inadequacy felt more real. That is because every time one clears a level of inadequacy and discouragement, one is better prepared to face the next, even deeper and more hurtful one a little further down the road. 51

我和妻子遇到看似无法逾越的障碍时，曾多次听到那令人沮丧的声音。迟早我们会突破这道障碍，走向更好的未来，但下一次再遇到同样的障碍时，那声音听起来更加令人信服，那种极度的沮丧和无力感也更加真实。这是因为，每当一个人克服了一层无力感和沮丧，他就能更好地应对未来道路上更深、更痛苦的挑战。<sup>51</sup>

The experience of wanting to give up due to a sense of failure and inadequacy in your relationship is a strong indicator that the phase of Introspection has begun. It is a time of great unraveling, where idols and ideals fall, doubts increase, and fantasies dissolve. The degree to which you made your partner your personal supplier of need fulfillment is the degree to which you will be tempted to come to the conclusion that you either chose the wrong partner, or the flame is simply out—and that either way, it’s time to go somewhere else.

在一段感情中，如果因为感到失败和无力而想要放弃，这强烈表明你已经进入了反思阶段。这是一个彻底瓦解的时期，偶像和理想会崩塌，疑虑会加剧，幻想会破灭。你越是把伴侣当作满足自身需求的来源，就越容易得出这样的结论：要么是你选错了人，要么是感情的火花已经熄灭——无论哪种情况，你都觉得是时候另寻新欢了。

The degree to which you have chosen to see your relationship as a learning path to unconditional love is the degree to which the grace that follows such commitments can support you through the “impossible situations,” to an experience of greater joy and intimacy. And some of the situations at this point will seem impossible. The subconscious traps may seem endless, and all your efforts futile. To get through these seemingly impenetrable blocks, one must learn the art of....

你选择将这段关系视为通往无条件之爱的学习之路的程度，决定了伴随这种承诺而来的恩典能在多大程度上支持你度过“不可能的困境”，最终体验到更大的喜悦和亲密。而此时此刻，有些困境看似无解。潜意识的陷阱似乎无穷无尽，你所有的努力似乎都徒劳无功。要突破这些看似无法逾越的障碍，你必须学会……

***

WALKING THROUGH WALLS

穿墙而过

———————————

“Stone walls do not a prison make, / nor iron bars a cage.”

“石墙不能筑成监狱，铁栏杆也不能囚禁牢笼。”

—From the poem “To Althea in Prison,” by Richard Lovelace

——摘自理查德·洛夫莱斯的诗作《致狱中的阿尔西娅》

The first time my marriage hit this stage, I began to seriously question whether relationships were purposely designed to fail. Despite the remarkable strides Su Mei and I had made in love, intimacy, trust, and respect, tendency for the relationship to become static seemed to keep creeping back. Routines and subconscious habits, along with the predisposition to avoid uncomfortable confrontations, kept attempting to drive a wedge of separation between us (at the time I knew many couples that did not avoid the uncomfortable confrontations, but engaged in them because a Power Struggle had more life to it than the deadly stagnation of the wall). Finally I found my face pressed so tightly up against this seemingly immovable barrier of separation between myself and my partner that I had to consider the possibilities that either relationships just weren’t meant to last forever, I was with the wrong person, or else there was something I had better learn—and quick!

我的婚姻第一次走到这一步时，我开始认真地质疑，是不是婚姻注定要失败。尽管我和苏梅在爱、亲密、信任和尊重方面取得了显著的进步，但关系停滞不前的趋势似乎总是悄然袭来。惯性思维和潜意识的习惯，以及回避尴尬冲突的倾向，不断地在我们之间筑起一道隔阂（当时我认识很多夫妻，他们并不回避尴尬的冲突，反而积极应对，因为权力斗争比死气沉沉的僵局更有活力）。最终，我发现自己紧紧贴着这道看似坚不可摧的隔阂，不得不考虑各种可能性：要么婚姻注定无法长久，要么我选错了人，要么我必须尽快学习一些重要的知识！

It was no use looking to my parents’ relationship for guidance. They did their best considering the poverty, the eight kids to take care of, the physical separation of World War 2, the social and religious pressures of the time, and the problems around alcoholism. Taking all these factors into account, my parents did an incredible job of staying together, but I wonder if they ever made it past the wall. I do recall that there came a time when they hardly spoke to each other, and no longer slept in the same room.

从父母的关系中寻求指导毫无意义。考虑到贫困、要养活八个孩子、二战造成的地理隔离、当时的社会和宗教压力，以及酗酒问题，他们已经尽力了。考虑到所有这些因素，我的父母能够维持婚姻关系实属不易，但我怀疑他们是否真正克服了婚姻中的“隔阂”。我记得，后来他们几乎不再说话，也不再睡在同一个房间。

A few years back I read a newspaper article which stated that the greatest secret shame in North American marriages was how many married couples slept in different rooms. 52 I took some perverse comfort from that article, grateful that, although my wife and I had problems, we weren’t that badly off. This small comfort did not last long, when I realized that unless I somehow overcame the inertia, and the desire to give up, my pride would not save our relationship. I had to answer some very important questions. Why is it so difficult to keep growing closer in a relationship? Why do I keep getting stuck, with the accompanying feeling of failure? How do I break through, past the wall?

几年前，我读到一篇报纸文章，文章指出北美婚姻中最大的秘密耻辱是许多夫妻分房睡。<sup>52</sup> 这篇文章让我感到一丝扭曲的安慰，庆幸虽然我和妻子之间存在问题，但我们的处境还不算太糟。然而，这种小小的安慰并没有持续多久，我意识到，除非我能克服惰性和放弃的念头，否则我的自尊心无法挽救我们的关系。我必须回答一些非常重要的问题：为什么维系一段关系如此艰难？为什么我总是陷入困境，并伴随着失败感？我该如何突破这道阻碍？

You might experience the stagnation of this relationship stage in any number of ways in your personal relationships, as well as in your work, creative endeavours, spiritual practice, or general sense of yourself. Some of the symptoms of “life at the wall” are: 53

你可能会在人际关系、工作、创作、灵修或自我认知等诸多方面感受到这种关系阶段的停滞。一些“人生停滞不前”的症状包括：53

• an intangible malaise

• 一种无形的不适

• boredom

• 无聊

• tiredness: emotional, mental, or physical.

• 疲劳：情绪上的、精神上的或身体上的。

• illness

• 疾病

• confusion or lack of focus

• 混乱或注意力不集中

• disinterest in most things, especially each other

• 对大多数事物漠不关心，尤其是彼此。

• a tendency to overindulge in mindless entertainment or pleasuring of the body

• 过度沉迷于无意义的娱乐或身体享乐的倾向

• advanced addictive behaviour

• 高级成瘾行为

• extensive fantasizing or daydreaming

• 过度沉浸于幻想或白日梦

• deadness in your sexual life 54 (including sexual dysfunctions)

• 性生活乏味54（包括性功能障碍）

• a depressing sense of unworthiness

• 一种令人沮丧的无价值感

• a repulsion towards your partner or a feeling that your partner finds you repulsive

• 对伴侣感到厌恶，或者觉得伴侣觉得你令人厌恶。

• an affair or a triangle relationship

•婚外情或三角关系

• a desire to quit, give up, or even die

• 想要放弃、退出甚至死亡的念头

• depression, loss of passion for life, the sense that you or the relationship are burnt out

• 抑郁、对生活失去热情、感觉自己或这段关系已经精疲力竭

• busyness—your partner’s or your own, which allows both of you to conveniently avoid spending time together

• 忙碌——无论是伴侣的忙碌还是你自己的忙碌，都让你们双方都能巧妙地避免相处。

• a sense of Assumed Inadequacy—that nothing you do will make any difference

• 一种无力感——认为自己做什么都无济于事。

• one of you files for divorce

• 你们其中一人提出离婚

• one of you tries to kill the other

• 你们其中一人试图杀死另一人

There is no doubt about it—life can become very difficult at the wall stage of Introspection, but it seems that we human beings have a propensity for further aggravating the discomfort by reacting to what is happening in the most unhealthy way. One of the key reasons for this unhealthy reaction is that, when someone runs up against the wall, they tend to believe there is something incurably wrong with the relationship. It is usually at this time that a client will tell me s/he made a mistake in marrying his/her partner in the first place. Some of the explanations that come out are:

毫无疑问，在内省的“碰壁”阶段，生活会变得异常艰难。但我们人类似乎有一种倾向，那就是以最不健康的方式应对现状，从而加剧这种不适感。造成这种不健康反应的关键原因之一是，当人们碰壁时，往往会认为这段关系存在无法挽回的问题。通常，正是在这个时候，我的客户会告诉我，他们当初结婚是个错误。他们给出的一些解释包括：

• “I never really loved him, not even when we first met.”

“我从来没有真正爱过他，甚至在我们初次见面的时候也没有。”

• “I just married her because I was tired of the dating scene.”

• “我娶她只是因为我厌倦了约会。”

• “I thought he was more passionate than he actually is.”

• “我原以为他比实际更有热情。”

• “We got married for all the wrong reasons.”

• “我们结婚的理由完全错误。”

• “She caught me on the rebound; I’m still in love with someone else.”

“她趁我失恋的空窗期抓到了我；我仍然爱着别人。”

• “I thought he would change once he settled down with me.”

“我以为他跟我安定下来后就会改变。”

• “She tricked me into marrying her.”

• “她骗我娶了她。”

• “We were too young to get married.”

“我们当时年纪太小，不适合结婚。”

• “Our parents pushed us into it.”

“是父母逼我们这么做的。”

• “Nobody else wanted me—she was the best I could do.”

“没有人想要我——她是我能找到的最好的人。”

• “I just wanted to get away from my family—I didn’t care who got me out.”

• “我只想逃离我的家人——我不在乎是谁救我出去。”

However the retrospectives are worded, the message is always the same, i.e.: it was a mistake—we really shouldn’t have gotten married in the first place. Of course not everyone second-guesses their motives for getting involved with a significant other. Other people do not regret getting married, but are simply dissatisfied with the state of the present relationship, their complaints sounding more like this:

无论这些回顾的措辞如何，传递的信息总是相同的，那就是：结婚是个错误——我们当初真不该结婚。当然，并非每个人都会质疑自己当初与伴侣结合的动机。有些人并不后悔结婚，只是对目前的婚姻状况不满，他们的抱怨听起来更像是这样：

• “I just don’t love him anymore.”

“我已经不再爱他了。”

• “There’s no spark left between us.”

• “我们之间已经没有火花了。”

• “It’s like living with my mother!”

“感觉就像和妈妈住在一起一样！”

• “We don’t do anything together. He reads all the time and I watch TV.”

• “我们俩什么都不一起做。他总是看书，我则看电视。”

• “I feel like I married my father.”

“我觉得我嫁给了我父亲。”

• “Our relationship is so claustrophobic—I can’t breathe.”

• “我们的关系太令人窒息了——我简直无法呼吸。”

• “We don’t know how to talk to each other anymore.”

• “我们已经不知道该如何沟通了。”

• “I’m just tired of always being the one that’s sacrificing!”

• “我只是厌倦了总是做牺牲的那个人！”

• “She’s not the same woman I married.”

• “她已经不是我娶的那个女人了。”

• “Hey! Where’s the sex?”

• “嘿！性爱呢？”

• “The fire’s out—I guess it’s time to move on.”

• “火已经扑灭了——我想是时候继续前进了。”

• “What happened? Where did we go wrong?”

• “发生了什么事？我们哪里做错了？”

From the list above you can get a sense of the deep disappointment, frustration, and/or lethargy that permeates a relationship once it hits the wall. Regardless of how animated and alive each partner might seem in social situations such as parties, work, or at various get-togethers, it is their interactions in private that really determines how stuck the relationship is. Inertia, stagnation, deadness, disinterest, or burnout are the most common signals that the relationship has hit the wall, and a process of introspection—or “soul searching”—must begin in order to give it a chance to keep growing.

从以上列举可以看出，一旦感情走到尽头，就会弥漫着深深的失望、沮丧和/或倦怠。无论伴侣在聚会、工作或各种社交场合中看起来多么神采奕奕，真正决定这段感情是否陷入僵局的，是他们在私下的互动。惰性、停滞、麻木、冷漠或倦怠是感情走到尽头最常见的信号，此时必须开始反思——或者说“灵魂拷问”——才能让这段感情有机会继续发展。

If you find yourself in this situation, please be careful how you respond. It may not seem like it, but the presence of this deadness is actually an indication that your life is about to take a drastic turn for the better. I spent a lot of years with my face pressed up against the wall—in relationships, work situations, friendships, and my personal development—and have become intimately acquainted with the bricks and mortar of this challenging human obstacle. I have discovered that there is always a choice to be made that determines the length of my stay in the shadow of the wall.

如果你发现自己身处这种境地，请务必谨慎应对。或许你感觉不到，但这种死气沉沉的状态实际上预示着你的生活即将迎来翻天覆地的转机。我曾多年感到寸步难行——无论是在人际关系、工作、友谊，还是个人发展方面——我对这种人生困境的根源早已了然于心。我发现，我总能做出一个选择，而这个选择将决定我在这堵墙的阴影下停留多久。

I always felt that I had a choice: stay and suffer, or get the hell out of the situation—run, boy! Run! Finally I learned that I did not have to keep leaving my relationship, quitting my job, or escaping the situation that I felt inhibited me from moving ahead. There was a way through, and that way was in the power of a choice that lay beyond the “either/or” dilemma I was caught in. To understand this choice better, it is of value to get a good look at what this wall really is. I have another name for it, which I call...

我一直觉得我只有两个选择：要么留下忍受痛苦，要么赶紧逃离——快跑，快跑！最终我明白，我不必总是离开这段感情，辞掉工作，或者逃离那些让我感觉阻碍我前进的困境。其实有一条出路，那就是超越我之前深陷的“非此即彼”困境的选择权。为了更好地理解这个选择，我们需要仔细审视一下这堵墙究竟是什么。我给它起了另一个名字，我称之为……

***

THE VICTIM PRISON

受害者监狱

———————————

“Come, let’s away to prison. We two alone will sing like birds I’ th’ cage.”

“来吧，我们一起去监狱。我们两个会像笼中鸟一样歌唱。”

—Shakespeare, King Lear

——莎士比亚，《李尔王》

Personally, the word “victim” makes me uncomfortable. It conjures up images of weakness, helplessness and fear, none of which I enjoy admitting that I have inside me. 55 However it is the most accurate word I can find to describe what keeps people locked into situations which, to an outside observer, might seem easy to resolve. When you are stuck in a problem, you are confined to only three positions from which to view your situation. Stephen Karpman designed a simple model called the Drama Triangle. 56

就我个人而言，“受害者”这个词让我感到不舒服。它让我联想到软弱、无助和恐惧，而我并不愿意承认自己内心深处存在这些感受。<sup>55</sup> 然而，它是我能找到的最准确的词，用来描述是什么让人们深陷困境，而这些困境在外人看来似乎很容易解决。当你身处困境时，你只能从三个角度来看待你的处境。斯蒂芬·卡普曼设计了一个简单的模型，叫做“戏剧三角”。<sup>56</sup>

When confronted with a problem, the first position you are likely to take—if even for only a few seconds—is that of the Victim. The Victim must struggle against a larger force than her/himself, with little or no chance of succeeding unless some bigger external force “miraculously” joins the Victim’s side. A Victim often feels overwhelmed by the problem, sometimes even incapacitated by it to the point of paralysis.

面对问题时，你最先采取的立场——哪怕只有短短几秒钟——很可能是受害者的立场。受害者必须与远超自身的力量抗争，除非有更强大的外力“奇迹般地”加入其阵营，否则几乎没有成功的可能。受害者常常感到被问题压得喘不过气来，有时甚至会因此而丧失行动能力，陷入瘫痪。

Other experiences that can indicate to you that you are feeling victimized are fear, self-pity, depression, frustration, indulgence in suffering, a tendency to complain, or a sense that you are being scapegoated—unfairly punished for a wrong you never committed. More aspects of the Victim are described on the chart.

其他可能表明你感到自己是受害者的经历包括：恐惧、自怜、抑郁、沮丧、沉溺于痛苦、抱怨的倾向，或者觉得自己成了替罪羊——因为从未犯过的错误而受到不公平的惩罚。图表中描述了受害者心态的更多方面。

Being a Victim is no fun at all. To stay in that position for any length of time would cause you to fear being further exposed to unfair treatment, punishment and other forms of victimization. After all, what else could a victim expect in life other than being victimized?

当受害者一点也不好玩。长时间处于这种境地会让你害怕遭受进一步的不公平待遇、惩罚和其他形式的伤害。毕竟，除了被伤害，受害者还能指望什么呢？

Thus the coping mechanism in the human ego drives you to find a better position from which to deal with your problem. The Persecutor is born out of this decision. Fuelled by blame, righteous superiority, and a compulsion for perfection, the Persecutor angrily seeks to escape suffering by making the problem someone else’s fault. If you can find someone else to blame, then you might get away with this approach—for a while, anyway. You see this happen a lot at sporting events. Whichever team is losing (Victim) usually becomes the angry team (Persecutor). 57 You will see them blaming the referees for making bad calls, attacking whatever player on the other team is “cheating” in their eyes, or criticizing their own team members for their perceived mistakes. In the end however, each member of the losing team must look up at the scoreboard and carry the burden of defeat on his/her shoulders into the locker room. Once in there, the Persecutor turns its attention inside, and the player starts blaming him/herself for not being “good enough” to carry the team to victory. 58

因此，人类自我中的应对机制驱使你寻找一个更好的角度来处理问题。迫害者正是在这种决定下产生的。迫害者受责备、自以为是和完美主义的驱使，愤怒地试图通过将问题归咎于他人来逃避痛苦。如果你能找到替罪羊，那么你或许可以侥幸逃脱惩罚——至少暂时如此。这种情况在体育赛事中屡见不鲜。通常情况下，输球的一方（受害者）会变成愤怒的一方（迫害者）。你会看到他们指责裁判误判，攻击对方球员在他们眼中“作弊”，或者批评自己队友的失误。然而最终，输球一方的每个成员都必须抬头看着记分牌，背负着失败的重担走进更衣室。一旦进入那种状态，迫害者的注意力就会转移到玩家自身，玩家会开始责怪自己不够“优秀”，无法带领团队取得胜利。58

Now why would you want to persecute yourself? Simply because when you run out of other people to accuse and blame, persecuting yourself allows you to maintain a safe distance from the experience of misery that you would feel as a Victim. Have you ever smacked yourself in the face or head when you made a mistake? Ever call yourself stupid, or verbally chastise yourself for some slip-up? That is the Persecutor rising up to suppress the Victim experience, and forcing you to do better. The perfectionist inside the Persecutor figures that it is the Victim’s imperfection that is the cause of all the misery. Anger allows you to deny any painful feelings, forcing the Victim in you to get up and keep trying to do better. Persecutors use self-righteousness to pump themselves up in an attempt to distance themselves from the weakness of the Victim.

那么，你为什么要自我迫害呢？原因很简单，当你找不到其他人可以指责和责备时，自我迫害能让你与作为受害者所感受到的痛苦保持安全距离。你犯错时有没有拍打过自己的脸或脑袋？有没有骂自己笨，或者因为一些小失误而责备自己？这就是迫害者在作祟，它试图压制受害者的体验，并强迫你做得更好。迫害者内心的完美主义者认为，受害者的不完美才是所有痛苦的根源。愤怒让你否认任何痛苦的感受，迫使你内心的受害者振作起来，继续努力做得更好。迫害者利用自以为是来激励自己，试图与受害者的软弱划清界限。

But still you are miserable, and although some people do not seem to mind living in a state of perpetual anger and critical perfectionism, most of us want to experience something a little nicer. That is where the Rescuer comes in. Image you had a sore shoulder; what is the first thing you do? Probably you try to reach the sore spot with your hand and start rubbing it. If it is really sore, you might try to find someone to massage it for you. You may also make an appointment with a professional masseuse, a chiropractor, a physiotherapist, or a doctor. Without knowing what actually caused the sore shoulder, you would try to fix it. While you are trying to fix it, of course, you might occasionally indulge in the odd complaint or two (Victim), and even get angry at possible causes such as the softness of the damn pillow or mattress (Persecutor). But your main goal will be to fix it (Rescuer), because you want the pain to go away—even if you never find out what caused it.

但你仍然感到痛苦，虽然有些人似乎并不介意生活在持续的愤怒和苛求完美的状态中，但我们大多数人都渴望体验一些更美好的事物。这时，“拯救者”就派上了用场。想象一下，你的肩膀疼，你会做的第一件事是什么？你可能会用手去按压疼痛的部位，开始揉搓。如果真的很疼，你可能会找人帮你按摩。你也可能预约专业的按摩师、脊椎按摩师、理疗师或医生。即使不知道肩膀疼痛的真正原因，你也会尝试去解决它。当然，在尝试解决的过程中，你偶尔可能会抱怨一两句（受害者），甚至会对一些可能的原因感到愤怒，比如该死的枕头或床垫太软（迫害者）。但你的主要目标仍然是解决问题（拯救者），因为你想让疼痛消失——即使你永远也找不到疼痛的真正原因。

The Rescuer is that part of us that strives to place us in an ideal state where there is no pain, and where problems do not exist. At its most positive it tends to pity the Victim as well as the Persecutor, offering nurturing and helpful advice. Self-sacrificing in its benevolent superiority, the Rescuer is always “there for you,” and never seems to have problems of its own. Using analysis, careful planning, tolerance and an air of moral superiority, the Rescuer will pick the Victim up and carry it forward, certain in its optimism that the Victim will one day walk on its own two feet again! It will constantly seek to appease the Persecutor’s anger and dissatisfaction. Most people fail to see that it is the Rescuer’s very attitude that keeps the Victim weak and helpless, and acts as an enabler for the Persecutor’s temperamental indulgences, as well as the Victim’s stuckness . Their continued existence sustains the Rescuer’s purpose for being.

“拯救者”是我们内心深处努力将我们置于理想状态的那一部分，在那里没有痛苦，也没有问题。在它最积极的时候，它往往会怜悯受害者和迫害者，提供关怀和有益的建议。出于仁慈的优越感，拯救者总是“为你着想”，而且似乎自身没有任何问题。它运用分析、周密的计划、宽容和一种道德优越感，将受害者扶起并带走，坚信受害者终有一天会重新站起来！它会不断地试图平息迫害者的愤怒和不满。大多数人没有意识到，正是拯救者的这种态度让受害者变得软弱无助，助长了迫害者的任性妄为，也让受害者深陷困境。他们的持续存在维系着救援者的存在意义。

When a problem enters your life, you might find yourself jumping from position to position in the Victim Prison, w hile enlisting the help of other people in your life to occupy the vacant corners. Sometimes you will jump from one corner to the other, and have a second and maybe even a third person jumping about as well. However it manifests, you will typically experience this prison’s three aspects from within you, or else see it projected outside of you. For instance, one morning I woke up with a very sore shoulder (problem). I got out of bed and complained to myself about how much it hurt (Victim). On my way to the shower, I got mad at my body for letting me down like that (Persecutor), and started to viciously massage my shoulder (Persecutor/Rescuer). After the shower, during which I focused a lot of time on having the warm water soothe my back (Rescuer), 59 I sat on the bed and complained (Victim) to my wife. Su Mei knelt behind me and massaged it (now, Su Mei is my Rescuer), and said the bed was too soft (Persecutor), and that we should get a new one (Rescuer). Afterwards, I phoned a couple of professional Rescuers—a masseuse and a chiropractor, and spent the next month being soothed and advised by them, allowing myself to stay in my Victim corner. But at least I was a sincere Victim! I was paying attention to my body and giving it the care I thought it needed, which included Tylenol and muscle relaxants (Rescuers), and more visits to the professionals. One herbal doctor gently criticized me (Rescuer/Persecutor) for exercising too hard, and not eating enough brown rice. 60

当问题闯入你的生活时，你可能会发现自己在“受害者牢笼”中不断变换角色，同时寻求身边人的帮助来填补空缺。有时，你会从一个角落跳到另一个角落，甚至可能还有第二个人、第三个人也跟着一起跳来跳去。无论以何种形式出现，你通常都会从内心深处体验到这个牢笼的三种面向，或者看到它投射到你之外。例如，一天早上我醒来时肩膀非常疼痛（问题）。我起床后，一边抱怨疼痛难忍（受害者）。在去淋浴的路上，我对自己身体如此“不负责任”感到愤怒（迫害者），开始用力按摩肩膀（迫害者/拯救者）。淋浴后，我花了很多时间让温水舒缓背部（拯救者），然后坐在床上向妻子抱怨（受害者）。苏梅跪在我身后帮我按摩（现在，苏梅是我的救星），说床太软了（迫害者），我们应该换张新的（救星）。之后，我给几个专业的救星打了电话——一个按摩师和一个脊椎按摩师，接下来的一个月里，我都在接受他们的安抚和建议，让自己继续扮演受害者的角色。但至少我是一个真诚的受害者！我开始关注自己的身体，并给予它我认为需要的照顾，包括服用泰诺和肌肉松弛剂（救星），以及更多地去看专业人士。一位中医温和地批评我（救星/迫害者）运动过度，而且糙米吃得不够。<sup>60</sup>

Then one day I went to a physiotherapist who happened to have unusual intuitive abilities, and guess what she told me? She informed me that my problem was not with my shoulder—it was down in my gallbladder, which was affecting my shoulder by some weird connection of tissues and muscles. I visited this physiotherapist for two months while she worked on my gallbladder. After two months she informed me that she had done all she could, but as far as she could tell the source of the problem was emotional. She suggested that I see a counsellor. “Wait a minute,” I thought to myself, “ I’m a counsellor!” After four months of this sore shoulder, I was brought back to myself. Here I was just wanting my body to be fixed, and all along my body was trying to get me to listen to it—it had something important to tell me and the pain was its way of getting my attention! 61

有一天，我去看了一位理疗师，她碰巧拥有非凡的直觉能力。你猜她告诉我什么？她告诉我，我的问题不在于肩膀，而在于胆囊，胆囊通过某种奇怪的组织和肌肉连接影响了我的肩膀。我接受了这位理疗师两个月的治疗，她一直在帮我处理胆囊问题。两个月后，她告诉我她已经尽力了，但据她判断，问题的根源在于情绪。她建议我去看心理咨询师。“等等，”我心想，“我本身就是个心理咨询师！” 肩膀疼痛了四个月后，我终于清醒过来。我之前一直只想治好自己的身体，而实际上，我的身体一直在试图让我倾听它的声音——它有重要的事情要告诉我，而疼痛正是它引起我注意的方式！<sup>61</sup>

It is at the Introspection stage of relationships that you have the opportunity to clearly see problems as indicators of something far greater than simple pain and suffering. You are given the chance to step out of the Victim Prison and experience the essential you . The problem is that by the time you reach the Introspection stage, you are often burned out and distracted by running from corner to corner of the Prison. By this time you have projected it fully onto your relationship; in other words, you see the relationship as the prison.

在关系的内省阶段，你有机会清晰地看到问题，并意识到它们远不止是简单的痛苦和磨难。你有机会走出“受害者牢笼”，体验真正的自我。问题在于，当你真正进入内省阶段时，你往往已经精疲力竭，疲于奔命地在“受害者牢笼”中奔波。此时，你已经将这种状态完全投射到你的关系中；换句话说，你把这段关系本身视为牢笼。

At this point your Rescuer is typically burnt out, reflected by you or your partner being too tired and disappointed to give any more in order to “make the relationship work.” As soon as you look at each other, one of you might become the Persecutor, not being able to stand the sight of the other. Possibly one of you will turn to silent or verbal complaints (Victim) about the other’s lack of caring, passion, communication, or concern for the health of the partnership. There are other instances as well, where one is in so much denial of the existence of any real problems (Rescuer) that the other partner feels like s/he is being patronized, unheard, made unimportant or abandoned emotionally (Victim). This is also a time when one, or both, of you turns to others for solace (Rescuer).

此时，你的“拯救者”通常已经精疲力竭，表现为你或你的伴侣感到疲惫不堪、失望至极，无力再为“维系这段关系”付出更多。你们彼此对视时，其中一人可能就会变成“迫害者”，无法忍受对方的存在。或许你们中的一方会以沉默或言语的方式抱怨（受害者），指责对方缺乏关心、激情、沟通，或对这段关系的健康漠不关心。还有一些情况下，一方极力否认任何实际问题的存在（拯救者），以至于另一方感觉自己被轻视、被忽视、被轻视或被情感抛弃（受害者）。此时，你们中的一方或双方也可能寻求他人的慰藉（拯救者）。

The elements of the Victim Prison were present in the Glamour Stage, but the denial, so prevalent in romanticism, would have you ignore its presence. In the Disillusionment Stage, the Victim/Persecutor/Rescuer tendencies become more apparent, but you might rely more on your powers of manipulation to change the other person rather than take responsibility for your Victim Prison reactions to your partner’s behaviour. If this is the case, it often seems too late when you reach the Introspection Stage. You may be too embedded in unproductive habits and patterns of relating to each other, comfortably entrenched (or comfortably numb) in your corners of the Prison, and well on your way to being convinced that there is no way out except through separation. But there is often another way.

受害者牢笼的种种要素在迷恋阶段就已经存在，但浪漫主义中普遍存在的否认心理会让你忽略它的存在。到了幻灭阶段，受害者/迫害者/拯救者的倾向会更加明显，但你可能会更依赖操控能力去改变对方，而不是为自己因伴侣行为而产生的受害者牢笼式反应负责。如果真是如此，当你进入内省阶段时，往往感觉为时已晚。你可能已经深陷于无效的相处习惯和模式中，安然地（或者麻木地）待在牢笼的角落里，并且逐渐确信除了分离别无出路。但通常还有另一种选择。

I have experienced life beyond the walls of this Prison. I say this not as a Rescuer who has a formula. There is no formula for relationship because we are far too unique to follow one approach. There are, however, certain principles that can be adapted to each individual’s uniqueness. Some of these principles are:

我体验过监狱之外的生活。我这么说并非出于救世主的心态，也并非想提供一套固定的模式。人际关系没有固定的模式，因为我们每个人都太过独特，无法套用同一种方法。然而，有一些原则可以根据每个人的独特性进行调整。这些原则包括：

a) A problem cannot be solved within the boundaries of the problem itself.

a) 问题无法在问题本身的范围内得到解决。

b) All problems are gifts and lessons in disguise.

b) 所有的问题都是伪装的礼物和教训。

c) Everything you perceive is a projection of your inner reality.

c) 你所感知的一切都是你内在现实的投射。

d) Every human being has the power to be 100% responsible for what he or she experiences in this life.

d) 每个人都有能力对自己在生活中所经历的一切负起100%的责任。

e) Freedom does not come from answers. It comes from questions.

e) 自由并非来自答案，而是来自提问。

f) There is no problem so great that love cannot resolve it.

f) 没有爱解决不了的问题。

If you look at each of these principles you may discover, as I did, some of the fundamental mistakes you are prone to making when presented with a problem in your life:

如果你仔细审视这些原则，你可能会像我一样，发现自己在生活中遇到问题时容易犯的一些根本性错误：

a) A problem cannot be solved within the boundaries of the problem itself. Carl Jung often said that problems are not solved, but one simply outgrows them. Einstein said the same thing from the viewpoint of physics—a problem cannot be resolved from within the boundaries of itself. In the Rescuer role, you may think you can figure out the answer to any problem—but the Rescuer is actually just a part of the problem. As such, you will believe there really are Victims in the world who are incapable of growing beyond their limitations without outside help. This denies the very important possibility that every human being has everything they need within themselves Secondly, the Rescuer is a mere creation of the Victim. It is created in an attempt to avoid pain, feel important, and feel “good.” The Rescuer is a compensator for the negative aspects of the Persecutor and the Victim. Therefore the Rescuer was created in reaction to a problem, and is thus locked inside the problem. It will run around looking for answers, but will rely on old “knowledge,” and therefore become dependent on the past rather than the direction that is being offered in the present moment.

a) 问题无法在问题本身的范围内得到解决。卡尔·荣格常说，问题不会被解决，人们只是超越了它们。爱因斯坦从物理学的角度也表达了同样的观点——问题无法在自身的范围内得到解决。扮演“拯救者”的角色，你或许认为自己可以找到任何问题的答案——但实际上，“拯救者”本身就是问题的一部分。因此，你会相信世界上真的存在受害者，他们没有外力帮助就无法超越自身的局限。这否定了一个非常重要的可能性：每个人都拥有自身所需的一切。其次，“拯救者”仅仅是受害者创造出来的。它的产生是为了逃避痛苦、获得重要感和“良好”的感受。“拯救者”是对迫害者和受害者负面特质的一种补偿。因此，“拯救者”是对问题的回应，因而也被困在了问题之中。它会四处奔走寻找答案，但会依赖旧的“知识”，因此会依赖过去，而不是依赖当下所提供的方向。

An example comes from a time when I cut my thumb with a very sharp knife. Not knowing what to do, I relied on some old information I had received as a child: I stuck my thumb in my mouth and sucked the blood. Then I remembered that cold water would help, so I put my thumb under the tap and ran cold water over it. Both of these approaches are very bad for the kind of cut I had. 62 The best response would have been to apply pressure to the thumb just below, almost on the cut, but my Rescuer was unaware of this knowledge. Instead it looked to old information to try to fix the problem. Suddenly something inside me said I’d better ask for help. I called a neighbour who had Red Cross training. She arrived just before I fainted (I had cut a nerve), and applied the proper treatment. I had to reach out to a source of knowledge beyond mine in order to learn the correct response. So it is with all problems that hold us back. They hold us back because we are trying to find answers to them from a limited source of information, rather than turning to our imagination and intuition to lead us beyond the boundaries of the problem. People never grow because of what they already know—they grow because of what they come to learn.

举个例子，有一次我用一把很锋利的刀割伤了拇指。当时我不知道该怎么办，就凭着小时候学到的一些老方法：把拇指放进嘴里吸血。后来我又想起冷水可以止血，于是就把拇指放在水龙头下冲。但这两种方法对我的伤口来说都非常糟糕。<sup>62</sup> 最好的处理方法应该是按压伤口下方，几乎就在伤口处，但我的“救命恩人”并不知道这一点。它反而依靠老方法试图解决问题。突然，我内心有个声音告诉我最好寻求帮助。我打电话给一位接受过红十字会培训的邻居。她在我昏倒前赶到（我割伤了神经），并进行了正确的处理。我必须向自身知识之外的人寻求帮助，才能学会正确的处理方法。所有阻碍我们前进的问题都是如此。它们阻碍了我们前进，因为我们试图从有限的信息来源中寻找答案，而不是依靠想象力和直觉来超越问题的局限。人们的成长并非源于已知的知识，而是源于学习新知。

b) All problems are gifts and lessons in disguise. You may have noticed that every time you resolved a problem completely, you learned something of great value and your life was enriched in some significant way. Maybe you gained more confidence, learned to trust life more, became wiser, or discovered a significant gift or talent in yourself. When you did not receive (or appreciate) the gift, or learn the valuable lesson, it was probably because you did not let go of something the problem caused you to lose (this is often true of people who have lost loved ones). 63

b) 所有的问题都是伪装的礼物和教训。你可能已经注意到，每次你彻底解决问题时，你都会学到一些非常有价值的东西，你的生活也会在某些方面得到显著的丰富。也许你变得更加自信，学会了更加信任生活，变得更加睿智，或者发现了自己身上一项重要的天赋或才能。当你没有收到（或珍惜）这份礼物，或者没有学到宝贵的教训时，很可能是因为你没有放下问题导致你失去的东西（这在失去亲人的人身上尤为常见）。<sup>63</sup>

This experience of recognizing the gift or lesson at the resolution of a problem has led me to understand that a beautiful gift and lesson rising from the depths of my soul are the actual cause of any crisis in my life. Whenever the soul takes a step forward in its purpose, a crisis occurs. The intensity of the suffering this step causes is mostly dependent on the degree of my surrender—or lack of surrender. The more attached I am to what the situation is threatening to take away from me, the more I fight the problem. The more I fight the problem, the more I delay the soul’s gift. When that happens all that is left for me is suffering.

这种在问题解决过程中领悟到其中蕴含的礼物或教训的经历，让我明白，源自灵魂深处的珍贵礼物和教训，才是我人生中所有危机的真正根源。每当灵魂朝着其使命迈出一步，危机便随之而来。这一步所带来的痛苦程度，主要取决于我臣服的程度——或者说，我是否臣服。我越是执着于困境可能夺走的东西，就越是抗拒问题。我越是抗拒问题，就越是拖延灵魂的馈赠。而当这种情况发生时，留给我的就只有痛苦。

There have been times, when confronted with a problem, I asked my soul what gift or lesson was being offered here. The answer soon came into my heart, and I chose to receive what I was being offered. That choice carried me beyond the problem to the gift in much less time than it would usually have taken me. The reason for that, I believe, is that I usually reacted to my problems with worry, anxiety, fear, panic, or outright terror. My fearful reaction brought the elements of struggle, doubt, procrastination, and resistance into the problem, thereby creating delays in the resolution. However, keeping my mind on the gift that lay beyond the problem brought hope and trust into my fears and allowed me to respond to the situation in a more effective way than either my Persecutor or Rescuer could offer.

有时，当我遇到问题时，我会问自己，这其中蕴含着怎样的礼物或教训。答案很快便浮现在我的心头，我选择接受它。这个选择让我超越了困境，更快地抵达了那份礼物。我相信，原因在于我通常面对问题时的反应是担忧、焦虑、恐惧、恐慌，甚至是极度的惊恐。恐惧的反应将挣扎、怀疑、拖延和抗拒等因素带入问题之中，从而延缓了问题的解决。然而，当我专注于问题背后那份礼物时，希望和信任便涌入我的恐惧，使我能够以比“迫害者”或“拯救者”都更有效的方式应对困境。

c) Everything you perceive is a projection of your inner reality. If you think your partner is persecuting you through attack, criticism, blame, teasing, or some other kind of abuse, listen closely. Is s/he saying anything to you that your own inner critic has not already said? If your partner is the Rescuer, is she/he giving you any advice that you have not heard—and rejected—in your own mind over the years? And if your partner is acting like a Victim, is it familiar to you, even if you have to dig back into your long-buried childhood experiences to see the similarity? Is your partner reflecting a part of you that you buried a long time ago, but never really came to peaceful terms with?

c) 你所感知的一切都是你内在现实的投射。如果你觉得你的伴侣在通过攻击、批评、指责、嘲弄或其他形式的虐待来迫害你，请仔细倾听。他/她对你说的话，你内心的批评家是否已经说过？如果你的伴侣扮演的是拯救者的角色，他/她给你的建议，你这些年来是否从未在自己的内心深处听到过——并且拒绝过？如果你的伴侣扮演的是受害者的角色，这种角色是否让你感到似曾相识，即使你需要回溯那些尘封已久的童年经历才能发现其中的相似之处？你的伴侣是否反映了你内心深处某个你很久以前就埋藏起来，却从未真正与之和平共处的部分？

In any challenging situation, the three aspects of the Victim Prison will manifest. People appear to enact the roles of your drama, which reflects the trap you have created through the power of your own mind. Sometimes you will be the Persecutor attacking your partner (the Victim) with righteous anger. At other times you will be the Rescuer and Persecutor attempting to lift your Victim partner out of his/her swamp with “tough love.” Or else you might choose to be the Rescuer, doing everything possible to help your partner, the Victim, lighten up. And sometimes you will be the Victim crying out for help to your Rescuer partner who suddenly loses patience with you and becomes your Persecutor. Still other times you may find yourself the Victim simultaneously asking for help, while at the same time rebelling against any helping hand that is offered. 64

在任何充满挑战的情境中，“受害者牢笼”的三个方面都会显现。人们似乎会扮演你戏剧中的角色，这反映了你通过自身思维的力量所设下的陷阱。有时，你会扮演迫害者的角色，义愤填膺地攻击你的伴侣（受害者）。有时，你会扮演拯救者和迫害者的角色，试图用“严厉的爱”将你的伴侣（受害者）从困境中拉出来。或者，你可能会选择扮演拯救者的角色，竭尽所能地帮助你的伴侣（受害者）放松下来。有时，你会扮演受害者的角色，向你的拯救者伴侣哭诉求助，而你的伴侣却突然失去耐心，变成了你的迫害者。还有一些时候，你可能会发现自己既是受害者，又在寻求帮助，同时又反抗任何伸出的援手。<sup>64</sup>

If you look at all the ways a Victim, Rescuer, and Persecutor can deploy to express themselves, the mathematical possibilities regarding what kinds of interaction can occur are vast. But when you realize the three corners of the prison are all aspects of your own mind, you are released from the experience of being only the Victim. This allows you to see yourself as the source of the situation—your soul has chosen to step forward in consciousness, causing upheavals in the status quo. You can then choose to cooperate with your soul, or perpetuate the problem by remaining stuck in Victim/Persecutor/Rescuer mode.

如果你仔细审视受害者、拯救者和迫害者这三种角色表达自我的所有方式，你会发现，他们之间可能发生的各种互动模式简直无穷无尽。但当你意识到这三个“牢笼”其实都是你自身思维的不同面向时，你便能从单纯的受害者体验中解脱出来。这让你意识到自己才是问题的根源——你的灵魂选择在意识层面挺身而出，打破了现状。此时，你可以选择与你的灵魂合作，也可以选择继续困于受害者/迫害者/拯救者的角色模式，从而延续问题。

d) Every human being has the power to be 100% responsible for what he or she experiences in this life. It is when you claim complete responsibility for what happens to you that you reclaim your power to choose. I am not stating this as one who is 100% accountable 100% of the time. The choice is made only on a moment-by-moment basis. When I have set the intention to be completely responsible for what happens in my life, I find a tranquility and clarity that allows me to choose what is best for everyone involved. Being 100% accountable for the situation you are presented with gives you the power to step out of your triangular prison and step into the realm of freedom. I see the evolution of responsibility in these stages:

d) 每个人都有能力对自己的人生经历负起百分之百的责任。当你对发生在你身上的一切承担起全部责任时，你就重新获得了选择的权力。我这么说并不是说自己时时刻刻都要百分之百负责。选择只是在当下时刻做出的。当我下定决心要对自己的人生负起全部责任时，我便会感到内心平静和清明，从而能够做出对所有相关人员都最有利的选择。对你所处的境况负起百分之百的责任，就能让你走出困境的牢笼，步入自由的领域。我认为责任的演变可以分为以下几个阶段：

1. Someone else is responsible for this shit, so someone else has to clean it up.

1. 这堆烂摊子是别人造成的，所以也得由别人来收拾残局。

2. Someone else is responsible for this shit, so they’re the bad guys; I’m just an innocent victim. 65

2. 这事是别人干的，所以他们是坏人；我只是个无辜的受害者。65

3. Someone else is responsible for this shit, and now, even though I’m stuck with it, I still have to clean it up.

3. 这都是别人的错，现在虽然我得承担后果，但我还是得收拾残局。

4. This shit is my fault, but I can’t help the way I am.

4. 这都是我的错，但我无法改变我的性格。

5. This shit is my fault, but I can rise above it.

5. 这都是我的错，但我可以克服它。

6. This situation is shit. Now how am I going to deal with it?

6. 这情况糟透了。现在我该怎么办？

7. Shit happens in life (shrug). You just have to learn how to handle it.

7. 人生不如意事十之八九（耸肩）。你只需要学会如何应对。

8. This shit is nobody’s fault. I have the power to respond to it in a way I can grow from.

8. 这事儿不是任何人的错。我有能力以一种能让我成长的方式来应对它。

9. I attracted this shit. Now I can choose something more appropriate for me at this time.

9. 我招来了这些破事。现在我可以选择一些更适合我的东西了。

10. I created this shit

10. 这玩意儿是我造的

11. This shit is a part of me.

11. 这玩意儿是我的一部分。

12. I am at peace—no shit!

12. 我内心很平静——真的！

As we grow in understanding, “responsibility” changes from a guilt—and shame-based word to one of responsiveness and freedom.

随着我们理解的加深，“责任”一词也从基于内疚和羞耻的词语转变为基于回应和自由的词语。

e) Freedom does not come from answers. It comes from questions. “Freedom From the Known” is a great book of discourses delivered by Krishnamurti. 66 It expresses the idea that what we “know” is not what gives us peace or a sense of who we really are. It is when we step beyond all the beliefs, which we mistakenly call “knowledge,” that we gain the freedom to expand limitlessly.

e) 自由并非源于答案，而是源于疑问。《摆脱已知》是克里希那穆提的一部伟大演讲集。<sup>66</sup> 它表达了这样一个观点：我们“知道”的东西并不能带给我们内心的平静，也不能让我们真正了解自己。只有当我们超越所有被我们误称为“知识”的信念时，我们才能获得无限扩展的自由。

When I was growing up, I found school to be extremely boring except for one particular high school history class. Our teacher, Mr. Werner, challenged us to question everything we took for the truth regarding current events, politics, history, and school itself. 67 He insisted that true knowledge was realized through the asking of questions that took us beyond the known. Most of my school knowledge to this point consisted of information I was spoon-fed (and sometimes force-fed), which I was discouraged from questioning and told to simply memorize. Suddenly Mr. Werner appeared and asked me a question I could not answer: “How do you know? All the information and knowledge you carry—how do you know if it is true?” Once you are outside the Victim Prison you are free to experience life in a state of innocence, where you are not confined by the limits of your beliefs. You can truly know yourself. “Then you shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free.”

在我成长的过程中，除了高中的一门历史课之外，我觉得学校生活极其枯燥乏味。我们的老师沃纳先生挑战我们质疑所有我们习以为常的关于时事、政治、历史乃至学校本身的“真理”。<sup>67</sup> 他坚持认为，真正的知识来自于提出问题，这些问题引领我们超越已知。在此之前，我的大部分学校知识都是被灌输（有时甚至是强迫灌输）的，老师不鼓励我质疑，只是让我死记硬背。突然，沃纳先生出现了，问了我一个我无法回答的问题：“你怎么知道？你所掌握的所有信息和知识——你怎么知道它们是真是假？”一旦你走出了“受害者牢笼”，你就能自由地体验一种纯真的生活，不再受制于你固有的信仰。你才能真正地认识自己。“那时，你们必晓得真理，真理必叫你们得以自由。”

It is through questions that you can begin to know yourself—questions that inquire about possibilities beyond your beliefs. Questions such as “What is the Truth here?”; “I wonder what gift (or lesson) my soul is offering me through this situation?”; “How can I fully accept this pain peacefully?”; “ What indisputable truth can I express to my partner that would bring peace to this conflict?”; “What do I really want in this situation?”; “How can I love my partner now?”; “What is the most important feeling I can feel right now?”; “I wonder what step I am being called to take at this moment?”; “Who am I being called to accept unconditionally?”; “ What am I being asked to understand about this situation?”

正是通过提问，你才能开始了解自己——这些问题探寻着超越你固有信念的可能性。例如：“真相是什么？”；“我想知道我的灵魂通过这种情况给予我的礼物（或教训）是什么？”；“我该如何平静地接受这份痛苦？”；“我能向伴侣表达什么无可辩驳的真理，从而化解这场冲突？”；“在这种情况下，我真正想要的是什么？”；“我现在该如何爱我的伴侣？”；“我现在最能感受到的是什么？”；“我想知道此刻我应该采取什么行动？”；“我被召唤去无条件地接纳谁？”；“关于这种情况，我需要理解什么？”

These are a few of the kinds of questions that, when asked with true innocence, take you beyond what you know into the realm of intuition—your soul’s thoughts. Once in that realm, you will be guided to the most direct route through your problem to an experience of conscious love.

这些问题，若以真诚的心态提出，便能引领你超越已知，进入直觉的领域——你灵魂深处的思考。一旦进入那个领域，你便会被指引找到解决问题的最直接途径，最终体验到觉知的爱。

Most of my questions have begun with “what” or “how,” but can also start with “who,” “when,” or “where.” The one that you want to be extra careful with is the word “Why.” It is one of the Victim’s favourite words when complaining or expressing its powerlessness, and so often leads to other “why”s. I do not mean to discourage its use, however. If expressed with innocence and wonder, it has as much power and effectiveness as any other question word.

我的问题大多以“什么”或“如何”开头，但也可能以“谁”、“何时”或“何地”开头。你需要格外注意的是“为什么”这个词。它是受害者在抱怨或表达无力感时最喜欢用的词之一，因此常常会引出更多的“为什么”。但我并非要阻止你使用这个词。如果带着天真和好奇的语气，它和其他任何疑问词一样，都具有强大的力量和效果。

f) There is no problem so great that love cannot resolve it. This principle needs no explanation. It requires only our trust in our soul’s nature.

f) 没有解决不了的巨大难题，爱可以化解。这个道理无需解释，只需要我们信任自己灵魂的本性。

My adaptation of the Karpman Triangle is the clearest and simplest representation I have found of the complex trap our ego has created in order to maintain separation in our relationships. 68 In order to heal this separation, it is important to consciously choose to move closer to our partners, friends, relatives and strangers, something that cannot be done within the confines of the prison. This is because whatever position you take on the triangle will determine where your “supporting cast” will end up. Sometimes you can create an artificial closeness by sharing the Victim spot with your partner. To do this you must create a Persecutor that threatens both of you. At other times you may share the Rescuer spot by both of you focusing on a Victim, or share the Persecutor corner by creating a scapegoat. 69

我对卡普曼三角的改编是我所发现的对我们自我为了维持人际关系中的分离而设下的复杂陷阱最清晰、最简洁的表述。<sup>68</sup> 为了治愈这种分离，重要的是要有意识地选择与伴侣、朋友、亲戚和陌生人走得更近，而这在“监狱”的束缚下是无法实现的。这是因为你在三角中占据的位置将决定你的“支持者”最终会在哪里。有时，你可以通过与伴侣共同扮演“受害者”的角色来营造一种虚假的亲密感。要做到这一点，你必须创造一个对你们双方都构成威胁的“迫害者”。有时，你们可以通过共同关注某个“受害者”来共同扮演“拯救者”的角色，或者通过创造一个替罪羊来共同扮演“迫害者”的角色。<sup>69</sup>

But, like chickens and curses, the Victim Prison will eventually come home to roost in your primary relationship. The false intimacy that was created by sharing a corner will disappear, leaving you with the necessity of having to deal with each other.

但是，就像鸡生祸害鸡一样，受害者心态最终也会在你们的主要关系中反噬自身。曾经通过共处一隅营造出的虚假亲密感会消失殆尽，最终你们不得不面对彼此。

The Victim Prison is designed to discourage loving relationships. The discouragement itself is a test of one’s commitment to what is true. It doesn’t matter if you are a Victim, Persecutor, or Rescuer, or how you justify staying in any of those positions. You will never get through the wall until you want what is true more than you want the false security of the Prison. To experience that Truth you need only ask. Asking a question that only your heart and soul can answer reflects your choice to know the Truth, and the commitment to know the response is your step through the wall and into the realm of Conscious Partnership.

受害者牢笼旨在阻碍爱的关系。这种阻碍本身就是对一个人坚持真理的考验。无论你是受害者、迫害者还是拯救者，无论你如何为自己身处这些角色辩解，都无关紧要。除非你对真理的渴望胜过对牢笼虚假安全的渴望，否则你永远无法突破这道墙。要体验真理，你只需开口询问。提出一个只有你的内心才能回答的问题，体现了你选择了解真理的决心；而你渴望知道答案的决心，就是你突破这道墙，进入觉知伴侣关系领域的一步。

As complicated as the traps in the Victim Prison are, it is the simplicity of sincere intention that sets you free. I would like to offer a few more examples of these traps, and explore with you the liberating possibilities that a commitment to Truth offers. Let’s start with....

尽管“受害者牢笼”中的陷阱错综复杂，但唯有真诚的意愿才能让你获得自由。我想再举几个例子来说明这些陷阱，并与你一同探索对真理的执着所带来的解放力量。让我们从……开始吧。

***

DILEMMA

困境

———————————

“Some people go this way...and some people go that way...but for myself I prefer the shortcut!”

“有些人走这条路……有些人走那条路……但我个人更喜欢走捷径！”

—The Cheshire Cat in “Alice in Wonderland,” by Lewis Carroll

——刘易斯·卡罗尔《爱丽丝梦游仙境》中的柴郡猫

Dilemma is experienced in situations when you feel the need to decide between one of two courses of action. The problem is that no matter which action you decide on, you will feel like you lost something valuable. Let me give you a few examples from case histories of some of my clients.

当你需要在两种行动方案中做出选择时，就会陷入两难境地。问题在于，无论你最终选择哪种方案，你都会感觉自己失去了某些宝贵的东西。让我举几个我客户的案例来说明一下。

➢ One man had to decide between his desire to be an artist, and the security of his office job. If he chose his art, he would be doing what he loved to do, but would not be assured of financial security. If he stayed at his office job, he would have financial security but would not experience any joy in his work. What to choose: doing what you love but no guaranteed money, or guaranteed money doing what you don’t love?

➢ 一位男士必须在成为艺术家的梦想和稳定的办公室工作之间做出抉择。如果他选择艺术，就能做自己热爱的事情，但无法保证经济保障。如果他继续留在办公室，虽然经济稳定，却无法从工作中获得任何乐趣。他该如何选择：做自己热爱但收入没有保障的事情，还是做自己不热爱但收入有保障的事情？

➢ A forty-year-old stay-at-home mother of three was having an affair with a very loving and passionate man. Her dilemma: stay with her husband and be unhappy in love and sex, or have an emotionally and sexually fulfilling relationship but lose the security of a stable family situation with her husband and children.

➢ 一位四十岁的全职妈妈，育有三个孩子，与一位非常体贴热情的男士发生了婚外情。她面临两难选择：是留在丈夫身边，忍受爱情和性生活的不幸福；还是拥有情感和性生活都令人满意的婚外情，但失去与丈夫和孩子共同生活的稳定安全感。

➢ A young man was working at his father’s bank, but was spiritually dissatisfied and wanted to discover his true purpose. The dilemma: If he quits, he can follow his dream, but his father will be very angry. If he stays he will make his father happy, but he is afraid he will grow old and regret never knowing his true purpose in life.

➢ 一位年轻人在他父亲的银行工作，但他内心感到空虚，渴望找到人生的真正意义。他面临两难的境地：如果他辞职，就能追寻梦想，但父亲会非常生气；如果他留下，父亲会很高兴，但他害怕自己年老时会后悔从未找到人生的真正意义。

➢ A mother owned a restaurant, and had a son and a daughter that did not get along. The mother wanted to retire and turn the business over to both her kids but they refused, insisting that she choose only one of them to take over the business. Of course each insisted on being the one she chose. How can she choose only one, without incurring the wrath and resentment of the other? Either way she loses.

一位母亲拥有一家餐馆，她有一儿一女，但两人关系不睦。母亲想退休，把餐馆交给两个孩子共同经营，但他们都拒绝了，坚持要母亲从中选一个接手。当然，他们都坚持要成为母亲选中的那个人。母亲该如何抉择，才能避免激怒另一个孩子呢？无论如何，她都注定要吃亏。

➢ A company owner who had to decide whether to expand his business into another country. If he did not expand he could spend more time at home with his family, but a rival company would move into that country, allowing it to get stronger while his own business eventually shrank, and possibly died. If he did expand it would mean more time away from his family, but he would probably become much more successful.

➢ 一位公司老板必须决定是否将业务拓展到另一个国家。如果不扩张，他可以有更多时间陪伴家人，但竞争对手会趁机进入该国，壮大自身实力，而他的公司最终可能会萎缩甚至倒闭。如果他选择扩张，虽然意味着要花更多时间远离家人，但他很可能会获得更大的成功。

Observing these situations from the outside, you may see an obvious solution, or at least recognize what you would do in that case, but have you ever talked to someone caught in a dilemma? No matter what course you suggest to them, they will give you a very good reason why they can’t do it. And if you fall into the Rescuer role, in very little time you may find yourself throwing up your hands in frustration and defeat, possibly even becoming a Persecutor and criticizing the dilemma Victim for being so weak and indecisive. Imagine for example a conversation between you (the Rescuer) and the forty-year-old woman who is in relationship triangle, caught between her stable husband (she calls him boring), and her red-hot lover:

从旁观者的角度来看，你或许能找到显而易见的解决方案，或者至少能意识到自己在这种情况下会怎么做。但你是否曾与身陷困境的人交谈过呢？无论你提出什么建议，他们都会给出充分的理由来解释为什么自己做不到。如果你扮演了“拯救者”的角色，很快你就会感到沮丧和无奈，甚至可能变成“迫害者”，指责陷入困境的“受害者”软弱无能、优柔寡断。例如，想象一下你（拯救者）与一位四十岁的女性的对话。她正处于三角恋中，一边是稳重的丈夫（她觉得他很无趣），一边是热情似火的情人：

You: So why don’t you leave your husband if you don’t feel anything for him any more?

你：既然你对丈夫已经没有任何感觉了，为什么不离开他呢？

Woman: I can’t. I just can’t break up our family—it would hurt our children so much!

女人：我不能。我绝对不能拆散我们的家庭——这会给我们的孩子带来太大的伤害！

You: Well then why don’t you stay and try to patch things up with your husband?

你：那你为什么不留下来，试着和你的丈夫和好呢？

Woman: I’ve been trying for years, but it’s no use. He just doesn’t want to deal with our problems.

女：我努力了好几年，但都没用。他就是不想处理我们的问题。

You: Well then it sounds like the marriage is over; why don’t you start working towards a friendly separation?

你：那听起来你们的婚姻已经结束了；为什么不开始努力友好分手呢？

Woman: But I’m afraid to be out there on my own—especially with the uncertain job market. And my husband doesn’t have enough money to support me in a home of my own. I’d have to go out and work, but I have no skills.

女：但我害怕独自在外闯荡——尤其是在就业市场如此不稳定的情况下。而且我丈夫没有足够的钱供我独自生活。我必须出去工作，但我没有任何技能。

You: So you have to stay.

你：所以你必须留下。

Woman: But I can’t stay! He’s so boring...so inattentive to my needs! I’ve done all the work in this relationship, and he does nothing in return!

女：但我不能留下来！他太无趣了……对我的需求漠不关心！在这段感情里，我一直都在付出，他却什么都不做！

You: So you better go to the man you love.

你：所以你最好去找你爱的人。

Woman: But I’m not really sure that would work either. I mean I love this other man... I think I do. But he’s an office worker who wants to be an artist. What if he decided to quit his job—how could he take care of me and the children? And would he want to be a father?

女人：但我也不确定那样行不行。我是说，我爱另一个男人……我想我是爱他的。但他是个上班族，想当艺术家。万一他辞职了——他怎么照顾我和孩子们？而且他愿意当父亲吗？

You: It sounds like you’re not too sure about this other guy. Maybe you’re better off staying in your marriage and trying to make it work.

你：听起来你对这个男人不太确定。或许你最好还是留在现在的婚姻里，努力维系这段关系。

Woman: I want to, but I can’t!

女人：我想，但我做不到！

You: Then leave.

你：那就离开吧。

Woman: I want to but I can’t!

女人：我想，但我做不到！

You: I quit!

你：我不干了！

Isn’t dilemma a marvellous invention of the ego? It is one of the most effective tools ever designed for causing huge, unproductive, and discouraging delays in your life. 70 It is so distracting in its ability to create convoluted dramas out of simple choices that its true purpose can be kept hidden for years, even a lifetime. What is its purpose? To keep you from taking a step towards Truth in your life. What feeds that purpose? Your personal fear of the Truth.

困境难道不是自我的一项绝妙发明吗？它是迄今为止最有效的工具之一，专门用来制造生活中巨大、无益且令人沮丧的延误。<sup>70</sup> 它能将简单的选择演变成错综复杂的戏剧，这种能力如此令人分心，以至于它的真正目的可以被隐藏数年，甚至一生。它的目的是什么？阻止你迈向人生的真理。是什么助长了它的目的？是你对真理的恐惧。

In the previous example you see what is really holding the woman back from making the correct choice is her fear. Since all fear is a fear of loss, you can see that she is afraid of losing what is familiar to her, what has given her a sense of security and some comfort in the world. She is afraid to take a step towards her husband in unconditional love because she would lose the familiar comfort of her prison walls. She is afraid to leave the marriage and lose the comfortable predictability of a stable family situation. She is afraid to trust life to take care of herself on her own, thereby losing the identity she has come to recognize as hers—even if that identity is one of a frightened, insecure, socially useless woman. Dilemma reinforces the victim mentality, and reinforces in everyone a fear of stepping forward in life.

在前一个例子中，我们可以看到真正阻碍这位女性做出正确选择的，是她的恐惧。由于所有恐惧都源于对失去的恐惧，我们可以看出，她害怕失去她所熟悉的一切，那些曾给予她安全感和慰藉的事物。她害怕向丈夫迈出无条件的爱的一步，因为她会失去牢笼般舒适的庇护。她害怕离开婚姻，失去稳定家庭带来的舒适和可预测性。她害怕相信生活能够照顾好自己，从而失去她已经认同的身份——即使这个身份是一个恐惧、缺乏安全感、在社交上无用的女人。这种两难困境强化了受害者心态，也强化了每个人心中对人生前进的恐惧。

The way through dilemma is simple. Choose the truth. Be willing to accept either of the two options the dilemma presents, or neither. This is a key point, because the dilemma would have you believe that there are only two choices. A willingness to let go of both options, and a sincere commitment to the truth, takes you out of the grasp of the dilemma to a place where anything can happen . For the sake of this model, I am defining the truth as that which offers the most beneficial experience for all parties concerned. Maybe in the above case it is better for the children to have divorced parents, rather than feeling like the parents are sacrificing their own happiness for the sake of their kids. Maybe the kids would be better off not living in a home where a lie is being lived. And maybe it would be better for the husband to get a divorce so he can start fresh, having learned how his uncorrected mistakes lead to the death of a relationship. For the woman, it might be better for her to face her insecurities and fears around her value as a member of the workforce so that she can have the chance to get a better sense of who she is and what she is truly capable of.

摆脱困境的方法很简单：选择真相。愿意接受困境提出的两个选项中的任何一个，或者两个都不接受。这一点至关重要，因为困境会让你觉得只有两种选择。愿意放弃这两个选项，并真诚地坚持真相，就能让你摆脱困境的束缚，进入一个一切皆有可能的境地。为了便于理解，我将真相定义为对所有相关方都最有利的体验。也许在上述案例中，父母离异对孩子更好，而不是让孩子觉得父母为了孩子牺牲了自己的幸福。也许孩子不应该生活在一个充满谎言的家庭中。也许对丈夫来说，离婚更好，这样他可以重新开始，吸取教训，明白自己未改正的错误是如何导致婚姻破裂的。对于女性而言，直面自己作为职场成员的价值方面的不安全感和恐惧或许更好，这样她才能有机会更好地了解自己是谁以及自己真正的能力是什么。

Or , it might be best for all if she remained in the marriage, and took steps towards accepting her husband as he is rather than what she expects him to be. Her kids would then be given an example of what True Partnership is. She and her husband would have the chance to see what love can bring into a seemingly dead relationship, and the lover would have a chance to move towards a relationship with a woman who is completely available.

或者，对所有人来说，最好的办法或许是她继续维持婚姻，并努力接受丈夫的本来面目，而不是固守她期望的样子。这样，她的孩子们就能从中看到真正的伴侣关系是什么样的。她和丈夫将有机会看到爱情能给一段看似死气沉沉的关系带来怎样的改变，而那个情人也有机会与一位完全敞开心扉的女性发展一段新的关系。

The fact is, nobody knows what would be best for that woman, her family, and the lover. The answer is in the woman’s heart. But she cannot hear her soul’s message in her heart if fear is clouding her thoughts. Being willing to have either option, or neither, will give her a serenity that will let her see beyond her fears, and allow her to hear what her heart has been saying all along.

事实上，没有人知道什么对那个女人、她的家人和她的爱人来说才是最好的。答案就在女人的内心深处。但如果恐惧蒙蔽了她的双眼，她就无法听到内心深处的呼唤。愿意接受两种选择，或者两者都不选，会让她获得内心的平静，让她超越恐惧，听到自己内心一直以来都在诉说的声音。

Dilemmas cause you to reject and hold on to what you have at the same time. This keeps you stuck. In the midst of a dilemma, extricate yourself from the drama—if you can—and express a commitment such as, “I am willing to accept either of these options, or neither of them. More than anything, I want the Truth.” As long as your intention is sincere, the appropriate step will appear. Maybe the woman will leave, or maybe she will stay. Maybe she will decide to sleep separately from her husband for a while, or maybe she will move out and start dating him again. One thing is for sure: whatever her heart guides her to do will be what is best for everyone involved, no matter the upheaval it initially causes. If you want the Truth more than anything else, the Truth will come to you.

两难困境会让你既想放弃又想保留，这会让你陷入困境。身处两难境地时，如果可以，尽量让自己从困境中抽身出来，并表达一个明确的承诺，例如：“我愿意接受这两个选择中的任何一个，或者两个都不接受。我最渴望的是真相。”只要你的意图是真诚的，合适的步骤自然会出现。也许她会离开，也许她会留下。也许她会决定暂时与丈夫分居，也许她会搬出去，重新开始与他约会。有一点可以肯定：无论她内心的指引如何，最终都会对所有人都有利，无论这最初会带来怎样的动荡。如果你比任何事都渴望真相，真相终将来到你身边。

# ↩

***

FAMILY LOYALTIES

家族忠诚

———————————

“A family that is united in love has no family ties, for there is no such thing as ‘family ties’ apart from the ties that bind.”

“一个因爱而团结的家庭没有家庭纽带，因为除了维系彼此的纽带之外，根本不存在所谓的‘家庭纽带’。”

—Anonymous

-匿名的

Please be aware that I may sound blasphemous for pointing out the limitations in one’s loyalty to the family. If so, you are probably associating loyalty with love and commitment. I do not believe you could ever be truly at peace with your family, unless you felt complete love (i.e. acceptance and appreciation) for every single member. However, loyalty to the family’s methods of “coping” with your feelings and life problems interferes with your ability to make responsible choices for yourself, whereas loving your family leaves you free to follow your heart’s calling.

请注意，我指出一个人对家庭忠诚的局限性，这或许听起来有些离经叛道。如果是这样，你可能将忠诚与爱和承诺混为一谈。我认为，除非你对家庭中的每一位成员都怀有完全的爱（即接纳和欣赏），否则你永远无法真正与家人和平相处。然而，忠于家庭“应对”你情绪和生活问题的方式会妨碍你为自己做出负责任的选择，而爱你的家人则能让你自由地追随内心的召唤。

Family Loyalties are the commandments you followed, sacrifices you made, beliefs you adopted, people you accepted or rejected, and coping behaviours you assumed for dealing with life situations, created within your family. “That’s the way we did it when I was a kid” is a popular statement of such loyalties. They were developed by imitating the words and actions of your parents, siblings, and relatives, thus moulding yourself in order to attain an identity. This in turn gave you a place in the family, whether negative or positive.

家庭忠诚指的是你在家庭中形成的，你所遵循的戒律、你做出的牺牲、你接受的信仰、你接纳或排斥的人，以及你应对生活境况所采取的行为模式。“我小时候我们家就是这么做的”是此类忠诚的常见体现。这些忠诚是通过模仿父母、兄弟姐妹和亲戚的言行而形成的，从而塑造自我，最终获得身份认同。这反过来又赋予你在家庭中的地位，无论这种地位是积极的还是消极的。

Although we imitated certain attitudes and pre-established patterns in order to earn the approval of the family and thus attain inclusion into that exclusive club, the choices we made to do so were not conscious ones. Most of our initial childhood learnings came from imitation. It is only normal then that when we experienced discouragement from unmet needs, we would imitate coping behaviours from those around us who were also dealing with the pain of discouragement. Somewhere along the line, our decision to imitate the “Family Way” combined with our unconscious need to survive; not belonging to our family would have meant death, as far as we were concerned. Therefore we secured ourselves a place by moulding ourselves according to the predetermined standards of behaviour that our parents adopted from their families. However, because the identity was moulded largely from a need to belong, it covered the soul’s true purpose, and hid away the genius of the individual.

尽管我们模仿某些态度和既定模式是为了赢得家庭的认可，从而融入这个精英圈子，但我们这样做并非出于自觉。我们童年早期的大部分学习都源于模仿。因此，当我们因需求未得到满足而感到沮丧时，模仿周围同样经历挫折的人的应对行为也就不足为奇了。在某种程度上，我们模仿“家庭模式”的决定，与我们潜意识中生存的需要相结合；在我们看来，不属于这个家庭就意味着死亡。因此，我们通过按照父母从他们各自的家庭继承而来的既定行为标准来塑造自己，从而确保自己在家庭中占有一席之地。然而，由于这种身份认同很大程度上源于归属感的需要，它掩盖了灵魂的真正目的，也隐藏了个人的天赋。

By “genius” I am referring to your inherent giftedness experienced through your creative thoughts, words, or behaviour. When influenced by your genius, you will feel a deep sense of joy, serenity, and/or purpose that radiates out through your actions. Even if those actions are basically the same ones you have performed many times, your genius will inspire you to perform them in a uniquely creative way. When acting from Family Loyalties, you are following patterns, rules and beliefs that may have been necessary in the past, but now serve only to limit you. You pledged obedience to this code of thought and behaviour in order to ensure a place for yourself in the family. Stepping away from this code towards your essence can initially bring up intense feelings of betrayal that have reduced many people to tears.

我所说的“天赋”指的是你与生俱来的才能，它体现在你的创造性思维、言语或行为中。当你的天赋发挥作用时，你会感受到一种深深的喜悦、宁静和/或使命感，这种感觉会通过你的行动散发出来。即使这些行动本质上与你以往多次做过的相同，你的天赋也会激励你以一种独特的创造性方式去完成它们。当你出于对家庭的忠诚而行事时，你遵循的模式、规则和信念在过去或许是必要的，但现在却只会限制你。你曾承诺遵守这套思想和行为准则，以确保自己在家庭中占有一席之地。背离这套准则，回归你的本真，最初可能会引发强烈的背叛感，这种感觉甚至会让许多人泪流满面。

In my work I have met people who are doctors, lawyers, bankers and politicians because they were loyal to what their family expected them to be. I have also met people in the same professions who are there because it is exactly where they want to be. There is a world of difference between the two kinds of professionals when it comes to inner peace and true success. But who loves their family more? The ones who freely chose their line of work typically seemed more at peace with—and often felt gratitude towards—their families. Those who chose their professions out of a sense of loyalty tended to be more ambiguous about their feelings towards their family.

在我的工作中，我遇到过一些人，他们成为医生、律师、银行家和政治家，是因为他们忠于家庭的期望。我也遇到过一些人，他们从事同样的职业，仅仅是因为这是他们真正想做的事。这两类职业人士在内心的平静和真正的成功方面有着天壤之别。但究竟谁更爱自己的家人呢？那些自由选择职业的人，通常与家人相处得更融洽，也常常对家人心怀感激。而那些出于忠诚而选择职业的人，往往对家人的感情更加复杂。

Family Loyalties are as effective as dilemmas in keeping us stuck and unable to step forward in our lives. They differ only in the way they cause us to behave. Where a dilemma will have you bouncing back and forth between two options, Family Loyalties will have you behaving according to predetermined patterns.

家庭忠诚和两难困境一样，都会让我们停滞不前，无法前进。它们的区别仅在于影响我们行为的方式。两难困境会让你在两个选择之间摇摆不定，而家庭忠诚则会让你按照预先设定的模式行事。

If your choice of profession originated from the need to belong, and never came from your heart, your experience of work will probably be very mundane. Many people drink because their parent(s) drank, work blue-collar jobs because they came from a blue-collar family, or drive Ford because they were born into a “Ford Family.” Did these people choose their actions or professions consciously, or did it all come from an unquestioned sense of what they “should” do? The following examples of the impact Family Loyalties have on us come from participants of workshops I have facilitated in Asia and North America:

如果你的职业选择源于归属感的需要，而非发自内心，那么你的工作体验很可能非常平庸。许多人喝酒是因为他们的父母喝酒，从事蓝领工作是因为他们出身于蓝领家庭，或者开福特车是因为他们出生在一个“福特家族”。这些人是经过深思熟虑才选择自己的行为或职业，还是仅仅出于一种不假思索的“应该”做什么的观念？以下例子来自我在亚洲和北美举办的研讨会的参与者，展现了家庭忠诚对我们产生的影响：

• A woman felt she had to choose a boyfriend that would meet with the approval of both her mother and father.

• 一位女士觉得她必须选择一个能同时得到父母认可的男朋友。

• A man complained that he had to take over the family business, even though he was very young and would have preferred to travel for a few years.

• 一名男子抱怨说，他不得不接管家族企业，尽管他很年轻，而且更愿意去旅行几年。

• A woman discovered that, because she took on the role of the “family slave”(taking care of household chores, raising the younger siblings, and going no further than grade school so both her parents could work and her brother could attend university), she tended to fall into a pattern of subservience in her important friendships and relationships. She never married, and was lost about what to do with her life.

一位女性发现，由于她扮演了“家庭奴隶”的角色（操持家务、照顾年幼的弟妹，并且为了让父母工作、哥哥上大学而只读到小学），她在重要的友谊和人际关系中往往陷入了一种顺从的模式。她终身未婚，对未来感到迷茫。

• A man had a hard time breaking the habit of stopping off at the bar for a couple of martinis after work. He realized he was following a routine of his father and grandfather.

• 一名男子很难改掉下班后去酒吧喝几杯马提尼的习惯。他意识到自己是在延续父亲和祖父的习惯。

• A woman had the habit of speaking very quietly because, when she was growing up, she was discouraged from speaking too loudly or calling attention to herself in her family environment. She was also afraid to approach her boss for a raise because that would be asking for “special attention.”

• 这位女士习惯说话声音很小，因为她从小在家庭环境中就被教导不要大声说话或引人注目。她也不敢向老板要求加薪，因为她觉得那样会被视为寻求“特殊照顾”。

My study of these Family Loyalties has led me to the awareness of the many ways I have imitated the “Moon behaviours” in my relationships—especially when I was unhappy. I could be angrily tight-lipped like my mother, and bitterly sarcastic like my father. Pretending not to care about a disappointment when it really hurt, avoiding social confrontations, worrying about money, being overly protective of the children, making a joke when feeling uncomfortable, silently pouting during the Power Struggles with my wife...I began to clearly see that the mannerisms and attitudes I employed closely resembled those that my mother, father, or siblings would use.

我对这些家庭忠诚的研究让我意识到，我在人际关系中模仿了许多人生中的“月亮行为”，尤其是在我不开心的时候。我会像母亲一样愤怒地沉默不语，也会像父亲一样尖酸刻薄。明明很伤心却假装不在乎，逃避社交冲突，为钱发愁，过度保护孩子，在感到不自在时开玩笑，在与妻子争执时默默生闷气……我开始清楚地看到，我的这些举止和态度与我的父母或兄弟姐妹非常相似。

The problem with this is that I sink into these behaviours automatically, without even thinking about it. Instead of coming up with a creative, spontaneous, loving, and truthful response to a given situation, I slip into a pattern that I created from imitating other family members. How do you know when you are being governed by these false loyalties? A good rule of thumb is: if you are not expressing the giftedness of your true genius, if what you are doing is not creative or inspired, or if you are reacting to a situation without consciously choosing your response, you are most likely serving a Family Loyalty: doing whatever you’re doing in pretty much the same way it’s been done for generations (with a few personal variations of course).

问题在于，我会不假思索地陷入这些行为模式。面对特定情境，我本应做出富有创意、自然流露、充满爱意且真诚的回应，但我却不由自主地陷入模仿其他家庭成员形成的模式。如何判断自己是否被这些虚假的忠诚所束缚？一个简单的判断方法是：如果你没有展现出真正的天赋，如果你所做的事情缺乏创意或灵感，或者如果你对情境的反应并非出于自觉选择，那么你很可能是在履行某种“家族忠诚”：你所做的一切，几乎都与几代人以来的方式如出一辙（当然，其中也包含一些个人化的差异）。
