There is an allusion to the unconscious origins of Family Loyalties in Judeo-Christian writings, concerning the sins of the father being visited upon the sons. 71 It’s interesting to note that “sin” is a Greek archery term which means “missing the mark,” i.e. a mistake. 72 Ergo if a parent makes a mistake, and does not correct it, the mistake gets passed on to the child, and the child’s child, etc., until someone finally hits the bullseye. It’s not unreasonable to conclude that we learned certain habits, purely because we imitated, rather than corrected, the misguided behaviours of our ancestors.

犹太教-基督教文献中暗示了家庭忠诚的无意识起源，其中提到父亲的罪孽会转嫁给儿子。<sup>71</sup>值得注意的是，“罪”（sin）一词源于希腊射箭术语，意为“脱靶”，即失误。<sup>72</sup>因此，如果父母犯了错却不加以纠正，这个错误就会传给孩子，再传给孩子的孩子，如此一代代，直到有人最终“射中靶心”。由此推断，我们之所以养成某些习惯，仅仅是因为我们模仿而非纠正了祖先的错误行为，这种结论并非毫无道理。

Even if you go through a phase of being “the problem kid” who is always rebelling against the status quo, asking inappropriate questions, and generally giving Mom and/or Dad trouble, your rejection of the “family way” can be just another way to be attached to it. Fighting against something strengthens it in your mind. I have talked to a number of clients who insisted that they were not bound by such false loyalties, and described behaviour in direct opposition to “the Family Way.” Upon a closer investigation into their family line, however, we always discovered an aunt, uncle or grandparent that rebelled in exactly the same way. The result was the same every time—they were still resisting their creative genius and relying on knee-jerk reactions to life situations in order to cope.

即使你经历了一段叛逆期，总是反抗现状，问一些不合时宜的问题，总之给父母添麻烦，你对“家庭模式”的拒绝，可能只是另一种形式的依附。反抗反而会在你心中强化它。我曾与许多客户交谈，他们坚称自己不受这种虚假忠诚的束缚，并描述了一些与“家庭模式”截然相反的行为。然而，当我们深入探究他们的家族史时，总会发现他们的叔叔、阿姨或祖父母也曾以同样的方式反抗过。结果总是相同的——他们仍然压抑着自己的创造力，依靠本能的反应来应对生活中的各种状况。

I would like to point out that, in researching the family influence, I have found in most cases—but not all—there were more helpful influences from the family than harmful ones, and the harmful ones did not have a permanent negative effect. Once you become aware that a self-harming action is actually a misguided behaviour you adopted from a family member, you can make a choice that is self-empowering and erases what might have been earlier perceived as a habit that you thought was an unchangeable part of you.

我想指出的是，在研究家庭影响的过程中，我发现大多数情况下（但并非所有情况），家庭带来的积极影响远大于消极影响，而且那些消极影响也不会造成永久性的负面影响。一旦你意识到某种自残行为实际上是从家庭成员那里学来的错误行为，你就可以做出一个能够增强自身力量的选择，从而消除你之前认为根深蒂固、无法改变的习惯。

The meaning of the previous sentence becomes clear when your relationship is up against the wall, and the only thing that will carry you through is an unprecedentedly creative, intuitive response. Family Loyalties are essential to reinforcing the stagnation that you find at the Introspection stage, and it is the mediocrity that Family Loyalties encourage that can block you from seeing more creative possibilities for resurrecting a dead relationship. You may be able to see what is keeping you stuck, but will react to that stuckness only with familiar coping mechanisms.

当你们的关系走到了尽头，唯一能让你渡过难关的，只有前所未有的、富有创造力的直觉式回应时，前一句话的含义就显而易见了。家庭忠诚会加剧你在内省阶段所感受到的停滞不前，而正是这种家庭忠诚所助长的平庸，会阻碍你发现更多挽救一段濒临破裂关系的创造性可能性。你或许能够看清是什么让你陷入困境，但你只会用熟悉的应对机制来应对这种困境。

Choosing the Truth can release you from this trap, creating a passage through the block to freedom; not only for yourself, but for your whole family as well. If one person can transcend a family pattern, it provides a path to freedom for all the others who are stuck in those same patterns.

选择真理能让你摆脱这种困境，开辟一条通往自由的道路；这不仅对你个人有益，对你的整个家庭也同样如此。如果一个人能够超越某种家庭模式，就能为所有深陷其中的人开辟一条通往自由的道路。

When it comes to this process, I found encouragement to move out of the deadness of the “same old same old” by recognizing that I was not doing this only for myself. I realized that if I did not break the hold of my Family Loyalties, I would pass them on to my children. I began to suspect that this process ran much deeper than I could initially see. What if so-called “hereditary disease” was another aspect? What if these loyalties attracted specific problems that were characteristic of my family line? Did my D.N.A. determine certain mental, physical, and emotional predispositions, or did my Family Loyalties influence my D.N.A.? Did I want my children to take on such burdens if there was a way I could prevent them?

在这个过程中，我意识到自己并非仅仅为了自己而努力，这给了我摆脱“一成不变”的沉闷生活的动力。我明白，如果我不打破家族忠诚的束缚，就会将它们传递给我的孩子。我开始怀疑，这个过程远比我最初看到的要深刻得多。所谓的“遗传疾病”会不会是另一个方面？如果这些忠诚招致了家族特有的某些问题呢？是我的DNA决定了某些心理、生理和情感上的倾向，还是我的家族忠诚影响了我的DNA？如果可以避免，我真的希望我的孩子背负这样的重担吗？

Besides my own kids, there were many other people stuck in similar loyalties who would benefit if they could see a better way. The first time I applied this understanding was at a point in my marriage where I was seized by a sense of supreme discouragement about myself as a worthy husband and father. A problem occurred between my wife and I that would not go away, but instead grew so large that it pushed us into distant corners. I soon found my face pushed up against the wall of my Victim Prison, and I reacted by coping with it the way I had taught myself to cope when I was a child. Petulantly withdrawing from Su Mei, I shut myself into the bedroom.

除了我的孩子，还有许多人也深陷类似的忠诚之中，如果他们能看到更好的出路，也会从中受益。我第一次运用这种理解，是在我婚姻中一个让我极度沮丧的时刻，那时我怀疑自己是否配得上一个好丈夫和好父亲的角色。我和妻子之间出现了一个问题，这个问题不仅没有消失，反而愈演愈烈，最终将我们逼到了隔阂的角落。我很快发现自己被困在了“受害者牢笼”的墙壁上，于是我用小时候学会的应对方式来应对。我任性地疏远了苏梅，把自己关进了卧室。

Laying on my bed, considering the advantages of divorce, I began thinking about how much easier death seemed than living. I was suddenly struck by an image of myself in a room with no doors or windows. A large group of people followed me around as I kept feeling the walls, hopelessly looking for a way out. Closest to me were my children Harmon and Tara, watching me and imitating my every action as if to say “Dad will show us how to get out of here—he knows everything.” I looked around at the other people and realized that I was not alone in my despair, but that there were many of us with similar problems. We were all looking for a way out, struggling with the temptation to simply give up on ourselves—to give up on life. One day my own children would face problems so overwhelming that they would be tempted to give up too. But what if I could show them that you never have to give up on life?

躺在床上，我琢磨着离婚的好处，开始觉得死亡似乎比活着容易得多。突然，我脑海中浮现出一幅画面：我身处一个没有门窗的房间。一大群人跟着我，我只能摸索着墙壁，绝望地寻找出路。离我最近的是我的孩子哈蒙和塔拉，他们看着我，模仿我的一举一动，仿佛在说：“爸爸会告诉我们怎么出去——他什么都知道。”我环顾四周，意识到自己并非孤身一人陷入绝望，很多人都面临着类似的困境。我们都在寻找出路，都在与放弃自我——放弃生命的诱惑作斗争。总有一天，我的孩子们也会面临难以承受的困境，他们也会想要放弃。但如果我能让他们明白，永远不要放弃生命呢？

I pulled myself off the bed, stood, and faced my pain of hopelessness and failure. Holding my children in my heart and thinking of the other people I had seen in my mind, I chose life. I refused to believe that this prison was real—my ultimate destiny—and I cried from my heart for the Truth.

我从床上爬起来，站起身，直面绝望和失败的痛苦。我心中怀着孩子们，脑海中浮现出其他人的身影，我选择了活下去。我拒绝相信这牢笼是真实的——这就是我最终的归宿——我发自内心地哭泣，渴望真理。

A loving feeling came into my pain, and with it came an inspired idea to reach out to my wife through my hurt. I left my room, approached Su Mei, and apologized, telling her how important she was to me. While I was talking to her, I was letting go of any desired results. I simply said what my heart directed me to say, and then went to the kitchen to make dinner. By the next day the problem had cleared itself up—as problems often do when you just leave them alone—and my marriage was full of life and passion again.

痛苦之中涌起一股爱意，随之而来的是一股灵感：透过伤痛去安慰我的妻子。我走出房间，走到苏梅面前，向她道歉，告诉她她对我有多么重要。和她说话的时候，我放下了所有期待的结果。我只是随心所欲地表达，然后就去厨房准备晚餐。第二天，问题就自然而然地解决了——就像很多问题一样，只要你顺其自然，它们就会自行消失——我的婚姻也重新充满了活力和激情。

I have spent a lot of time up against the wall. My blind attachment to Family Loyalties caused me to react to my problems according to familiar patterns that kept me going nowhere. Sometimes I quickly remembered to choose the Truth, while at other times I delayed for weeks before coming to the inevitable conclusion that only a creative, inspired response would release me from my situation. I am sure there will be many more opportunities to examine where my commitment lies, but of this I am also certain: Family Loyalties are not the Truth. They do not inspire a loving experience and therefore they are not true. I can free myself of them by asking for a creative response to my situation that only my soul can provide, because my soul is not chained to any false allegiances. I can confront the most important (often the most painful) feeling with all my heart, recognize that pain is not the Truth, and desire the Truth more than the suffering. I can remember the people at the wall with me, looking for an example of hope in this world, and I can choose for them.

我曾多次陷入困境。我对家庭忠诚的盲目执着，使我以熟悉的模式应对问题，结果却原地踏步。有时，我能迅速想起要选择真理；有时，我却拖延数周，最终才不得不承认，唯有创造性的、充满灵感的回应才能让我摆脱困境。我相信，未来还有很多机会让我审视自己的信念所在，但我也确信一点：家庭忠诚并非真理。它们无法激发爱的体验，因此它们并非真理。我可以通过祈求灵魂赐予的、唯有灵魂才能提供的创造性回应，来摆脱它们的束缚，因为我的灵魂并未被任何虚假的忠诚所束缚。我可以全心全意地面对最重要（也往往最痛苦）的感受，认识到痛苦并非真理，并渴望真理胜过痛苦本身。我可以记起那些与我一同在困境中寻求希望的人们，我可以为他们做出选择。

Lastly, I can choose to value my partner more than any false loyalties, and take a step towards her in my heart. This possibility is often overlooked in relationships because the deadness that can often exist between the partners at the stage of Introspection, but for me it is the most immediate and effective response to the stagnation that Family Loyalties reinforce.

最后，我可以选择将伴侣的价值置于任何虚假的忠诚之上，并在心中向她靠近。这种可能性在人际关系中常常被忽视，因为在反思阶段，伴侣之间常常会存在隔阂，但对我而言，这是应对家庭忠诚所加剧的停滞状态最直接、最有效的方法。

The stagnating deadness discourages loving feelings, and often leads one or both partners to believe that the love is gone and will never come back. All that is left to do is either leave, or cope with the deadness the way we learned to in our childhood. It is certainly true that the sentiment and need which we mistook for love has died; but real love cannot die, or else it would not be real love. If we prefer the sentiment and romance, as well as the other aspects of Glamourous love, we can always consider leaving the romantic graveyard of the Victim Prison and begin our search again for our “perfect mate.” But if we would prefer an experience of the love that comes from the soul, valuing our partner more than the deadness gives us that opportunity. How do you value him or her when things seem so hopelessly stuck? Want to . Want to more than anything else. Result equals intention.

这种停滞不前的死寂会扼杀爱的萌芽，常常让伴侣中的一方或双方都觉得爱情已经逝去，永不复返。剩下的只有离开，或者像我们小时候那样，用我们习以为常的方式去应对这种死寂。诚然，我们曾误以为是爱的那些情感和需求已经消逝；但真正的爱不会消亡，否则它就不是真正的爱。如果我们更喜欢浪漫的情感、浪漫的氛围以及其他“魅力爱情”的元素，我们当然可以考虑离开“受害者监狱”的浪漫坟场，重新开始寻找我们的“完美伴侣”。但如果我们渴望体验源自灵魂的爱，那么，比起死寂的现状，更加珍视我们的伴侣，就能让我们拥有这样的机会。当一切看似毫无希望地陷入僵局时，你该如何珍视他/她呢？想要珍视。比任何事都更渴望珍视。结果取决于意图。

***

SACRIFICE

牺牲

———————————

“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice.”

“因为我喜爱怜悯，不喜爱祭祀。”

—Hosea 6:6

何西阿书 6:6

You can tell when you are in a state of sacrifice simply by exploring your feelings around two words: yes and no. If you are asked to do something and you feel too guilty to say no, or you are joyless when saying yes, you are probably being led into sacrifice by your guilt. In our childhood we took on a great number of sacrificial roles in an attempt to feel like a good person, thus nullifying the guilt that kept threatening to attack us. I’m sure I am not the only kid who assumed guilt for upsetting Mom or Dad. Many people felt that they were troublemakers, burdens, or destroyers of the family.

只需探究你对“是”和“否”这两个词的感受，就能判断你是否处于一种牺牲的状态。如果有人请你做某事，你却因为内疚而无法拒绝，或者即使答应了也毫无喜悦，那么你很可能是被内疚感驱使着去牺牲自己。在童年时期，我们为了觉得自己是个好人，承担了许多牺牲的角色，以此来消除那挥之不去的内疚感。我相信，我不是唯一一个因为惹父母生气而感到内疚的孩子。许多人觉得自己是麻烦制造者、负担，或是家庭的破坏者。

But where did I get the idea that my family was unhappy, and why was it my job to cheer them up? The answer to both questions is “guilt.” It doesn’t matter that the answer makes no real sense. I believed that my family’s unhappiness was my fault, and I also believed that I had to make up for causing their unhappiness (maybe this idea does not make sense to you, so let me give you an example: Have you ever been in a room or office where something was lost or stolen, and the way some people looked at you made you feel like you had to prove your innocence—even though you didn’t do it? Your defensiveness is irrational, but the guilt that causes the defensiveness is really there. Guilt doesn’t have to make sense for it to be effective). But the guilt debt never gets paid off. Most people live out their lives trying to heal their guilt through making sacrifices. 73

但我究竟是从哪里得出“我的家人不快乐”这种想法的？为什么我有责任让他们开心起来？这两个问题的答案都是“内疚”。即便这个答案听起来毫无道理，也无关紧要。我坚信家人的不快乐是我的错，我也坚信我必须弥补我给他们带来的不快乐（也许你无法理解这种想法，让我举个例子：你是否曾经身处一个丢失或被盗物品的房间或办公室，而某些人的眼神让你感觉自己必须证明清白——即使你并没有做这件事？你的辩解是非理性的，但引发这种辩解的内疚感却是真实存在的。内疚感并不需要合乎逻辑才能发挥作用）。然而，这种内疚感的债务永远无法偿还。大多数人终其一生都在试图通过做出牺牲来治愈这种内疚感。<sup>73</sup>

When you reach the Introspection stage of relationships, you begin to question how much of your “giving” in the relationship comes from heartfelt desire, and how much comes purely from a sense of obligation. You feel the exhaustion of your sacrificial behaviour, and are confronted with the question of whether you have really been yourself throughout the time you’ve shared with your partner. If you do not want to be responsible for your actions, you will blame your partner for forcing you into that position; but if you are honest with yourself, you can see that your behaviour is only an adult version of your childhood sacrifices.

当关系发展到内省阶段，你会开始质疑自己在关系中的“付出”有多少是发自内心的渴望，又有多少纯粹出于责任感。你会感到自己牺牲奉献的行为令人疲惫，并开始反思在与伴侣相处的这段时间里，你是否真正活出了自我。如果你不想为自己的行为负责，你会责怪伴侣把你逼入这种境地；但如果你对自己诚实，就会发现你的行为只不过是童年时期牺牲奉献的成人版。

If you were the “hero” as a child who got the best grades, kept the house spotless, did all the cooking, or was a star on the track and field team, you’ll probably be the adult hero who gives the family all the best while doing the job of three people at work, never getting sick or run-down. Oh, and you’ll likely be the head of the P.T.A. and the Girl Guides or Boy Scouts too (maybe I’m exaggerating, but you get the idea).

如果你小时候是家里的“英雄”，成绩最好，家里一尘不染，包揽所有烹饪，或者还是田径队的明星，那么你长大后很可能也会是家里的英雄，尽心尽力照顾家人，同时在工作中承担三个人的工作量，而且从不生病或疲惫。哦，对了，你很可能还会担任家长教师协会和女童子军或男童子军的负责人（也许我有点夸张，但你明白我的意思）。

If you were the “invisible child” who tiptoed around the house, never spoke too loud, and never caused a disturbance, you might in your adult life be inclined to avoid confrontations with your partner and make yourself unavailable at such times—reasoning, as you did when you were young, that your presence was the cause of the unhappiness and so disappearing would make everyone’s life easier.

如果你小时候是那个在家里蹑手蹑脚、从不大声说话、从不惹是生非的“隐形孩子”，那么长大后你可能会倾向于避免与伴侣发生冲突，并在冲突发生时让自己不出现——就像你小时候那样，你会认为自己的存在是不快乐的根源，所以消失会让每个人都过得更轻松。

If you were the sweet, adorable, charismatic, “charmer,” you might feel the obligation to always be sweet and cheerful when your partner is feeling down. It always worked on Mom or Dad!

如果你是那种温柔可爱、魅力四射的“万人迷”，你可能会觉得有义务在伴侣情绪低落时始终保持温柔和快乐。这招对父母总是很管用！

If you were the “scapegoat” or “problem child,” you’ll act in a way that invites attack from your partner, allowing him/her to relieve frustrations by blaming you for his/ her misery. In the experience of righteousness your partner could feel better, and you could pay off your debt for being the cause of your partner’s—and family’s—misery.

如果你是“替罪羊”或“问题儿童”，你的行为会招致伴侣的攻击，让他/她通过责怪你来发泄不满，为自己的痛苦负责。在这种“正义感”的驱使下，你的伴侣可能会感觉好一些，而你也能借此偿还自己作为伴侣乃至家庭痛苦根源的“债务”。

Finally, if you were the “martyr,” you might sacrifice your physical, emotional or mental wellbeing, taking the problem into you and dying for it (if necessary). That way your loved one can forget his/her unhappiness while standing over your sickbed, or grave, and you can finally be together again—just like you tried to do with your family.

最后，如果你是“殉道者”，你可能会牺牲自己的身体、情感或精神健康，将问题深埋心底，甚至为此献出生命（如有必要）。这样，你的亲人站在你的病床或墓前，就能忘却心中的不快，你们最终也能再次团聚——就像你曾努力与家人重聚一样。

From the descriptions above you may catch a glimpse of yourself in one or more of the five major sacrificial roles outlined by Dr. Spezzano that most people choose as they grow up. People caught in other sacrificial patterns—such as “the nice guy,” “helper,” “silent sufferer,” “super achiever,” “Good Time Charley,” “entertainer,” “clown,” “chronically ill,” “misfit,” “strong, silent type,” “rogue,” “peacekeeper,” “pleaser,” “rebel without a pause,” to name a few—when acting out one of these sacrifices for their partners find that there is no true joy, fun, or peacefulness in the way they are giving.

从以上描述中，你或许能瞥见自己身处斯佩扎诺博士提出的五种主要牺牲型角色中的一种或多种，而大多数人在成长过程中都会选择这些角色。那些陷入其他牺牲模式的人——例如“好好先生”、“帮手”、“默默承受痛苦者”、“超级成功者”、“玩乐达人”、“娱乐者”、“小丑”、“慢性病患者”、“格格不入者”、“沉默寡言的坚强者”、“浪子”、“和平缔造者”、“讨好者”、“不折不扣的叛逆者”等等——当他们为了伴侣做出这些牺牲时，会发现这种付出方式并不能带来真正的快乐、乐趣或平静。

Introspection allows you to realize that the sacrifices you make in your life are actually compensations for the “bad guy” that lurks underneath. To understand this better, I envision a model like this:

内省能让你意识到，你人生中做出的牺牲，实际上是为了弥补潜藏在你内心深处的“坏人”。为了更好地理解这一点，我设想这样一个模型：

SACRIFICER

牺牲

-------------------

TORMENTOR

折磨者

-------------------

“BAD GUY”

“坏家伙”

-------------------

EMOTIONS

情绪

-------------------

FEELINGS (EMPTINESS)

感受（空虚感）

-------------------

ESSENCE (SOUL)

精髓（灵魂）

-------------------

The tormentor is the part of your mind that keeps you in sacrifice, even when you are fed up with it, or burned out by the lack of fulfillment in your actions. This form of the Persecutor is a strong disciplinarian, using shame or threats of punishment and exclusion to keep you focused on the debt that you must pay before you can be forgiven. Just look at what happens when a sacrificer tries to change:

折磨你的那部分心灵，即使你已经厌倦了，或者因为行动缺乏成就感而精疲力竭，它仍然让你继续牺牲。这种迫害者就像一个严厉的纪律执行者，利用羞耻感、惩罚威胁和排斥，让你时刻关注必须偿还的债务，只有偿还了债务，你才能获得宽恕。看看当一个牺牲者试图改变时会发生什么：

A friend of mine told me once of his attempts to climb out of his “quiet guy” tendencies. He would always allow his wife to dominate the conversation, even if he was not interested in what she was saying and wanted to change the subject. Whenever he attempted to step out of his role he felt frustrated, because he really didn’t know what he wanted to say. Eventually he decided that he could not win. If he kept quiet he felt used by his wife, who did not care what he had to say, but if he tried to speak out he found himself at a loss for words and felt foolish and inadequate.

我的一位朋友曾跟我讲过他如何努力摆脱自己“沉默寡言”的性格。他总是让妻子主导谈话，即使他对妻子说的话不感兴趣，只想换个话题。每当他试图打破这种角色，都会感到沮丧，因为他真的不知道自己想说什么。最终，他意识到自己进退两难。如果他保持沉默，会觉得自己被妻子利用，妻子根本不在乎他的想法；但如果他试图开口，又会发现自己词穷，觉得自己很愚蠢、很无能。

The frustration built until he reached a point of starting heated arguments every time she began to talk. No matter what she said, he would attack her with an opposing point of view. It didn’t matter whether he believed what he was saying; he would argue just to give himself something to say. Although he could see how shocked and hurt his wife was, he felt he had to be angry and argumentative, or he would cave in to his old pattern of sacrificial silence. His anger was the only weapon he had to combat his inner tormentor’s accusations that he was being a “bad boy” for speaking out. It often happens that when someone wants to rid themselves of the burden of sacrifice, they will indulge in behaviour which is opposite to their usual habit. My friend was simply not ready to face his guilt, and thus defended himself against it. The more upset she looked, the more his guilt threatened him, driving him to argue even more vehemently.

他的挫败感与日俱增，最终演变成只要妻子开口，他便会与她激烈争吵。无论妻子说什么，他都会用相反的观点反驳她。他并不相信自己所说的话，只是为了让自己有话说而争辩。尽管他能看出妻子有多么震惊和伤心，但他觉得自己必须愤怒地争辩，否则就会重蹈覆辙，再次陷入默默牺牲的境地。愤怒是他对抗内心折磨者指责他“不该说真话”的唯一武器。通常情况下，当一个人想要摆脱牺牲的重担时，他们会放纵自己，做出与平时习惯截然相反的行为。我的朋友只是还没准备好面对自己的愧疚，所以才为自己辩护。妻子越是伤心难过，他的愧疚感就越强烈，这驱使他更加激烈地争吵。

After he calmed down and approached his problem in a healthier way, he discovered that his “bad boy” was really just someone who would question things if they did not “feel right.” In his family, questioning the authority of his elders was strongly forbidden, so as a child he had deduced that his questioning ways were a threat to his wellbeing in the family. In order to feel safe he decided to keep his mouth shut, and let others do the talking. 74 This understanding only came about for my friend when he was willing to be the so-called “bad boy” without judging or defending himself. He re-experienced the sad emotion and guilt that so often accompany that part of ourselves, and kept asking to know the Truth about himself. This quest brought him to deep feelings of loneliness—one of the primary feelings one discovers in the emptiness within. By responding to the loneliness with a peaceful resolve to accept it, and thereby accept himself, his confidence grew in time and the need to argue diminished. He became a happier man as well as an effective communicator.

冷静下来后，他以一种更健康的方式处理自己的问题，发现自己所谓的“坏男孩”其实只是在感觉不对劲的时候会质疑一些事情。在他的家庭里，质疑长辈的权威是被严格禁止的，所以他从小就认为自己的质疑会威胁到自己在家庭中的安全。为了感到安全，他决定保持沉默，让别人替他说话。<sup>74</sup> 我的朋友只有在愿意做那个所谓的“坏男孩”，不去评判自己或为自己辩解的时候，才真正理解了这一点。他重新体验到了伴随我们内心这一部分而来的悲伤和内疚，并不断地追寻关于自己的真相。这种探索让他感受到了深深的孤独——这是人们在内心空虚中发现的主要感受之一。通过平和地接受孤独，从而接受自己，他的自信心逐渐增强，争辩的欲望也随之减少。他变得更加快乐，沟通能力也更强了。

Sacrifice can deaden your relationship in three ways. The first is that you can become so resentful of the feeling of being forced to keep sacrificing that the resentment will turn into a repulsion or even hatred towards your mate. You will typically think that she/he is expecting you to act in a way that brings no reward. A second destructive effect of sacrifice is that, in trying to escape the sacrificial behaviour, you may swing the other direction—as my friend did—and indulge in actions that are hurtful to the other. The third effect is burnout. You simply become exhausted by the burden of endless sacrifice and are strongly tempted to leave the relationship for your health or sanity. These results come about largely because of an unwillingness to honestly confront the real cause of the sacrificial behaviour.

牺牲会从三个方面扼杀你们的关系。首先，你会对被迫不断牺牲的感觉感到怨恨，这种怨恨会演变成对伴侣的厌恶甚至仇恨。你通常会认为对方期望你做一些毫无回报的事情。其次，牺牲的破坏性影响是，为了逃避这种牺牲行为，你可能会走向另一个极端——就像我的朋友那样——做出伤害对方的行为。第三种影响是精疲力竭。你会被无休止的牺牲压得喘不过气来，并强烈地想要为了身心健康而离开这段关系。这些结果的出现，很大程度上是因为你不愿意诚实地面对牺牲行为的真正原因。

From the outside, it may be impossible to see the difference between a sacrificial role and a free act of giving. On the inside however, it is easy to tell them apart: when you’re in sacrifice, you cannot receive . You are merely performing an action to assuage and compensate for your truckload of guilt. It’s like paying off a huge financial debt. Not just huge but enormous . 75 At first there may be a feeling of relief that you’re able to make your payments, but after a while the sense of never reaching an end to your debt starts to make you feel tired, drained, and poor. 76

从表面上看，牺牲和无偿付出之间似乎难以区分。然而，在内心深处，二者却很容易区分：当你做出牺牲时，你无法接受任何回报。你只是在用行动来减轻和弥补你内心沉重的愧疚感。这就像偿还一笔巨额债务。不仅是巨额，而是天文数字。<sup>75</sup> 起初，你或许会因为能够偿还债务而感到如释重负，但过了一段时间后，那种永远无法还清债务的感觉会让你感到疲惫不堪、精疲力竭，甚至觉得自己一贫如洗。<sup>76</sup>

It’s the same with sacrifice. There is no life to what you to what you give—no joy or enthusiasm. Maybe at first your sacrifices were appreciated, way back in the Glamour stage. At the Introspection stage, however, your sacrifices just aren’t enough. Being a loyal, attentive partner doesn’t get you the passionate appreciation it used to. It’s still expected of you, so you keep doing it—but there’s no more payoff, and you begin to realize that there never was any payoff for you. It was all for the role you were playing.

牺牲也是如此。你付出的东西失去了生命力——没有喜悦，也没有热情。或许在最初的魅力阶段，你的牺牲还曾被感激。然而，到了内省阶段，你的牺牲却远远不够。做一个忠诚体贴的伴侣，不再能换来曾经的热情赞赏。人们仍然期待你这样做，所以你继续做下去——但你不再有任何回报，你开始意识到，你从未真正得到过任何回报。这一切都只是为了扮演一个角色。

In a relationship that is stuck, when you start hearing phrases like, “I’ve given you the best years of my life, and what did I get in return?! Nothing! ” you can be pretty sure that someone is close to walking out, or collapsing under the sacrifice. Unfortunately, what that person gave was not the best.

一段陷入僵局的关系中，当你开始听到类似“我把人生中最美好的时光都给了你，结果你给了我什么回报？！什么都没有！”这样的话时，你几乎可以肯定，一方已经濒临离开，或者已经不堪重负。不幸的是，这个人付出的并非最好的。

Giving from your heart is a completely different experience. You do not get emotionally drained, you do not feel resentful if appreciation is not forthcoming, and you are not acting to pay off your guilt. You are not expecting any results from your giving at all. You are acting from your heart, and are doing so because you know it is for everyone’s good to give in this way (remember that “everyone” includes you). If love, or the desire to know love, is your motivator, you will concern yourself with the experience of giving itself and will repeatedly see that it is in truly giving that you receive.

发自内心的付出是一种截然不同的体验。你不会感到情绪耗竭，也不会因为得不到感激而心生怨恨，更不会为了弥补内心的愧疚而行动。你完全不期待任何回报。你发自内心地付出，因为你知道这样做对每个人都有益（记住，“每个人”也包括你自己）。如果爱，或者说对爱的渴望是你的动力，你就会专注于付出本身，并反复体会到，唯有在真心付出中，你才能真正有所收获。

The biggest help to ending sacrificial patterns is awareness and accountability. Being 100% accountable for our lives challenges us to see our sacrificial roles without blame. It is too easy to say that we behave the way we do because our parents or family forced us into it. Maybe the choice to act in sacrifice was unconscious. Perhaps it was made out of a need for love, or from a misguided attempt to give love. Maybe it was made for the sake of survival. Whatever the motivation behind our choice, it is absolutely crucial to recognize that the choice came from somewhere inside of us, whether as a mistake or a necessary choice. Once we accept that responsibility, we claim for ourselves the power to choose something better for ourselves.

打破牺牲模式的关键在于觉察和责任感。对自己的生活负起百分之百的责任，能让我们客观地看待自己曾经扮演的牺牲角色，而不自责。我们很容易把行为归咎于父母或家庭的强迫。或许，我们做出牺牲的选择是无意识的。或许是出于对爱的渴望，或许是出于一种错误的爱的表达。或许是为了生存。无论我们选择背后的动机是什么，至关重要的是要认识到，无论出于错误还是迫不得已，这个选择都源于我们内心深处。一旦我们接受了这份责任，我们就拥有了为自己选择更好人生的力量。

Awareness has a magnificent quality that can profoundly affect our consciousness. It has the potential to diminish whatever is not true, and enhance what is true. If you bring your full awareness to a negative emotion, the emotion will quickly dissolve into pure energy. If you focus your full awareness on a loving, joyful, or peaceful feeling, the experience of love, peace or joy will grow within you. How big it can get depends on how much joy you can contain.

觉察力拥有一种奇妙的特质，能够深刻地影响我们的意识。它能够削弱一切不真实的事物，并增强真实的事物。如果你将全部的觉察力集中于一种负面情绪，这种情绪会迅速消融为纯粹的能量。如果你将全部的觉察力集中于一种充满爱、喜悦或平和的感觉，爱、平和或喜悦的体验就会在你心中增长。它能增长到什么程度，取决于你能容纳多少喜悦。

Being fully aware of the feelings and emotions that push you towards sacrifice will ultimately allow you to see that sacrificial roles are not conducive to loving relationships. As draining and unrewarding as they are, we continue our sacrifices because it is easier to do so than face the torment and guilt that lurks beneath our seemingly noble behaviour. It is a greater challenge to peacefully accept our sacrificial tendency as something that no longer serves us, turn away from it and experience the uncomfortable influences of the tormentor and “bad person.” 77 Consistent awareness without reaction and a sincere commitment to be true to ourselves will gradually transform us.

充分觉察那些驱使你做出牺牲的感受和情绪，最终会让你明白，牺牲型角色不利于建立充满爱的关系。尽管牺牲令人精疲力竭且毫无回报，我们仍然继续这样做，因为这样做比面对潜藏在我们看似高尚行为之下的痛苦和愧疚要容易得多。更难的是，我们要平静地接受自己不再有益于自身的牺牲倾向，转身离开，去体验折磨者和“坏人”带来的不适影响。77 持续的觉察而不做出反应，并真诚地致力于忠于自我，将逐渐改变我们。

With time and willingness, you can overcome the gravity of the sacrificer/tormentor/bad person, and give to your partner what you truly want to give. In the giving you will come to know your essential self.

只要有时间和意愿，你就能克服那个牺牲者/折磨者/坏人的阴影，给予你的伴侣你真正想给予的东西。在付出的过程中，你会逐渐认识真正的自己。

***

RELATIONSHIPS SWING LIKE A PENDULUM DOES

人际关系就像钟摆一样摇摆不定

———————————

“It takes two to Tango.”

“跳探戈需要两个人。”

—Proverb

-谚语

I would like to point out one last aspect of sacrifice before we go on to other traps in the Victim Prison. This last item is related to what I call the “pendulum effect.” The premise of this model is that if you are sacrificing for your mate, then you will see him/her as someone who takes advantage of you, the sacrificer, by not pulling his or her own weight. The degree to which one sacrifices will equal the degree of apparent indulgence in the other. Every sacrificer requires such an “indulger” to exist.

在继续探讨“受害者牢笼”中的其他陷阱之前，我想指出牺牲的最后一个方面。这一点与我称之为“钟摆效应”的现象有关。这个模型的前提是，如果你为伴侣牺牲，那么你就会觉得他/她利用了你这个牺牲者，因为他/她没有尽到自己的责任。一方牺牲的程度与另一方表面上表现出的纵容程度成正比。每一个牺牲者都需要这样一个“纵容者”的存在。

How could you always be picking up after someone unless that someone was always leaving things around to be picked up? How could you sacrifice yourself to listening to someone chatter on endlessly unless there was someone to do the chattering? For every sacrificer there is an indulger and vice versa. If you are the sacrificer you cannot change your partner unless you give up your sacrifice. You cannot give up your sacrifice until you recognize that it is not your “job” to change your partner or compensate for his/her behaviour. If your mate indulges in anger, it is not your god-given mission to try and maintain peace. If your partner is addicted to gambling, it is not your job to make up for the lack of money in the house by overworking. His/her alcoholism is not your burden, so you are not required to relinquish your spontaneity and passion in order to provide a stable and predictable environment to compensate for your partner’s instability and unpredictability. After saying all this, I will follow up by saying that, although it is not your job to compensate for your partner’s indulgences, your partner’s indulgences are your responsibility. That is, you have the power to respond to your partner without sacrifice.

除非对方总是乱扔东西让你收拾，否则你怎么可能总是替别人收拾烂摊子？除非有人喋喋不休，否则你怎么可能甘愿牺牲自己去倾听别人没完没了的唠叨？每个付出者都对应着一个放纵者，反之亦然。如果你是付出者，除非你放弃付出，否则你无法改变你的伴侣。而只有当你意识到改变伴侣或弥补其行为并非你的“责任”时，你才能放弃付出。如果你的伴侣沉溺于愤怒，维持家庭和平并非你的天职。如果你的伴侣沉迷赌博，你无需通过过度工作来弥补家庭经济的不足。他/她的酗酒并非你的负担，因此你无需为了弥补伴侣的不稳定和不可预测性而放弃你的热情和活力，去营造一个稳定可预测的环境。说了这么多，我还要补充一点：虽然你没有义务弥补伴侣的放纵，但伴侣的放纵却是你的责任。也就是说，你有能力在不做出牺牲的情况下回应伴侣。

It’s easy to forget that both parties are 100% responsible for what happens in the relationship. Often you may see a situation where one person is working his/her buns off while the other one in the relationship is not pulling an equal share of the load. An alcoholic relationship is often depicted as having one long-suffering partner, slaving to keep the relationship or family together, while the other is indulging in selfish pursuit of pleasure. But in the last few decades, it has been shown that the sacrificer is equally responsible for the dysfunction in that situation. If you have sacrifice in your life, it will attract a corresponding indulgence. 78

人们很容易忘记，双方对关系中发生的一切负有百分之百的责任。我们常常会看到这样的情况：一方拼命工作，而另一方却没有承担同等的负担。酗酒关系通常被描绘成一方长期忍受痛苦，为了维系关系或家庭而辛勤付出，而另一方则沉溺于自私的享乐之中。但近几十年的研究表明，在这种关系中，付出的一方同样要为关系的失衡负责。如果你在生活中有所付出，就会吸引相应的放纵。78

This dynamic can be played out by two people, where one indulges while the other sacrifices; but if you want to see something really fascinating, ask each of those people privately which one sacrifices more. Most often, the reply will be that the one you are talking to is most burdened with the debt of living. Even if the one you are talking to may seem to be less active or productive at the moment, that is only because s/he is “resting” from a hard week at work, a tough month, a rough year, maybe even a miserable childhood. Indulgers will often justify their tendencies with a story of sacrifice in their life. This points to a very important understanding: sacrifice is not in the action. Sacrifice is in the mind . Washing dishes may be either a fun time or a horrendous drag. The experience is determined purely by the attitude. How to change the attitude? I start by wanting to, but I also recognize that I need some extraordinary help to pull me out of this lifetime pattern that began before I was even conscious of what I was choosing to do. I sacrificed myself for my family out of an instinct for physical and emotional survival.

这种动态可以在两个人身上体现出来，一个人放纵享乐，另一个人则做出牺牲；但如果你想看到真正引人入胜的现象，不妨私下问问他们，谁的牺牲更多。通常情况下，答案会是那个背负着生活重担的人。即使你正在交谈的那个人此刻看起来不那么活跃或高效，那也只是因为他/她正在从辛苦的工作周、艰难的月份、难熬的一年，甚至可能是悲惨的童年中“休息”。放纵者常常会用自己生活中的牺牲故事来为自己的倾向辩解。这引出了一个非常重要的道理：牺牲不在于行动，而在于心态。洗碗可能是一件乐事，也可能是一件令人痛苦不堪的事。这种体验完全取决于你的态度。如何改变这种态度呢？我首先是想改变，但我同时也意识到，我需要一些非凡的帮助才能摆脱这种在我意识到自己选择之前就已经形成的终身模式。出于对身体和情感生存的本能，我为家人牺牲了自己。

If you look at the pendulum model, you can deduce that the further you are away from the centre, the more extreme the levels of sacrifice and indulgence. Since they are in a symbiotic relationship, if you end one you also end the other. I have found that whatever side I’m swinging to, I can always call on the power in the centre to help me. In the centre I find the power of my soul—or essence—giving me all the support I could ever need. Since my soul doesn’t judge me or punish me, I can trust it to lovingly guide me out of the indulgence or sacrifice.

如果你观察钟摆模型，你会发现，离中心越远，牺牲和放纵的程度就越极端。由于它们之间存在共生关系，如果你停止其中一方，另一方也会随之停止。我发现，无论我摇摆到哪一边，我总能借助中心的力量来帮助我。在中心，我找到了我灵魂——或者说本质——的力量，它给予我所需的一切支持。因为我的灵魂不会评判我，也不会惩罚我，所以我可以信任它，它会充满爱地引导我走出放纵或牺牲的泥沼。

Once you become consciously aware of the sacrifice, you can focus on the power at the centre and ask for love to guide you out. Sacrifice is in the mind. Only love can reach into the mind and transform the pattern of giving without receiving (sacrifice) and taking without enjoying (indulgence) into an experience of true giving and heartfelt receiving. All that we need do—indeed, pretty well all we can do—is allow the love of our soul to guide us back to our centre, where the love abides. Practice, practice, practice.

一旦你意识到自己做出了牺牲，你就可以专注于内心深处的力量，并祈求爱指引你走出困境。牺牲存在于你的头脑中。只有爱才能深入你的头脑，将只付出不回报（牺牲）和只索取不享受（放纵）的模式，转化为真正付出和发自内心的接受。我们所需要做的——实际上，几乎是我们所能做的一切——就是让灵魂的爱指引我们回到内心深处，回到爱的所在。练习，练习，再练习。

***

FUSION—THE TIES THAT BIND

融合——维系纽带

———————————

“A cage went in search of a bird.”

“一个笼子去寻找一只鸟。”

—Franz Kafka

——弗朗茨·卡夫卡

My wife and I had been married for three months when it happened. Su Mei was in her first trimester and not feeling well physically or emotionally. I was sitting at a desk in the hallway of our house, doodling on a piece of paper when she walked by behind me. Immediately, I jumped up and looked around for the vacuum cleaner, as I had suddenly decided to do some house cleaning. Then I would do the dishes, chop some wood for the fire, fold the laundry and...and then I realized it was 11:45 P.M.! Five minutes earlier, the big job I was contemplating was pulling back the covers and going to bed. Now I was seconds away from renovating the living room! Then I recognized what I was feeling. I remembered when I was seven or eight, and my mother was going through some very unhappy times. I felt cut off from her, and somehow to blame for her unhappiness, so I deduced that it was my job to cure her. She was always commenting on the perpetual disorder and mess in the house (small wonder with eight kids and a dog), so I figured that maybe if I kept the house clean, she would cheer up. If she were happy, I’d feel more secure, and maybe she’d like me again—maybe even love me! Twenty-five years later I found myself once again in the presence of an unhappy mother, and through all that time I had never come up with a better solution than cleaning the house. Before I was even aware of my motives, I was unconsciously reaching for the vacuum cleaner.

我和妻子结婚三个月后，这件事发生了。苏梅当时正处于孕早期，身心都有些不适。我坐在家里走廊的桌子旁，在一张纸上涂鸦，她从我身后走过。我立刻跳起来四处寻找吸尘器，因为我突然决定要打扫一下房子。然后我还要洗碗、劈柴、叠衣服……然后我才意识到已经是晚上11点45分了！五分钟前，我还在琢磨着掀开被子睡觉呢。现在我却差点就要开始翻修客厅了！这时我才意识到自己当时的感受。我想起了七八岁的时候，母亲经历了一段非常不愉快的时光。我感觉和她很疏远，好像她的不快乐都是我的错，所以我认定我的责任就是治愈她。她总是抱怨家里永远乱糟糟的（八个孩子加一条狗，难怪），所以我寻思着，如果我把家里收拾干净，她或许会高兴起来。她开心了，我也会更有安全感，说不定她还会喜欢我——甚至爱上我！二十五年后，我又一次面对着一位不开心的母亲，这么多年来，我始终没能想到比打扫房子更好的办法。甚至在我意识到自己的动机之前，我就下意识地拿起了吸尘器。

When we urgently need a parent to love us, while at the same time feeling that we are not worthy of that love, sometimes we will do anything—no matter what the cost to ourselves—to make sure that parent doesn’t exclude us. In my case, I threw away every part of myself that I deemed unattractive to my mother and did my best to become the perfect son. I became her charming little helper, and in that way moulded myself to meet what I thought were her needs. I threw away huge chunks of myself so I could fit her requirements, and clung to her—emotionally, if not physically—like a kitten halfway up a curtain. This is an example of fusion: it is a tremendous sacrifice we make to ensure that we are not abandoned. We sacrifice ourselves.

当我们迫切需要父母的爱，同时又觉得自己不配得到这份爱时，有时我们会不惜一切代价——无论付出多大的代价——也要确保父母不会抛弃我们。就我而言，我抛弃了所有我认为不符合母亲心意的特质，竭尽全力成为她眼中完美的儿子。我成了她讨人喜欢的小帮手，并以此塑造自己，以满足我认为她的需求。我舍弃了自己很大一部分，只为符合她的要求，像一只攀附在窗帘上的小猫一样，在情感上（而非身体上）紧紧依偎着她。这就是融合的一个例子：为了不被抛弃，我们做出了巨大的牺牲。我们牺牲了自己。

Fusion can start as early as three years of age and continue until we approach adolescence, so it’s easy to see how it could become a major aspect of who we think we are. 79 Imagine a child throwing away her aggression and willfulness to please Dad, rejecting her intelligence to seem harmless and dependent on someone much wiser than she, becoming blind to her artistic qualities to assure Dad she would be a practical little girl, becoming less outgoing so she could stay closer to home, or rejecting her solitude so that her father would be proud of how popular she is. Imagine if all this and more had been the choice of one child? How quickly would she become a one-dimensional human being with very predictable characteristics? She would have thrown away every aspect of herself that did not fit what she thought her father wanted from her. And what her father wanted from his daughter would be what he felt he was lacking in his life. Like a half of a broken heart, he would be searching for the other half that would fit him perfectly, and she would try to shape herself into that other half so that they could “bond.” Think of the incredible sacrifice that she would have to make in order to “belong.” That is the price of fusion, an inauthentic form of bonding. Its motive is need and its glue is sacrifice. It is not in fact bonding at all—it is bondage.

融合最早可从三岁开始，一直持续到青春期，因此很容易理解它如何成为我们自我认知的重要组成部分。<sup>79</sup> 想象一下，一个孩子为了取悦父亲而抛弃自己的攻击性和任性，为了显得无害且依赖比她更有智慧的人而否定自己的智慧，为了向父亲保证自己会是一个务实的小女孩而对自己的艺术天赋视而不见，为了待在家里而变得内向，或者为了让父亲为她的受欢迎程度而拒绝独处。想象一下，如果所有这些，甚至更多，都是一个孩子所做出的选择，她会多么迅速地变成一个性格单一、特征可预测的人？她会抛弃所有不符合她认为父亲期望的特质。而她父亲想要从女儿身上得到的，正是他觉得自己生活中所缺失的。就像一颗破碎的心，他会寻找另一半，一个与他完美契合的灵魂；而她则会努力塑造自己，成为他生命中的另一半，以便彼此“结合”。想想她为了“归属”需要做出多么巨大的牺牲。这就是融合的代价，一种虚假的结合。它的动机是需要，它的粘合剂是牺牲。它根本不是结合，而是束缚。

To help you better understand fusion, perhaps a mental picture would serve. Imagine the parent you are most fused to is standing in front of you. Then visualize that you are somehow inescapably bound to that person. Perhaps you each have tentacles like two octopuses tangled with each other. Perhaps you are fused together at the hip like Siamese twins. Maybe a huge chain is wrapped around both of you. A female client came up with the scenario of half her body caught in a huge leg-hold trap that was chained to her father. One very popular image of fusion is that of an umbilical cord attached at both belly buttons. Whatever the image, the form of bondage is representative of the emotional attachment that keeps you in a state of sacrifice from which there seems to be no escape. The person caught in the fusion may feel frustrated by the containment, straitjacketed or smothered—as if the parent were sucking away the very air around him/her.

为了帮助你更好地理解融合，或许一个形象的画面会有所帮助。想象一下，你最亲近的父母站在你面前。然后想象你与这个人之间有着某种无法挣脱的联系。也许你们就像两只章鱼一样，触手缠绕在一起。也许你们像连体婴一样，髋部融合在一起。也许一条巨大的锁链缠绕着你们。一位女性客户设想，她半个身体被一个巨大的夹腿陷阱困住，而这个陷阱又被锁链拴在她父亲身上。融合的一个非常流行的形象是，脐带连接在两个人的肚脐上。无论是什么形象，这种束缚形式都代表着一种情感上的依恋，它让你处于一种牺牲的状态，似乎无法摆脱。被困在融合中的人可能会因为这种束缚而感到沮丧、沮丧或窒息——仿佛父母正在吸走他/她周围的空气。

For most people a survival mechanism will kick in, causing the individual to push away from this inauthentic form of bonding and flee to independence from that parent. This attempt at breaking away tends to take time, and intensifies as the child approaches adolescence. But the fusion is not broken, and you discover this as soon as you enter an important relationship with someone of the same sex as the parent you were fused to. You gradually begin to realize you are relating to that person in the same way that you did with that parent. You even begin to feel like you are living with that parent.

对大多数人来说，一种生存机制会启动，促使个体摆脱这种不真实的依恋形式，并寻求独立于父母之外。这种挣脱的过程往往需要时间，并且随着孩子接近青春期而愈发强烈。但这种融合并未真正消失，当你与一位与你曾经融合的父母性别相同的人建立重要关系时，你就会发现这一点。你会逐渐意识到，你与这个人相处的方式，与你曾经与那位父母相处的方式如出一辙。你甚至会开始感觉自己仿佛与那位父母生活在一起。

To summarize, then: when, as a child, you lose the sense of bonding—or human love—with one or both of your parents, you become torn between the need to belong and the sense that you are not good enough to be loved. Therefore you mould yourself around what you think will cause that parent to keep you close, throwing away aspects of your personality in order to form an inauthentic form of bonding called fusion. When you break out of the stranglehold, you do not necessarily dissolve the fusion—you temporarily distance yourself from it. As soon as you spend time around a person towards whom you feel some degree of dependency (e.g. a sexual partner, an authority figure, a creditor, etc.), you will find yourself behaving in a way that does not really benefit you or make you feel good about yourself. But you would feel too fearful of being excluded to act any other way.

总而言之：当孩童时期，你与父母一方或双方失去亲密感——或者说人与人之间的爱——你便会在归属感的渴望和觉得自己不够好、不值得被爱的矛盾心理之间挣扎。因此，你会努力塑造自己，以期获得父母的关爱，抛弃自身性格的某些方面，从而形成一种虚假的亲密关系，称为“融合”。当你挣脱这种束缚时，你未必能消除融合——你只是暂时与它保持距离。一旦你与某个你感到某种程度依赖的人（例如性伴侣、权威人士、债主等）相处，你就会发现自己的行为方式实际上对你并无益处，也无法让你感到自我价值。但你又害怕被排斥，所以不敢采取其他任何行动。

At a certain point your fusion to your parent(s) is largely transferred to your partner, and its smothering effects tend to be felt most strongly in the Introspection stage. The person experiencing it will often feel that s/he does not have a life of her/his own, and is tempted to blame the partner for taking that life away. If this happens to you, it is important to realize that what is happening is a re-experience of an old feeling. The temptation to push away the partner is actually a re-visitation of the desire to reject the parent to which you were fused. It is not always necessary to throw away your relationship to end the fusion. 80 Along with awareness, your willingness and determination to reclaim the parts of you that you threw away will assist you in healing the wounds of fusion. Be aware of the physical and emotional sensations of the fusion, and notice how familiar they are—how long you have been carrying them inside you.

在某个阶段，你与父母的融合很大程度上会转移到你的伴侣身上，这种窒息感在内省阶段往往最为强烈。经历这种融合的人常常会感到自己没有属于自己的生活，并会忍不住责怪伴侣夺走了自己的生活。如果你也经历这种情况，重要的是要意识到，这其实是对旧有感受的重现。想要推开伴侣的冲动，实际上是对曾经与你融合的父母的拒绝欲望的重新体验。结束这种融合并不总是需要放弃你们的关系。80 除了觉察之外，你重新找回那些被你抛弃的自我部分的意愿和决心，将有助于你疗愈融合带来的创伤。觉察融合带来的生理和情感感受，并留意它们是多么熟悉——你已经在内心深处承受了多久。

Imagine that you were given the opportunity to paint a picture of your emotional fusion to your partner. See the picture in your mind as best you can, so that you can now see what you have been doing emotionally. Whatever your partner’s mood, you had to adjust. Wherever his/her moods have taken your partner, you had to go as well, surrendering your choice to the fusion. Be aware of any feelings of resentment, fear, frustration, or anxiety that may be present as you view this scene. Next, state your intention to be free of this bondage, calling upon your determination to fuel your will. Either verbally or mentally express to your partner that it is no longer true to continue this false relationship, and that what you are choosing is what is best for both of you. Then visualize a picture of you breaking free from the bondage. Experience all the feelings connected to this image, and then paint a third picture of the two of you—how you will appear once the bondage is ended. If there is still conflict or lack of peace in this picture make note of it, then draw another one in your mind. You may need a number of pictures until you can envision both of you as you are really meant to be in the relationship. The reason for this is that, even when ended peacefully, the severing of the fusion can cause adverse reactions in both of you as you seek to establish foundations based on Truth. Typically, people caught in the fusion trap have a very deep fear of losing their false security, and one will be less willing to let go than the other. It takes courage and trust to be yourself in any relationship, and your determination to do so will set off a chain reaction that is not always pleasant. Drawing pictures in your mind (it may be more effective to put them down on paper, in clay, or represent them through some other artistic medium) allows you to intuitively see what lays ahead for you.

想象一下，你有机会描绘你与伴侣情感融合的画面。尽可能清晰地在脑海中呈现这幅画面，以便看清你一直以来的情感状态。无论伴侣的情绪如何，你都必须做出调整。无论伴侣的情绪将他/她带向何方，你也必须随之而去，将自己的选择交付于这种融合。在描绘这幅画面时，请留意任何可能存在的怨恨、恐惧、沮丧或焦虑等情绪。接下来，表达你想要摆脱这种束缚的意愿，并运用你的决心来增强你的意志力。用言语或在心中向伴侣表达，继续这段虚假的关系已经不再合适，而你现在的选择对你们双方都是最好的。然后，想象你挣脱束缚的画面。体验与这幅画面相关的所有感受，然后描绘第三幅你们两人的画面——当束缚解除后，你们将会是什么样子。如果这幅画面中仍然存在冲突或不和谐，请记录下来，然后在脑海中绘制另一幅画面。你可能需要描绘许多画面，才能真正想象出你们在关系中应有的样子。这是因为，即使和平分手，当你们试图建立基于真理的基础时，融合的断裂也会在你们双方心中引发负面反应。通常，陷入融合陷阱的人内心深处都害怕失去虚假的安全感，其中一方往往比另一方更不愿意放手。在任何关系中做自己都需要勇气和信任，而你这样做的决心会引发一系列连锁反应，这些反应并不总是令人愉快的。在脑海中描绘画面（或许用纸笔、黏土或其他艺术媒介来表现会更有效），能让你凭直觉预见未来。

The power of this exercise rests in your intention to reclaim your true nature, and your willingness to actualize this intention. Actualization occurs when you are clear about what you want—what you intuitively sense is good for you—and your willingness to accept that your partner does not have to be your source. As you become clearer about who you are, you step towards the Truth. Often, you will see your partner take that same step—in his/her time. At this point you have reclaimed the power of your own choice, and can choose your partner again; not from need this time, but from a sense of what is right for you. 81

这项练习的力量在于你重拾真我的意愿，以及你实现这一意愿的决心。当你清楚自己想要什么——你凭直觉感受到什么对你有益——并且愿意接受伴侣不必是你的唯一依靠时，愿望便得以实现。随着你越来越了解自己，你便迈向真理。通常，你会看到你的伴侣也在他/她认为合适的时机迈出同样的步伐。此时，你已经重新掌握了选择的主动权，可以再次选择你的伴侣；这一次，不是出于需要，而是出于对自身真正需求的感知。<sup>81</sup>

***

MIRROR, MIRROR ON THE WALL

魔镜魔镜告诉我

———————————

“Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men? The shadow knows.”

谁知道人心中潜藏着怎样的邪恶？只有阴影知道。

From the 1930s radio show called “The Shadow,” by Walter Gibson

出自沃尔特·吉布森创作于 20 世纪 30 年代的广播剧《影子》。

I read a great story in the newspaper many years ago—long before I even knew the universal implications of its message. It was a true account of a group of well meaning Christians who travelled to remote villages in India to tell the villagers about Jesus. They came to a farming area that was not very advanced technologically. In fact the villagers there had never seen television or movies, and had just been introduced to electricity. To give these simple people a better understanding of who Jesus was, the Christian group brought a big movie projector, and set up a huge screen on a hillside. Thousands of local men, women and children, came out when the sun went down and sat on the ground to watch the movie. The audience became completely absorbed in the story, so much so that when Jesus’ crucifixion was depicted, the crowd went wild. At the sight of the nails being driven into his hands, the audience rose up and charged the screen, attempting to save Jesus by pulling him off the cross. I had a good laugh at this story and the childlike naïveté of those simple people. Fifteen years later I came to recognize how much like those uninformed villagers I actually was. It took me that long to comprehend projection.

很多年前，我在报纸上读到一篇精彩的故事——那时我甚至还不了解它所传递信息的普世意义。故事讲述的是一群心地善良的基督徒前往印度偏远村庄，向村民们讲述耶稣的故事。他们来到一个科技落后的农业区。事实上，那里的村民从未见过电视或电影，电力也才刚刚普及。为了让这些淳朴的村民更好地了解耶稣，这群基督徒带来了一台大型电影放映机，并在山坡上架起了一块巨大的银幕。日落之后，成千上万的当地男女老少来到山上，坐在地上观看电影。观众们完全沉浸在故事中，以至于当耶稣被钉十字架的场景出现时，人群沸腾了。当钉子钉入耶稣的手时，观众们纷纷起身冲向银幕，试图将耶稣从十字架上拉下来。读到这个故事，以及那些淳朴村民孩童般的纯真，我不禁开怀大笑。十五年后，我才意识到自己其实和那些不明真相的村民有多么相似。我花了那么长时间才理解投射的含义。

We tend to have a lot of opinions about other people. Some of them are complimentary while others are harsh and judgmental. It seems that the more we get to know someone, the more opinions—good and bad—we form about them. It’s all part of becoming “familiar” with somebody. But we rarely question where these opinions come from. Basically, the opinions we form come from observing the other person’s actions and interpreting their meaning to suit some inner requirement of ours.

我们往往对他人有很多看法。有些是赞扬，有些则是苛刻和评判。似乎我们越了解一个人，就越会形成关于他的看法——好的和坏的都有。这都是“熟悉”一个人的过程。但我们很少质疑这些看法从何而来。基本上，我们形成的看法源于观察他人的行为，并根据我们内心的某种需求去解读这些行为的含义。

Two people watch a well-dressed man give a homeless person a dollar. One of the observers opines that the well-dressed man is generous and kind; the other observer opines that the man is cheap and arrogant. Who’s right? In reality neither of the observers were right—or wrong, for that matter. Both of them were projecting certain values that they hold about themselves onto the well-dressed man. All our interpretations of what we see in another are simply projections of our evaluations and core beliefs about ourselves.

两个人看着一个衣着考究的男人给一个流浪汉一美元。其中一人认为这个男人慷慨善良；另一人则认为他吝啬傲慢。谁是对的？实际上，两人都说得不对，或者说都说得不对。他们都把自己的一些价值观投射到了这个男人身上。我们对他人行为的所有解读，其实都只是我们自身评价和核心信念的投射。

When I first heard about projections, I refused to believe any of it. I was adamant that I was me and everyone else was everyone else, and my judgments and opinions of others were not reflections of me. One day that all changed. I was talking to a friend of mine, criticizing a co-worker for certain obvious faults. Suddenly my friend turned to me and said, “It sounds like you’re talking about yourself there, Chris.” The more I insisted that I was not at all like this other jerk, the more my friend laughed, until I could no longer object. Smiling in spite of my shame, I admitted to my friend that he was right.

我第一次听说“投射”这个词时，完全不相信。我坚信我就是我，别人就是别人，我对别人的评判和看法与我自身毫无关系。直到有一天，一切都改变了。当时我和一个朋友聊天，正在批评一位同事的几个显而易见的缺点。突然，朋友转过头对我说：“克里斯，你这话听起来好像是在说你自己。”我越是坚持说我跟那个混蛋完全不一样，朋友就越是笑个不停，直到我再也无言以对。尽管羞愧难当，我还是笑着承认朋友说得对。

Since then I have often realized that everything we see is a reflection of what is already inside us. Whatever we judge in someone else is what we believe to be true about ourselves. If I reject someone for being too critical, I am projecting how harshly I reject my own critical nature. Maybe that one is a bit obvious—criticizing someone for being critical—but it is the same for all my opinions. What I attack in someone else is what I am unconsciously attacking in me. Unfortunately I usually remain unaware that I am simply seeing myself in a mirror (which is too bad, because there are a lot of gifted people that I waste time envying when I could be recognizing my own giftedness through them).

从那时起，我常常意识到，我们所看到的一切都是我们内心世界的反映。我们对别人的评判，其实就是我们认为自身存在的某种特质。如果我因为别人过于挑剔而拒绝他们，那其实是我在投射自己对自身挑剔性格的苛刻否定。或许这一点显而易见——批评别人挑剔——但这同样适用于我的所有观点。我攻击别人身上的缺点，其实是我在潜意识里攻击自己身上的缺点。可惜的是，我通常意识不到自己只是在照镜子（这很遗憾，因为我浪费时间去羡慕那些才华横溢的人，而我本可以从他们身上发现自身的天赋）。

A Shadow Figure is an individual who possesses the qualities that you judge to be the worst parts of yourself. Of course, when you first meet that person you don’t immediately realize (if you ever do) that you are seeing yourself. That’s because this individual carries one or more negative attributes that you completely and utterly rejected in yourself to the point that you have denied their very existence within you.

阴影人物指的是一个拥有你认为自身最糟糕的特质的人。当然，当你第一次遇到这个人时，你不会立刻意识到（或者即使意识到了）你看到的正是你自己。这是因为这个人身上携带着一种或多种你完全彻底地排斥的负面特质，以至于你否认了它们在你内心深处的存在。

Although projection often begins to show up in the Disillusionment Stage, it really starts to rear its ugly head at Introspection, when your partner assumes the role of Shadow Figure. You will judge him or her to be objectionable to the point of repulsion, and you may even develop a burning hatred of him or her. Jung suggested that to completely accept your Shadow Figure calls for the highest moral courage; in my experience, though, my highest moral courage was not enough. I needed a miracle. The miracle came through my curiosity.

虽然投射现象通常在幻灭阶段开始显现，但它真正开始肆虐是在内省阶段，此时你的伴侣会扮演阴影人物的角色。你会觉得他/她令人反感，甚至厌恶，你甚至可能对他/她产生强烈的憎恨。荣格认为，完全接纳你的阴影人物需要极高的道德勇气；然而，就我的经验而言，即使拥有极高的道德勇气也远远不够。我需要一个奇迹。而奇迹就来自我的好奇心。

I began to wonder if I was wrong about my conviction that Shadow Figures defied the laws of projection and were simply the incarnation of evil in the world. I developed this conviction in my early teens, and had it reinforced until I was in my mid thirties. During those years there was rarely a time when there was not some S.O.B. making my life miserable. Sometimes it was a co-worker; other times it was a close friend who just “changed” all of a sudden and became the bane of my existence. Honestly, there were times when my thoughts would be completely preoccupied with fantasies of my Shadow Figure’s death. Then the miracle occurred as a simple thought that asked me, “What if it’s you, Christopher? What if what you hate about that person is really you—and since you would never want to acknowledge that part of yourself, you would control your behaviour so that you never acted that way?”

我开始怀疑自己之前关于“阴影人物”的信念是否错误，我原以为他们违背了投射法则，仅仅是世间邪恶的化身。这种信念在我十几岁时就已形成，并一直强化到三十多岁。在那几年里，几乎总有一些混蛋让我痛苦不堪。有时是同事，有时是突然“变了”的好朋友，成了我生命中的噩梦。说实话，有好几次，我的脑海里全是“阴影人物”死亡的幻想。然后，奇迹发生了，一个简单的念头让我恍然大悟：“如果那个人就是你自己呢，克里斯托弗？如果你憎恨的那个人其实就是你自己——而你永远不愿承认自己有这样的一面，所以你会控制自己的行为，让自己永远不会那样做呢？”

My curiosity got the better of me. I asked myself to imagine what would make a person act like a complete jerk. So he talks too much—what would make him do that? The answer that came to me was “Insecurity.” And what about you, Christopher? Do you feel insecure? Well yes, but I don’t act like that! Of course not, you don’t criticize people out loud because that isn’t nice. But what do you suppose makes him so loudly critical of other people’s mistakes? Because he believes he’s a failure. Correct, just like you do. But instead of being loudly critical, Christopher, you keep your criticisms to yourself because you think people will like you more if you are nice. So you’re a quiet failure and he’s a loud one.

我的好奇心战胜了理智。我问自己，究竟是什么让一个人表现得像个十足的混蛋？比如他话太多——是什么让他这样？我想到的答案是“缺乏安全感”。克里斯托弗，你呢？你缺乏安全感吗？嗯，是的，但我不会那样做！当然不会，你不会大声批评别人，因为那样不礼貌。但你觉得是什么让他如此大声地批评别人的错误呢？因为他觉得自己是个失败者。没错，就像你一样。但克里斯托弗，你不会大声批评别人，而是把批评藏在心里，因为你觉得如果你表现得友善，别人会更喜欢你。所以你是个默默的失败者，而他是个大声的失败者。

My exploration continued. With every step, I realized how much alike my Shadow and I were on the inside. We had vastly different—and usually opposite ways—of compensating for what we rejected about ourselves, but we were rejecting the very same painful, limiting feelings and beliefs we carried inside. Like most people, I thought it was my Shadow Figure’s behaviour that was bothering me. But my judgment of the behaviour was merely the righteousness of my Persecutor, compensating for my recognition of the negative quality I was seeing beneath the behaviour. In the example above, I was acting quietly as a compensation for my sense of failure, while my Shadow Figure was acting loudly to compensate for the same sense of failure. I looked at my quiet compensator as being better than his loud one, thus distancing myself from the real shadow beneath both of our behaviours.

我的探索仍在继续。每走一步，我都意识到我和我的阴影在内心深处是多么相似。我们用截然不同——通常是相反的方式——来弥补我们自己所排斥的那些特质，但我们排斥的，恰恰是内心深处那些痛苦的、限制性的感受和信念。和大多数人一样，我以为困扰我的是我的阴影人物的行为。但我对这种行为的评判，其实只是迫害者的自以为是，它掩盖了我对这种行为背后负面特质的认知。在上面的例子中，我默默地行事是为了弥补我的失败感，而我的阴影人物则大声喧哗，同样是为了弥补这种失败感。我把默默的补偿者看作比大声的补偿者更好，从而让自己远离了隐藏在我们两人行为背后的真正阴影。

For years I have practiced the following method of integrating my Shadow Figures. Sometimes it is slow going, for there are still aspects of myself which I am scared to admit are actually me. But with determination, willingness, and the help of my soul, I have consistently seen that my Shadow is me. If you are confronted with a partner, friend, acquaintance, relative, or even a stranger that you find it impossible to tolerate, much less love and accept, this exercise may be a great help to you:

多年来，我一直实践以下方法来整合我的阴影人格。有时进展缓慢，因为我仍然害怕承认自己身上存在一些我不敢承认的面向。但凭借决心、意愿和灵魂的指引，我始终能够看到，我的阴影就是我。如果你遇到一位伴侣、朋友、熟人、亲戚，甚至是陌生人，你发现自己无法容忍，更遑论爱和接纳，那么这个练习或许能对你大有帮助：

1. What is the negative attribute of the person that causes you to react? Remember to stay away from behaviour and focus on inner qualities. If you focus on behaviour, ask yourself what your Shadow must be believing or feeling about him/her self to cause the behaviour.

1. 是什么负面特质导致你对这个人产生反应？记住，不要只关注行为，而要关注内在品质。如果你确实关注了行为，那就问问自己，你的阴影面一定是这样看待自己，才会产生这种行为。

2. Once you get the answer to #1, find the belief or feeling in you that is the same as your Shadow’s. Accept that part of yourself as best you can. Own it. Your shadow is your mirror image. When you lift your right hand, your reflection lifts what seems to be its left hand. But you’re both lifting your hand for the same reason. The behaviour may be opposite, but the motive is identical.

2. 一旦你找到了第一个问题的答案，就找到你内心与你的阴影相同的信念或感受。尽可能地接纳你内心的这一部分，并坦然接受它。你的阴影是你的镜像。当你举起右手时，你的倒影也会举起看似是左手的那只手。但你们举手的原因其实是一样的。行为可能相反，但动机却完全相同。

3. You may feel a little uncomfortable once you decide to accept the part of yourself that you were rejecting,. It is not pleasant to acknowledge your hateful judgments as being self-judgments, but the discomfort will not last long. As a matter of fact the discomfort is a sign that the process is working, for Truth is sometimes a bitter medicine.

3. 当你决定接受自己一直以来所排斥的那部分自我时，你可能会感到有些不自在。承认自己那些充满憎恨的评判其实是自我评判，这并不容易，但这种不适感不会持续太久。事实上，这种不适感恰恰表明这个过程正在奏效，因为真理有时是一剂苦药。

4. Now express your appreciation of something you admire about that person. This step I found to be a very expedient way to transform the Shadow Figure. By looking for something you can admire and respect, you open your heart to this other person. If the Shadow Figure is your partner, this step has the power to reignite a flame that you may have thought was extinguished. Also, since projections can be positive as well as negative, when you appreciate a gift in someone else you make it possible to own that same quality in yourself.

4. 现在，表达你对对方身上你欣赏的某个特质的赞赏。我发现这一步是转化阴影人物非常有效的方法。通过寻找你欣赏和尊重的事物，你就能敞开心扉接纳对方。如果阴影人物是你的伴侣，这一步能够重新点燃你可能以为已经熄灭的火焰。此外，由于投射既可以是积极的也可以是消极的，当你欣赏他人身上的某种特质时，你也有可能在自己身上拥有同样的品质。

5. Go back to #1. Keep following these four steps until you feel close to the other person and the Shadow has disappeared. Remember that the closer you are emotionally to your Shadow Figure, the more intense and challenging this process will be—and the more rewarding. For once you have integrated your Shadow, all the gifts that you rejected in your past can now return. You have reopened the door to your soul.

5. 回到第一步。重复这四个步骤，直到你感觉与对方亲近，阴影消失。记住，你在情感上与你的阴影越亲近，这个过程就越强烈、越具有挑战性——但也越有意义。一旦你整合了你的阴影，所有你过去拒绝的礼物都可以回归。你已经重新打开了通往你灵魂的大门。

***

SEXUAL GUILT

性方面的罪恶感

———————————

“It’s your choice: sex without guilt, or guilt without sex.”

“这是你的选择：要么无愧于心地享受性爱，要么带着愧疚而放弃性爱。”

—Anonymous

-匿名的

In a movie I saw once, Woody Allen was playing a character who was being praised by a woman for being a great lover. He acknowledged his expertise proudly, explaining that he practiced a lot when he was by himself. Unfortunately many people do not always have such confidence and positive feelings regarding their sexuality, and can often remain unaware of some personal block until they are involved in a significant emotional relationship.

我曾经看过一部电影，伍迪·艾伦饰演的角色被一位女士称赞为情场高手。他自豪地承认自己的“本领”，并解释说这是他独处时经常练习的结果。可惜的是，很多人对自己的性能力并没有这样的自信和积极的态度，而且往往直到进入一段重要的情感关系后，才会意识到自身存在的某些障碍。

The growth of sexual guilt at the Introspection Stage can lead to deadness in the bedroom, sexual difficulties, a man’s sense of lost potency, a woman’s sense of lost attractiveness, temptations towards other sexual partners, busyness, tiredness, physical repulsion towards the partner, triangle relationships, and divorce or separation. Some of the remarks I have heard around this particular process are:

在内省阶段，性内疚感的增长会导致性生活冷淡、性功能障碍、男性性能力下降、女性魅力受损、对其他性伴侣产生诱惑、忙碌、疲惫、对伴侣产生生理上的厌恶感、三角关系，甚至离婚或分居。我听到的一些关于这一过程的评论包括：

• “I’d rather just spend my time reading a good book.”

“我宁愿把时间花在读一本好书上。”

• “Sometimes when I’m making love, I feel like I’m having sex with my mother!”

• “有时候做爱的时候，我感觉就像在和我妈妈做爱一样！”

• “I feel so uptight—I just can’t get it up.”

• “我感觉好紧张——我根本硬不起来。”

• “The thought of making love to him makes me want to throw up.”

• “一想到要和他做爱，我就想吐。”

• “I’m ready to go any time, but she/he is almost never into it.”

• “我随时都准备好了，但她/他几乎从来都不感兴趣。”

• “We’re just too busy for it now. What with the kids, our jobs, and taking care of the house, there’s just no time.”

• “我们现在实在太忙了。要照顾孩子，要工作，还要打理家务，根本没时间。”

Once again, because this is an unconscious process, one isn’t aware that one is losing interest in, being turned off from, denying, or being denied, sex because of guilt. One of the biggest problems in understanding our sexuality comes from the widely held identification of our sexuality to specific locations in the body. This identification was established in our early adult life when the volcanic power of sexual energy that erupted in us during adolescence seemed to abate in our twenties, and became more or less localized in our genitalia. Of course our genitals were always extremely sensitive to the force of sexual energy, but you might remember that when puberty came upon us it was a complete body experience, just as it was when we were infants. In both infant-hood and adolescence the energy was eventually contained. I suggest that the power of guilt acts as a suitable container for such an awesome energy. 82

再次强调，由于这是一个无意识的过程，人们往往意识不到自己因为内疚而对性失去兴趣、感到厌恶、拒绝或被拒绝。理解自身性欲的最大障碍之一，源于人们普遍将性欲与身体的特定部位联系起来。这种观念形成于我们成年早期，那时青春期喷涌而出的性能量似乎在二十多岁时有所减弱，并或多或少地局限于生殖器。当然，我们的生殖器一直对性能量极其敏感，但你或许还记得，青春期到来时，它是一种全身性的体验，就像婴儿时期一样。无论是在婴儿期还是青春期，这种能量最终都会被抑制。我认为，内疚的力量恰好为这种强大的能量提供了一个合适的容器。<sup>82</sup>

I do not want to explore the source of sexual guilt, or even give case histories and bibliographies to support its validity. I am aware that there are those who do not even believe in its pervasiveness throughout humanity. Whether it exists in many or only a few, I am writing about it because many of those I have met in my profession have been convinced that once the sex dies, the marriage is over. In fact I have often witnessed a lack of sexual enthusiasm being used as a very convincing argument for ending the relationship. However, upon further exploration I have inevitably found that the sexual deadness is only one aspect of an overall malaise that has infiltrated the relationship. It’s just that some people tend to react more strongly when the sex goes.

我不想探究性愧疚的根源，甚至不想提供案例和参考书目来佐证其真实性。我知道有些人根本不相信性愧疚在人类社会普遍存在。无论它存在于许多人还是少数人之中，我之所以要写这篇文章，是因为我在工作中遇到的许多人都坚信，一旦性生活消失，婚姻也就走到了尽头。事实上，我经常看到性欲减退被用作结束关系的有力理由。然而，经过进一步的探究，我最终发现，性冷淡只是渗透到这段关系中的一种整体不适感的一个方面。只不过，有些人对性生活的消失反应更为强烈而已。

The truth is that the sex is not really gone; it is just not as focused on your personal plumbing as it may have been previously. One way to look at sexual energy is as a magnetic force that can end the separation between two seemingly opposite polarities. To my mind, anything that heals separation is, by nature, loving. Since love never dies, neither can sexual energy.

事实是，性并没有真正消失；它只是不再像以前那样专注于你的生理需求。我们可以把性能量看作一种磁力，它能够消除看似对立的两极之间的隔阂。在我看来，任何能够治愈分离的事物，其本质都是爱。既然爱永不消逝，性能量也同样如此。

If you are in a situation where you and your partner are not enjoying sexual interaction through your sexual organs, 83 my first question would be, how much do you want your partner? Not just the use of his/her body to pleasure yourself, or the reassurance of his/her desire for you—how much do you want to experience an intimate connection with the most important person in your life? There comes a point in most relationships when physical stimulation or even fantasy is not enough to maintain sexual arousal around your partner, because your soul is calling for more of who you really are to be with who your mate really is. Sometimes in order to reach a more essential you, the bad feelings you have about yourself, your body, and your sexual identity, along with fusion issues, come to the fore and diminish or inhibit the enjoyment of your sexuality. These in turn can bring on feelings of personal failure, anxiety, or frustration. You will either be aware of these within you, or see them reflected in your partner’s response to you. Of the many stressful factors in a relationship, sexual issues are right near the top of the list.

如果你和伴侣无法享受性爱带来的愉悦，我的第一个问题是：你究竟有多渴望你的伴侣？不仅仅是利用他/她的身体来取悦自己，或者确认他/她对你的渴望——你究竟有多渴望与生命中最重要的人建立亲密的联结？大多数关系都会经历这样一个阶段：仅仅依靠身体刺激甚至性幻想，已经不足以维持你对伴侣的性唤起，因为你的灵魂渴望与真实的自我相伴。有时，为了触及更真实的自我，你对自身、身体和性身份的负面感受，以及融合问题，会浮现出来，削弱或抑制你享受性爱的乐趣。这些反过来又会引发个人失败感、焦虑感或挫败感。你会在内心深处感受到这些，或者从伴侣的反应中看到它们的反映。在一段关系中诸多压力因素中，性问题往往名列前茅。

But what if you were to view what is happening as a chance to learn more about yourself and your capacity to love unconditionally. What if you were to simply focus on loving your partner—as a friend, a companion, and a wonderful gift in your life? Would you be more willing then to share your secret world, your fears, your resentments toward the opposite sex (if that applies), your fantasies, your insecurities, and your pain, and let the love and trust of true friendship grow? Out of that friendship will likely come the poignancy and power of true intimacy; for intimacy involves being truly, nakedly yourself, and sharing that self with your chosen partner. It is not a plateau that, once reached, can be considered conquered. Many times I have experienced deep intimacy with my wife, only to find it mysteriously elusive a day later, for the Soul’s call is unrelenting, urging you always to reach further for your self. But once experienced, such intimacy can lead you to a sense of sexual naturalness which can melt away the layers of deeply embedded guilt that have suppressed the boundless energy of the “kundalini.” As the kundalini uncoils, gradually stretching itself upwards, the entire body becomes the instrument of love it was intended to be.

但如果你把正在发生的一切看作是一个了解自己、认识自己无条件爱的能力的机会呢？如果你只是专注于爱你的伴侣——把她当作朋友、伴侣，以及生命中一份美好的礼物呢？那时，你是否更愿意分享你的秘密世界、你的恐惧、你对异性的怨恨（如果存在的话）、你的幻想、你的不安和你的痛苦，让真挚友谊的爱与信任生根发芽？从这份友谊中，很可能会孕育出真正亲密关系的深刻与力量；因为亲密关系意味着真实、坦诚地做自己，并将这个真实的自我分享给你选择的伴侣。它并非一个一旦达到便可征服的高峰。我曾多次与妻子体验到深厚的亲密，却发现第二天它又神秘地消失不见，因为灵魂的召唤永不停歇，它敦促你不断探索自我，追求更深层次的成长。但一旦体验过这种亲密关系，就能让你感受到性爱的自然之美，从而融化那些压抑着“昆达里尼”无限能量的根深蒂固的罪恶感。随着昆达里尼能量逐渐释放，向上延伸，整个身体都成为了它原本就应该成为的爱的工具。

***

COMPETITION

竞赛

———————————

“It’s lonely at the top, but who cares? It’s lonely at the bottom too!”

“高处不胜寒，但谁在乎呢？低处也很孤独！”

—Anonymous

-匿名的

The root of competition is scarcity—the belief that there is not enough for everybody. When you hold such a belief, and combine it with the need to be special, you perceive the world through this scarcity and see that there is not enough love out there for you—you will need to beat all other people who are vying for the same goal as you are.

竞争的根源在于稀缺性——认为资源不足以满足所有人的需求。当你抱持这种观念，并结合渴望与众不同的需求时，你就会透过这种稀缺性来看待世界，觉得世上没有足够的爱留给你——你必须击败所有与你争夺同一目标的人。

The same competition for specialness takes place in your most important relationships. You may enter the contest against your mate, using your friends, your neighbours, or your children as the prize (“Who do you love more—Mommy or Daddy?”); or you may simply want to prove to your partner alone that you are more special than she/he is. As a basis of proof you might use your intelligence, parenting skills, arguing abilities, knowledge of the world, past experiences, previous relationships, popularity, cleanliness, or driving expertise, to name a few. Whatever arena you and your partner choose to enter to prove your supreme specialness, I guarantee one thing: you will both lose. That is because the basis of your competition is a lie. Either we are all loved equally or there is no love.

在最重要的关系中，也存在着同样的“特殊性”竞争。你可能会和伴侣展开这场较量，把朋友、邻居甚至孩子当作奖品（“你更爱爸爸还是妈妈？”）；或者，你可能只是想向伴侣证明，你比他/她更特别。为了证明这一点，你可能会拿出自己的智慧、育儿技巧、辩论能力、见识、过往经历、人际关系、人缘、爱干净程度，或者驾驶技术等等。无论你和伴侣选择在哪个领域证明自己最特别，我都可以保证一点：你们都会输。因为你们竞争的基础是一个谎言。要么我们都被平等地爱着，要么根本就没有爱。

With some shame, I admit that there were times when I was seized by the Lobster Effect, a term that was inspired by seeing lobsters in a pail in a restaurant kitchen. Every time one tried to climb out of the pail, the others would grab its legs and pull it back in. 84 I found myself hoping that my friends would fail—or at least, not completely succeed—in their pursuit of happiness, whether that happiness involved money, work, relationship, creativity, spiritual pursuits, or any other goals they might set their sights on. The fear that I would be left behind if my friends started to “get away,” caused me to use manipulation, gossip, and sabotage to try to undo their attempts to become greater people. Fear of being left behind leads to a sense of scarcity—the conviction that you are not good enough to go forward toward success as well.

我有些羞愧地承认，我曾一度深受“龙虾效应”的困扰。这个词的灵感来源于我在一家餐馆厨房里看到的一桶龙虾。每当一只龙虾试图爬出桶外，其他的龙虾就会抓住它的腿，把它拉回去。<sup>84</sup> 我发现自己竟然希望我的朋友们在追求幸福的道路上失败——或者至少无法完全成功——无论这种幸福是关于金钱、工作、人际关系、创造力、精神追求，还是他们可能设定的任何其他目标。我害怕如果朋友们开始“飞黄腾达”，我就会被落下，这种恐惧驱使我使用操纵、散播谣言和破坏等手段，试图阻止他们成为更优秀的人。害怕被落下会导致一种匮乏感——一种觉得自己不够优秀，无法像他们一样走向成功的信念。

It was not hard for me to see my competitive compulsions when I examined most of my life, but when it came to my relationship I couldn’t really believe it. I mean, why would I want to compete with my own wife? I’m supposed to love her, aren’t I? Why would I want to win any contest at her expense, and what contests would we ever get involved in in the first place? When I posed these questions to myself, I soon became painfully aware of the answers. I competed with Su Mei over who was more liked by our friends and more loved by our children, who was right about any given disagreement, who was more independent than the other, and who was a better person in general. When I thought about it, I realized the competition came down to a battle that would determine who was more special.

回顾我的人生，我很容易发现自己有好胜心，但当涉及到我的感情关系时，我却难以置信。我的意思是，我为什么要和自己的妻子竞争呢？我应该爱她才对，不是吗？我为什么要不惜一切代价去赢得任何比赛，而且我们之间又有什么比赛可言呢？当我问自己这些问题时，我很快就痛苦地意识到了答案。我和苏梅竞争的焦点在于谁更受朋友欢迎，谁更受孩子喜爱，谁在争论中更有道理，谁更独立，以及谁才是更好的人。仔细想想，我意识到这场竞争最终演变成一场决定谁更特别的较量。

When you bring competition into your relationship, your drive to be special and your fear of abandonment can keep both of you struggling in battle while your true giftedness and purpose remain quietly hidden. Competition can be found in many negative experiences such as jealousy, comparison, envy, the need to be right, Power Struggle, and holding your partner back.

当你在感情中引入竞争时，你渴望与众不同的驱动力和害怕被抛弃的恐惧会让你们陷入无休止的争斗，而你真正的天赋和人生目标却会被悄然掩盖。嫉妒、攀比、羡慕、总想证明自己是对的、权力斗争以及阻碍伴侣发展等负面情绪都可能体现竞争。

The voice of the soul is so quiet that only a tranquil mind can hear it. But the mind will never be quiet so long as the drive to compete holds sway. Ending the competition involves waking up and honestly confronting your attitude in the relationship. Some people are like me: in such great denial that they simply do not wish to admit the existence of competition with their partner. It is not a thing that someone else can prove to us, for we can easily rationalize away the proof. It’s up to us to acknowledge it and admit to ourselves, our partners and our friends. Sure we will feel great discomfort exposing it. Competition always works best when done in secrecy; exposing it to the world is no easy task, as we will likely be confronted by our shame or guilt.

灵魂的声音如此轻柔，唯有内心平静之人方能聆听。然而，只要竞争的欲望占据主导，内心便永无宁日。结束竞争需要我们觉醒，并坦诚面对自己在关系中的态度。有些人和我一样：极力否认，根本不愿承认与伴侣之间存在竞争。这并非他人能够证明的，因为我们可以轻易地找到各种理由来推翻它。我们必须承认它的存在，并坦诚地告诉自己、伴侣和朋友。当然，坦白一切会让我们感到极度不适。竞争在暗中进行往往最为有效；将其公之于众绝非易事，因为我们很可能要面对内心的羞愧或愧疚。

To take the risk of bringing my competition out in the open, I must ask myself three questions: 1) Is my partner valuable enough to me that I would be willing to risk facing my guilt and shame, in order to admit my competition with her? 2) Am I—that is, is my uniquely gifted self—worth taking this risk for? 3) Do I value the Truth enough to do this? If I can answer “yes” to these, I will find the strength to choose an end to the competition. Then I can start giving my beloved lobster a boost to freedom. Who knows? Maybe when my arms are stretched up in order to give her a last push over the top, I’ll find a claw reaching down to lift me out.

为了冒着将竞争对手公之于众的风险，我必须问自己三个问题：1）我的伴侣对我来说是否足够重要，以至于我愿意冒着面对内疚和羞耻的风险，承认我与她之间的竞争？2）我——也就是说，我这天赋异禀的自我——是否值得我冒这个险？3）我是否足够珍视真相，以至于愿意这样做？如果我对这三个问题的答案都是“是”，我就会找到结束竞争的力量。然后，我就可以开始帮助我心爱的龙虾获得自由。谁知道呢？也许当我伸出双臂，想要给她最后一推，让她跃过顶峰时，我会发现一只爪子伸下来，把我拉了出来。

***

DEATH, WHERE IS THY STING?

死亡啊，你的毒钩在哪里？

———————————

“Those who aren’t busy being born are busy dying.”

“那些不忙着出生的人，都在忙着死亡。”

—Bob Dylan,

——鲍勃·迪伦

“There are a lot of things worth dying for, but love is the only thing worth living for.”

“有很多东西值得为之献身，但唯有爱才值得为之活下去。”

—Anonymous

-匿名的

Sylavano, an old high school friend of mine, once told me his experience of being taken rock climbing for the first time. He said that he was halfway up the rock face when he was gripped by an overwhelming fear. He could not find a reliable hand hold within reach, and suddenly became terrified. He knew he couldn’t go down, and could see no way up either, even though his experienced friend was ahead of him, directing his progress. The fear had simply paralyzed Sylvano. “At that point” he said, “I wanted to throw myself off the rock face, just to kill the fear.” 85 Years later I began to see that such a “death temptation” is much more typical than I imagined.

我的高中老朋友西尔瓦诺曾跟我讲过他第一次攀岩的经历。他说，他爬到岩壁一半的时候，突然被一种难以抑制的恐惧攫住了。他找不到任何可以抓握的地方，顿时感到一阵恐慌。他知道自己无法下去，也看不到任何上去的路，尽管他经验丰富的朋友就在前面，指引着他前进。恐惧彻底麻痹了西尔瓦诺。“当时，”他说，“我真想从岩壁上跳下去，就为了摆脱这种恐惧。”85年后，我开始意识到，这种“死亡诱惑”比我想象的要普遍得多。

Sometimes during the Introspection stage, your relationship experience can be too difficult to bear, and the wish that it would all be over can creep in. The absolute discouragement of Assumed Inadequacy can make you feel there’s no point in going on. You may not express it as a desire to die, but the dread of having to go on facing a seemingly unchangeable reality is very close to a death wish. Whenever life presents us with such a challenge, if we reject the feelings that this situation makes us aware of, we are rejecting life. It is like saying, “I never want to feel like that again—I’d rather die.” 86 If that statement becomes our motto, whether we choose to leave or stay, we will likely approach relationships more cautiously, and our sense of faith and trust in life will be diminished. In effect, we are expecting death to erase our pain, and looking at life as the enemy.

有时在内省阶段，你的感情经历可能难以承受，甚至会产生想要结束这一切的念头。这种“假定自身不足”带来的彻底沮丧会让你觉得继续下去毫无意义。你或许不会将其表达为求死的念头，但面对看似无法改变的现实，那种恐惧感与求死非常接近。每当生活给我们带来这样的挑战时，如果我们拒绝接受这种境况所引发的感受，我们就等于拒绝了生命。这就像在说：“我再也不想经历那种感觉了——我宁愿去死。”<sup>86</sup> 如果这句话成为我们的座右铭，无论我们选择离开还是留下，我们都可能会更加谨慎地对待感情，对生活的信念和信任也会逐渐减弱。实际上，我们期待死亡来消除痛苦，并将生命视为敌人。

There is a powerful momentum to the death direction, and so it is only by a very sincere choice for life that these death desires can truly be overcome. Whatever you decide to do in your situation, it is important that your decision be made from a life-affirming intention. If your choice is made out of fear, anger, or hatred, recognize that those feelings point you in a death direction. If you choose with an intention to do what you sincerely believe is best for all involved, you are choosing a life direction. There is an amazing boost of support that comes with choosing life. With that choice comes hope, wisdom, and clarity of purpose. The more you choose it, the more is inspired in you a sense of wonder and awe. Gradually you begin to see what an awesome gift and opportunity life has given you. Even when in pain that wonder can still be felt, offering you comfort and inspiration. The power of life will re-enter, resurrecting what you thought had died and left forever, and instilling in you a sense of hope and strength to fully face your process with trust and love.

死亡的诱惑力强大，唯有发自内心地选择生命，才能真正战胜这种死亡的念头。无论你最终做出怎样的决定，重要的是你的决定必须出于对生命的肯定。如果你的选择是出于恐惧、愤怒或仇恨，那么你要意识到，这些情绪正将你引向死亡。如果你选择去做你真心相信对所有相关人员都最有利的事情，那么你就是在选择生命。选择生命会带来一股强大的力量。伴随这一选择而来的是希望、智慧和清晰的目标。你越是选择生命，就越能感受到生命带给你的惊奇和敬畏。你会逐渐明白，生命给予你的是多么珍贵的礼物和机遇。即使在痛苦中，你依然能感受到这份惊奇，它会给你带来慰藉和力量。生命的力量将会重新注入你的生命，唤醒你以为已经消逝的一切，并赋予你希望和力量，让你能够以信任和爱去面对人生的种种挑战。

When you find yourself paralyzed in your relationship, either unable or unwilling to move closer to your partner, be aware of what force is behind that paralysis. Is it a loving power that is holding you back, or is it a fear-based force that is at work here? 87 If it is fear-based, it is harmful to you, as well as your partner, and not life-enhancing. When tempted by one of death’s many facets, choose life with all your heart. Your commitment to life will lift the veil, revealing one of the ego’s greatest secrets....

当你发现自己在感情中陷入僵局，无法或不愿与伴侣更亲近时，要觉察到这种僵局背后的力量是什么。是爱的力量在阻碍你，还是恐惧的力量在作祟？87 如果是恐惧，它不仅对你有害，对你的伴侣也有害，而且无益于你们的生活。当死亡的种种诱惑袭来时，要全心全意地选择生命。你对生命的执着将揭开面纱，展现出自我最大的秘密之一……

* **

THE CONSPIRACY OF DOUBT

怀疑的阴谋

———————————

“Thinking comes from personality, and doubt is the epitome of thinking.”

“思考源于个性，而怀疑则是思考的极致体现。”

—Chuck Spezzano

——查克·斯佩扎诺

At last we come to the purpose of the introspection stage, which is to reveal to us the ultimate problem creator in our lives. Through introspection you are offered the opportunity to look within, and uncover an insidious conspiracy created by your “egoic mind” to stop you from knowing your true nature. Using doubt as its favoured weapon, your mind tries to keep you trapped in a complex maze: preoccupying you with problems of a small or gargantuan nature, waylaying you with tempting distractions and confusing you with faulty memories of your past. Its goal is to ensure that you do not perceive the truly gifted person that you are. At the heart of the conspiracy is the fear of stepping towards your essence.

最终，我们来到了内省阶段的目的，那就是揭示我们生活中问题的终极制造者。通过内省，你有机会审视内心，揭开你“自我意识”精心策划的阴谋，阻止你认识真正的自我。你的意识惯用怀疑作为武器，试图将你困在一个复杂的迷宫中：让你沉浸于各种大小问题，用诱人的干扰分散你的注意力，用错误的记忆迷惑你。它的目标是让你无法认识到自己真正的天赋。这个阴谋的核心在于害怕接近你的本质。

Before you take an important step in your life, you will be besieged by voices of doubt. They will torment you with fear, anxiety, and dread, and attempt to convince you that you are in no way equipped to do what you are about to do. Before you take the step, doubt will tell you that you can’t do it. You are not good enough, not prepared enough, not strong enough, or not deserving enough. I slowly became aware of the nature of doubt over the course of my career as a workshop facilitator and public speaker. The effectiveness of my work depends on my willingness to trust and follow my intuition. Listening to my intuition means paying attention to the voice of my soul. In order to do this I do not prepare speeches, or set agendas for the workshop, but instead simply speak and act according to the direction that’s given to me on a moment-to-moment basis. This involves spontaneity, and relying on the inspiration and creativity of my soul.

在你人生迈出重要一步之前，你会被怀疑的声音所包围。它们会用恐惧、焦虑和畏惧折磨你，试图让你相信你根本没有能力去做即将要做的事情。在你迈出那一步之前，怀疑会告诉你你做不到。你不够好，准备不够充分，不够坚强，或者不够配得上。在我作为工作坊导师和公众演讲者的职业生涯中，我逐渐意识到怀疑的本质。我的工作成效取决于我是否愿意信任并跟随我的直觉。倾听我的直觉意味着关注我灵魂的声音。为了做到这一点，我不会准备演讲稿，也不会为工作坊设定议程，而是根据当下传递给我的指引来说话和行动。这需要自发性，需要依靠我灵魂的灵感和创造力。

When I started this work I felt that I was not very creative or inspired, and wasn’t confident of my connection to soul. Thus I would rely on the methods of other great teachers and more or less do it their way. Before my first workshop, I prepared the program so I would know what to do on an hourly basis. I was terrified at the thought of standing in front of a group of people and not knowing what to do next. When a participant presented an issue, I would think back to the way a teacher had responded to a similar issue and repeat what he or she had said and done. All in all it worked pretty well—for about one day. After that I was bored with the work, and embarrassed to find myself repeating other teachers’ words and philosophies. Somebody pointed out that I was even standing and walking like one of those teachers. All the things I was doing just weren’t me.
